chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Thank goodness, studying or instructing geometry is behind me,” remarked Nell Harcourt, rather vengefully, while she slammed a slightly worn copy of Euclid into a large book chest, struck the cover closed victoriously, and perched on it, gazing at Isolde Duckett across the Grey Shutters attic, with morning-sky-like gray eyes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: A shadowy, suggestive, and delightful place was the garret, just as every garret ought to be. Sitting beside the open window, Nell felt the sweet, scented, sun-warm air of the August afternoon blow past; outdoors, poplar boughs were rustling and tossing in the wind; further off lay the woods, through which Linger Lane snaked its enchanted path, along with the old apple orchard that continued to yield its rosy harvests generously. Moreover, towering above everything in the blue southern sky was a vast mountain range of snowy clouds. Looking out the opposite window revealed a view of a far-off, white-capped, blue sea—the lovely St. Lawrence Gulf, where Abegweit floats like a jewel, though its softer, sweeter Indian name was abandoned long ago for the more prosaic title of St. Brendan’s Island.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: Having aged three years since our previous encounter, Isolde Duckett was now rather matronly. Nevertheless, her eyes retained their blackness and brilliance, her cheeks their rosiness, and her dimples their enchantment, just as they were during those past days when an oath of everlasting friendship was sworn by her and Nell Harcourt within the Pear Hill garden. Nestled in her arms was a tiny, slumbering child with black curls, who throughout two joyful years had been called “Small Nell Lucinda” by the Brierley community. Naturally, the residents of Brierley understood the reason Isolde gave her the name Nell, yet those same Brierley residents felt confused regarding the Lucinda. No individual named Lucinda had ever existed within the Pembroke or Duckett families. It was suggested by Mrs. Gorham Pullen that Isolde had likely discovered the moniker inside a cheap book, while she expressed surprise that Gideon lacked the wisdom to forbid it. Isolde and Nell, however, exchanged a smile. The origin of Small Nell Lucinda’s name was something only they understood.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “It was always geometry that you disliked,” Isolde remarked, smiling in recollection. “Anyhow, I would imagine you must be truly pleased to have finished with teaching.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Oh, geometry aside, I have constantly enjoyed instruction. My previous three years spent in Eastmere were quite agreeable. Upon my return, Mrs. Gorham Pullen informed me of the unlikelihood that I would consider matrimony so much superior to teaching as I anticipated. Mrs. Gorham obviously shares Hamlet’s view that enduring our present troubles might be preferable to rushing toward unfamiliar ones.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: A laugh from Nell—just as cheerful and captivating as in past times, though now carrying a new tone of gentleness and adulthood—echoed across the attic room. Downstairs in the kitchen, Thirza was preparing blue plum preserve when the sound reached her, bringing a smile to her face; she then sighed upon reflecting that the future would rarely hear that cherished laughter reverberating inside Grey Shutters. The realization that Nell intended to wed Hugh Carrow had brought Thirza greater delight than any other event in her existence; yet every delight inevitably casts its own small shadow of sadness. Throughout those three years spent in Eastmere, Nell had frequently returned home to stay for breaks and weekends; however, following this event, one could expect nothing more than a twice-yearly stay.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “What Mrs. Gorham says doesn’t need to worry you,” Isolde said, possessing the peaceful confidence of a woman married for four years. “Naturally, there are ups and downs in married life. Expecting all things to proceed smoothly all the time is a mistake. However, Nell, I can give you my assurance that life is happy, provided your husband is the right man.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: Nell hid a smile. The grand, experienced manner that Isolde put on had always brought her a bit of amusement.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “It is likely I will be wearing them as well, once four years of marriage have passed for me,” occurred to her. “However, my sense of humor will undoubtedly save me from that.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Has the location of your future home been decided yet?” inquired Isolde, holding Small Nell Lucinda close with that matchless maternal touch that perpetually caused a sensation—partly unalloyed delight and partly an unusual, otherworldly ache—to course through the heart of Nell, which was laden with tender, unspoken aspirations and longings.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Indeed. I intended to inform you of that when I rang you to travel down here today. Incidentally, I am unable to grasp that telephones are actually present in Brierley at this moment. For this sweet, unhurried ancient location, it seems so absurdly current and contemporary.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “The A. V. I. S. deserves our gratitude for those,” Isolde remarked. “Had they not embraced the issue and driven it to completion, we would not have secured the line. So much discouragement was aimed at them that it would have dampened any organization. Even so, they persevered. Nell, establishing that society was a magnificent service to Brierley. The fun we experienced during our gatherings was unforgettable! Is the blue hall, along with Judson Tibbs’s plan to put medicine ads on his fence, something you will ever erase from your memory?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “I am not entirely sure of my gratitude toward the A. V. I. S. regarding the telephone,” Nell remarked. “Certainly, it is extremely useful—surpassing even our previous method of communicating through candlelight signals! Furthermore, as Mrs. Agatha notes, 'Brierley must keep up with the procession, that’s what.’ Yet I possess a lingering feeling against Brierley being ruined by the things Mr. Pettifer terms 'modern inconveniences’ when attempting humor. My desire would be to preserve it perpetually as it existed during those beloved past times. Such a wish is foolish—and sentimental—and impossible. Consequently, I will turn wise, practical, and possible without delay. The telephone, by Mr. Pettifer’s admission, represents 'a buster of a good thing’—notwithstanding the awareness that roughly six curious individuals are likely overhearing everything on the circuit.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “That’s the most dreadful part,” Isolde uttered with a sigh. “Hearing the earpieces being replaced every time you make a call is terribly irritating. People claim that Mrs. Gorham Pullen demanded her ’phone be placed inside their kitchen for the sole purpose of eavesdropping every time it chimed while simultaneously watching over the meal. Earlier today, upon your call to me, the chiming of that strange Tulk clock reached my ears clearly. Consequently, Flossie or Tibby was undoubtedly eavesdropping.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Ah, that explains your remark, ‘You’ve got a new clock at Grey Shutters, haven’t you?’ Your meaning completely escaped me. The moment you finished speaking, a sharp click reached my ears. The Tulk receiver was being slammed down with cursed force, I presume. Regardless, let us forget about the Tulks. To quote Mrs. Agatha, ‘Tulks they always were and Tulks they always will be, world without end, amen.’ My desire is to discuss more agreeable subjects. The location of my future residence has been fully decided.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Oh, Nell, where? Near here is where I truly hope it is.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “No-o-o, the disadvantage lies right there. Hugh intends to make his home in Seven Gulls Harbor, which is sixty miles away.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Sixty! It could just as easily be six hundred,” Isolde sighed. “Now, I am never able to travel any farther from home than Port Marlow.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “You must visit Seven Gulls. On the Island, no harbor surpasses its beauty. At its head lies a small settlement named Glen St. Agnes, where Dr. David Carrow has been a practitioner for half a century. As you are aware, he is the great-uncle of Hugh. Upon his retirement, Hugh will assume his medical practice. Since Dr. Carrow intends to remain in his home, however, we must secure a residence of our own. Although its true identity and location remain unknown to me for now, my imagination has fully appointed a modest house o’dreams—a small, enchanting castle in Spain.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “To what location will you travel for your honeymoon?” Isolde inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “To no place at all. Please do not appear shocked, dearest Isolde. You propose Mrs. Gorham Pullen. Unquestionably, she will patronizingly observe that individuals unable to pay for wedding 'towers’ show genuine good sense by foregoing them; subsequently, she will prompt my memory that Odette traveled to Europe for her own. It is my desire to pass MY honeymoon at Seven Gulls inside my very own cherished dream house.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “And you have chosen to forgo having a bridesmaid?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “No candidates are available. Regarding matrimony, you, Cressy, Honora, and Odette got ahead of me; meanwhile, Mabel works as a teacher in Vancouver. I do not possess any additional 'kindred soul' and refuse to accept a bridesmaid who lacks that qualification.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Isolde asked anxiously, “Will you not be wearing a veil, though?””

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Indeed, that's true. Without one, I would not feel like a bride. I recall saying to Obed, on that night when he escorted me to Grey Shutters, that my expectations of becoming a bride were non-existent because my appearance was so plain that nobody would ever desire to take me as a wife—except perhaps a foreign missionary. At that time, I believed that foreign missionaries could not be picky about appearances if they needed a woman to jeopardize her life amid cannibals. You ought to have beheld the foreign missionary who married Honora. He possessed the good looks and mystery of those fantasies we once intended to wed ourselves, Isolde; no man I ever encountered was better dressed, and he gushed about Honora’s 'ethereal, golden beauty.’ Naturally, though, Japan has no cannibals.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “At any rate, your bridal gown is heavenly,” Isolde uttered with a sigh of delight. “Being so tall and slight, you will resemble a complete queen wearing it. Nell, in what manner DO you remain so thin? My weight has increased even more—before long, my waist will completely disappear.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Being heavy or thin appears to be predetermined,” Nell remarked. “In any case, the comment Mrs. Gorham Pullen made to me upon my return from Eastmere, 'Well, Nell, you’re just about as skinny as ever,’ cannot be directed at you. Calling someone 'slender’ conveys a certain romance, whereas 'skinny’ carries a distinctly altered flavor.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Mrs. Gorham was speaking regarding your trousseau. It is as lovely as Odette’s, she acknowledges, even though she remarks that Odette wed a millionaire while you are merely marrying a 'poor young doctor without a cent to his name.'”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: A laugh came from Nell.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “My gowns ARE lovely. Pretty items are things I adore. The initial attractive frock I possessed comes to mind—the brown gloria provided to me by Obed for our school performance. Up until then, all my possessions were terribly unattractive. That evening, it felt as though I entered a different realm.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “During that evening, Hugh performed 'Bingen on the Rhine,' turning his gaze toward you as he uttered, 'There’s another, NOT a sister.’ Furthermore, you felt such intense rage when he placed your pink tissue rose into his breast pocket! Back at that time, you hardly envisioned that he would one day become your husband.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 IN THE GARRET OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Oh, well, another case of predestination is right there,” Nell laughed, while they walked down the stairs from the garret.

Never in the entire history of Grey Shutters had the atmosphere held such intense excitement. Thirza herself was so thrilled that she was unable to hide it, an occurrence that bordered on the extraordinary.

“No wedding has ever taken place in this house,” she mentioned to Mrs. Agatha Sowerby, sounding somewhat apologetic. “During my childhood, an elderly clergyman remarked that a home fails to become a genuine one prior to being hallowed by a birth, a marriage, and a passing. Deaths have occurred in this place—both my mother and father passed away here, in addition to Obed; moreover, a birth has taken place here as well. A great while back, right after our relocation to this residence, a wedded farmhand worked for us briefly, and a infant was born to his wife here. Yet a marriage has never occurred previously. Thinking about Nell getting wedded feels incredibly odd. To an extent, she appears to me like nothing more than the young girl Obed carried home to this place fourteen years back. It is impossible for me to grasp her adulthood. My emotions upon witnessing Obed carrying in a GIRL will remain with me forever. I ponder the outcome of the boy who would have joined us had an error not transpired. I ponder the nature of HIS destiny.”

“Indeed, the error turned out to be lucky,” Mrs. Agatha Sowerby remarked, “even if, remember, I didn't hold that view initially—on the night I visited Nell and she made a huge fuss for us. A great deal has shifted since that moment, indeed.”
Mrs. Agatha let out a sigh, but she quickly became lively once more. If there were marriages to be arranged, Mrs. Agatha was willing to allow bygone days to be forgotten.

“Two of my cotton warp spreads are going to Nell,” she continued. “One with a tobacco stripe and another with an apple leaf. According to her, their popularity is actually returning. Regardless of what is fashionable, my opinion remains that a lovely apple-leaf spread is unmatched in beauty for a guest bed, and that is my final word. Bleaching them is something I need to attend to soon. Since the death of Thomas, I have kept them encased in cotton sacks, so their shade is surely terrible by now. Nevertheless, with a full month remaining, exposing them to dew will produce amazing results.”
Merely one month! Thirza let out a sigh, after which she remarked with pride:

“I am bestowing upon Nell the six braided rugs stored in my garret. It never occurred to me that she would desire them—they are terribly out of date, and modern preference seems entirely focused on hooked mats. Nevertheless, she requested them from me—stating that they were her absolute preference for her floors. Indeed, they ARE lovely. I crafted them using the finest rags, forming them into braided stripes. Creating them provided such companionship throughout these recent winters. Additionally, I intend to prepare a sufficient amount of blue plum preserve to supply her jam closet for a full year. It appears truly peculiar. Those blue plum trees failed to produce a single flower for three years, leading me to believe they should probably be chopped down. Yet this past spring they bloomed completely white, yielding a plum harvest larger than any I can recall at Grey Shutters.”

“Well, I am so grateful that Nell and Hugh are actually getting married in the end. I have constantly prayed for this,” Mrs. Agatha stated, speaking like someone who is pleasantly confident that her supplications accomplished a great deal. “Discovering that she actually had no intention of marrying the Portmaris man brought much peace of mind. Granted, he possessed wealth, whereas Hugh lacks money—at the outset, anyway; however, he is an Island boy.”

“He’s Hugh Carrow,” Thirza stated with satisfaction. Before expressing the idea that constantly lingered in the rear of her thoughts whenever she had observed Hugh since he was a child—the notion that he could have been HER son if not for her own stubborn pride a very long time ago—Thirza would have submitted to death itself. It seemed to Thirza that, through some odd mechanism, that past error would be corrected by his wedding to Nell. From the badness of the old resentment, something good had emerged.

Regarding Nell personally, her joy was so immense that it nearly terrified her. Ancient folklore claims that the gods dislike seeing humans who are exceedingly joyful. At the very least, it is true that particular people object to it. A pair of such individuals came down upon Nell one purple twilight and set about doing everything within their power to pop the iridescent sphere of her contentment. Should she believe she was securing any special catch in young Dr. Carrow, or should she fancy that his devotion to her remained as passionate as it perhaps was during his youth, they felt obligated to present the situation to her from a different viewpoint. Nevertheless, these two respectable women were not Nell's foes; rather, they were actually rather affectionate toward her, and they would have protected her like their own offspring if a third party had assailed her. Consistency is not required of human nature.

Mrs. Inglis—formerly Odette Pullen, as the Daily Enterprise described her—arrived alongside her mother and Mrs. Jasper Bell. However, time spent in marital arguments had failed to sour the gentle disposition within Odette. She had enjoyed a fortunate life. Although she had wed a wealthy man—a point Mrs. Agatha Sowerby would be sure to mention—her union had remained a joyful one. She remained uncorrupted by riches. She maintained the same tranquil, pleasant, rosy-faced nature that Odette had shown in the former group of four, sharing in the joy of her longtime friend and possessing a deep fascination with every delicate aspect of Nell’s trousseau, treating it with as much enthusiasm as if it were comparable to her own luxurious, gem-encrusted wardrobe. Cleverness was not Odette's strong suit, and she had likely never uttered a single notable thought throughout her existence; yet she refrained from speaking words that might injure the sentiments of others—a trait that, while passive, remains an uncommon and desirable quality.

“So Hugh did not betray your trust in the end,” Mrs. Gorham Pullen remarked, managing to infuse her voice with a hint of astonishment. “Indeed, the members of the Carrow family usually adhere to their promises after giving them, regardless of the circumstances. Let me think—you have reached twenty-five years of age, have you not, Nell? During my youth, turning twenty-five marked the initial milestone. Nevertheless, your appearance is remarkably youthful. Individuals with red hair invariably retain that look.”

“Very fashionable now is red hair,” Nell remarked, attempting a smile, though her tone was somewhat cool. Experience had fostered within her a humorous outlook that assisted her through numerous troubles; nevertheless, up to this point, no resource had succeeded in hardening her to any mention of her hair.

“Indeed it is—indeed it is,” Mrs. Gorham acknowledged. “No one can predict the odd whims that style will adopt. Now, Nell, your possessions are quite lovely, as well as being entirely appropriate for your social standing, wouldn't you say, Odette? My desire is that you find great joy. Be assured that you possess my finest hopes. An extended courtship rarely ends favorably. Nevertheless, given your circumstances, it was naturally unavoidable.”

“People may not put great trust in Hugh because he appears quite youthful for a physician,” Mrs. Jasper Bell remarked dejectedly. Following this, her lips pressed firmly together, signaling that she had fulfilled her obligation and absolved her mind. She fit the description of those individuals who perpetually wear a limp black plume in their headgear and have loose wisps of hair trailing down their necks.

The brief eclipse of Nell’s superficial joy in her lovely wedding attire quickly passed, leaving the profound depths of her underlying bliss untouched; furthermore, the minor gibes from Mesdames Bell and Pullen vanished from her mind upon Hugh’s arrival that evening, whereupon the couple strolled toward the brookside birches, which had grown from the young shoots present when Nell first arrived at Grey Shutters into majestic, pale pillars inside an enchanted realm of dusk and starlight. Sheltered by those dark shapes, Nell and Hugh conversed as sweethearts do regarding the residence they would share and the future that lay ahead for them both.
“I’ve discovered a home for us, Nell.”
“Ah, in what location? Surely not directly within the village, I trust. I would not entirely appreciate that.”

“No. In the village, a house could not be found. Halfway between Glen St. Agnes and Seven Gulls Point, on the harbor shore, stands this small white house. It is somewhat remote, though that will be less important once a ’phone is installed. Its location is lovely. Facing the sunset, it overlooks the vast blue harbor. Not far off are the sand-dunes, which the ocean winds sweep across and the sea spray soaks.”
“Yet what about the residence, Hugh,—the initial dwelling of OURS? How does it appear?”

“It isn’t particularly big, yet it will be big enough for our needs. On the ground floor, you'll find a magnificent living room containing a fireplace, along with a dining room facing the harbor, plus a small room that can serve as my office. Its age is around sixty years—making it the most ancient house situated in Seven Gulls. However, it has been maintained in quite decent condition, having undergone a complete renovation approximately fifteen years back—it was shingled, plastered, and fitted with new flooring. From the start, the construction was sturdy. I gather that an element of romance was attached to how it was built, though the individual from whom I leased it was unaware of the details.”
“He stated that Captain Saul was the sole person able to tell that ancient tale at present.”
“What person is Captain Saul?”

“The lighthouse tender at Seven Gulls Point. That Seven Gulls light will delight you, Nell. Its beam rotates, winking through the dusk similar to a grand star. From the windows of our living room and our front entrance, it is visible to us.”
“To whom does the house belong?”

“Well, the Glen St. Agnes Presbyterian Church owns it currently, since I leased the place from its trustees. However, a very elderly woman, Miss Elizabeth Russell, was the owner until recently. Following her death this past spring, the Glen St. Agnes Church inherited her estate because no close kin survived her. The residence continues to hold her furnishings, a major portion of which I purchased—one could claim I got it for a mere song, as the trustees lost hope of finding a buyer due to its completely outdated style. I suspect the people of Glen St. Agnes have a preference for plush brocade along with sideboards that feature mirrors and decorative details. All the same, Miss Russell’s furnishings are of high quality, and I am certain it will appeal to you, Nell.”

“Up to this point, fine,” said Nell, giving a careful nod of agreement. “However, Hugh, individuals are unable to subsist on furniture by itself. You still have not brought up a single highly crucial detail. Do TREES exist around this house?”

“A great deal of them, oh, dryad! Situated behind it is a large grove of fir trees, running down the lane are two rows of Lombardy poplars, and encircling a most charming garden is a ring of white birches. Right into the garden is where our front door opens, yet a second entrance exists—a small gate suspended between two firs. On one trunk are the hinges, while on the other is the catch. Overhead, an arch is created by their boughs.”

“Oh, I am deeply relieved! Residing in a place devoid of trees would be impossible for me—a crucial part of my spirit would perish from hunger. Indeed, following that admission, inquiring whether a stream exists nearby is pointless. Expecting THAT would be overstepping.”
“However, a brook DOES exist—and it truly flows through a single corner of the garden.”
“Then,” Nell remarked, letting out an extended sigh of complete contentment, “the residence you located IS the exact house of my dreams.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Nell, have you decided whom you will invite to the wedding?” inquired Mrs. Agatha Sowerby, while she busily hemstitched table napkins. “Even if they are just going to be informal, it is time for your invitations to go out.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “It is not my intention to have a large number,” Nell remarked. “Our desire is simply for those held dearest by us to witness our wedding. The family of Hugh, along with Mr. and Mrs. Wace, plus Mr. and Mrs. Pettifer.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “You would scarcely have counted Mr. Pettifer as one of your closest companions in the past,” Thirza remarked drily.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Indeed, I did not feel a VERY powerful draw toward him when we first met,” admitted Nell, laughing as she remembered it. “However, getting to know Mr. Pettifer better has raised my opinion of him, while Mrs. Pettifer is truly sweet. Additionally, we must not forget Miss Rosalind and Cedric.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Did they make up their minds to visit the Island during this summer? It was my understanding that they intended to travel to Europe.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Their perspective shifted once my letter informed them of my upcoming marriage. A communication from Cedric arrived for me today. He states that he MUST attend my wedding, regardless of the situation in Europe.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “You were always idolised by that child,” Mrs. Agatha remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Mrs. Sowerby, that ‘child’ has grown into a nineteen-year-old young man now.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “How time does fly!” was the brilliant and original reply made by Mrs. Sowerby.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Belinda the Fourth might accompany them. Through Cedric, she passed along word that she would attend provided her husband allowed it. I ponder if those huge blue bows are still worn by her, and if she is addressed by her husband as Belinda or Leonora. Having Belinda present at my wedding would be a delight for me. A long time ago, a wedding was attended by Belinda and me. At Echo Cottage, their arrival is anticipated next week. Additionally, Cressy and the Reverend Ez—— are expected”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “It sounds terrible to hear you talk about a clergyman in such a manner, Nell,” Mrs. Agatha remarked sternly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “He is called that by his wife.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Then she ought to show greater reverence for his sacred calling,” Mrs. Agatha fired back.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “I’ve listened to you rebuke clergymen rather severely on your own,” Nell jested.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Yes, but my actions are respectful,” Mrs. Sowerby objected. “You have never known me to bestow a NICKNAME upon a minister.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: Nell concealed a grin.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Indeed, Isolde, Gideon, little Gideon, and Small Nell Lucinda are present—along with Odette Pullen. My desire would be to invite Miss Stacey, Aunt Euphemia, Honora, and Mabel as well. Nevertheless, Mabel resides in Vancouver, Nonie has moved to Japan, Miss Stacey is wed and living in California, and Aunt Euphemia, despite her fear of snakes, has traveled to India so she can investigate the mission field of her daughter. How individuals become dispersed across the world is truly terrible.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “The Lord never intended it, that’s what,” declared Mrs. Agatha with authority. “During my youth, folk reached adulthood and wedded and took up residence where they had been born, or fairly close to it. Thank goodness you have remained on the Island, Nell. I worried that Hugh would demand to hurry away to the furthest corners of the world upon finishing college, and pull you along with him.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Locations would become crowded in a short time, Mrs. Sowerby, if each person remained in the place of his birth.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Oh, I won’t debate this with you, Nell. A B.A. is something I am not. At what hour of the day will the ceremony take place?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “It is noon that we have chosen—high noon, as it is phrased by the society reporters. From then, we will possess sufficient time for catching the evening train bound for Glen St. Agnes.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “And the wedding will take place in the parlor?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “No—not unless there is rain. It is our intention to be wed in the orchard—with the blue sky above us and the sunshine surrounding us. If it were possible, do you know the time and place I would choose to be married? It would occur at dawn—a June dawn, accompanied by a magnificent sunrise, and roses flowering in the gardens; and I would quietly go down and join Hugh, and the two of us would walk together to the center of the beech woods,—and in that spot, beneath the green arches which would resemble a grand cathedral, our marriage would take place.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: A disdainful sniff came from Thirza, while a look of shock appeared on Mrs. Sowerby.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “However, that would be exceedingly strange, Nell. Indeed, it would hardly appear lawful. Furthermore, what would be the reaction of Mrs. Gorham Pullen?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Ah, that is the difficulty,” Nell sighed. “A great many actions in this existence remain undone simply owing to our dread of Mrs. Gorham Pullen’s remarks. ‘'Tis true, ’tis pity, and pity ’tis, ’tis true.’ What wonderful activities we could engage in if Mrs. Gorham Pullen did not exist!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “At times, Nell, I am not entirely certain that I completely comprehend you,” Mrs. Sowerby grumbled.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “In fairness, Nell possessed a romantic nature,” Thirza offered by way of excuse.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Well, wedded existence will in all probability heal her of it,” Mrs. Agatha replied consolingly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: Nell chuckled and stole off toward Linger Lane, the spot where Hugh discovered her; and it appeared that neither one harbored much dread, or expectation, that their life together in wedlock would rid them of romance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: The individuals from Echo Cottage arrived during the following week, filling Grey Shutters with the excitement of their presence. Miss Rosalind was so unchanged that the three years following her previous Island trip could have been merely a watch in the night; Nell, however, was breathless with wonder regarding Cedric. Was it possible that this impressive six-foot man was the small Cedric from the Brierley school period?

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Cedric, you truly cause me to feel aged,” remarked Nell. “How about that, I am forced to look upward at you!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Teacher, you will never age,” Cedric remarked. “You belong to those lucky human beings who discovered and imbibed the Fountain of Youth,—you alongside Mother Rosalind. Look at this! After you get married, calling you Mrs. Carrow is something I WILL NOT do. For me, your name will forever be 'Teacher’—the instructor who gave me the finest lessons I was ever taught. There is something I want you to see.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: That “something” proved to be a pocketbook filled with poems. Cedric had turned a number of his lovely imaginings into poetry, and the editors of magazines had not shown the lack of appreciation that people occasionally attribute to them. Nell perused the poems of Cedric with genuine joy. Charm and promise abounded within them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Cedric, you are going to be celebrated one day. It was ever my ambition to instruct a single renowned student. My expectation was a university head—yet an extraordinary poet would surpass that. In the future, I will have the chance to brag about beating the renowned Cedric Stanhope. Although, I did not actually beat you, did I, Cedric? That was a wasted chance! Nevertheless, I believe I forced you to stay inside during recess.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “It is possible that you are well-known as well, Teacher. Over these past three years, I have come across much of what you have done.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “No. I am aware of my own capabilities. I am able to compose lovely, imaginative brief pieces that delight youngsters and prompt editors to mail agreeable payments. However, I am incapable of producing anything grand. The sole opportunity I have for lasting fame in this world is a space within your Memoirs.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: Belinda the Fourth no longer wore the blue bows, although her freckles remained just as visible.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “I certainly never believed I would descend to taking a Yankee as my husband, Miss Harcourt, ma’am,” she stated. “However, what lies ahead remains a mystery, and he cannot be blamed for it. He was simply born as one.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Belinda, because you have taken a Yankee for a husband, you are now a Yankee too.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “I am NOT, Miss Harcourt, ma’am! Even if a dozen Yankees became my husbands, I still would not be! There is a certain niceness to Tom. Furthermore, it occurred to me that I ought not to be overly picky, since a second opportunity might never come my way. Between his meals, Tom does not grumble about having to labor, nor does he take to drink, and taking everything into account, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, I am contented.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Is Leonora the name he uses for you?” Nell inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Gracious, no, Miss Harcourt, ma’am. I would not have any idea who he was referring to if he did. Naturally, at the time we were wed he was required to recite, 'I take thee, Leonora,’ and I swear to you, Miss Harcourt, ma’am, I have carried the most terrible impression ever since that he was not speaking to me and I have not been properly wedded whatsoever. And thus you are about to be wedded your own self, Miss Harcourt, ma’am? I ever imagined I should enjoy being wed to a physician. It would be exceedingly useful whenever the little ones contracted measles and croup. Tom is merely a bricklayer, yet he possesses a truly fine disposition. When I remarked to him, says I, 'Tom, may I attend Miss Harcourt’s wedding? I intend to go regardless, yet I should prefer to possess your permission,’ he simply responds, 'Suit yourself, Belinda, and you’ll suit me.’ That is a truly agreeable sort of spouse to possess, Miss Harcourt, ma’am.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: It was the day prior to the nuptials when Cressida and her Reverend Ez came to Grey Shutters. Nell and Cressy shared an ecstatic reunion that soon settled into an intimate, warm conversation regarding everything that had occurred and everything that was on the verge of happening.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Queen Nell, your majesty remains unchanged. I have grown dreadfully skinny following the arrival of the infants. My looks are not nearly as pleasant as before; however, I believe Ez prefers it this way. You see, the difference in our appearances is no longer so sharp. Furthermore, oh, your upcoming marriage to Hugh is absolutely wonderful. Cyril Lisle would have been completely unsuitable, completely. Although I experienced terrible disappointment back then, I am able to recognize that now. You must admit, Nell, your treatment of Cyril was exceedingly poor.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “I gather he has gotten better,” Nell smiled.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Oh, yes. He has a wife, and she is a sweet little thing, and their happiness is complete. All things work together for good. That is stated by Ez and the Bible, which are fairly reliable authorities.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Have Hector and Orlando gotten married yet?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Hector is, though Orlando isn’t. Talking with you brings back those sweet past times at Tabby’s Place so vividly, Nell! We enjoyed such great fun!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Did you visit Tabby’s Place recently?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Indeed, my visits are frequent. Miss Tabby alongside Miss Maria continue sitting near the hearth to do their knitting. That brings to mind—there is a marriage present for you that we carried from those two, Nell. Try to deduce its identity.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “I was always unable to. In what way were they aware that my marriage was about to take place?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Oh, I informed them. My visit occurred last week. They showed such great interest, in fact. Miss Tabby sent me a note two days back requesting that I drop by; she then inquired whether I'd bring her present to you. What item from Tabby’s Place would you desire above all else, Nell?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Is it possible that I have been sent her china dogs by Miss Tabby?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Ascend to the top. This exact second, they are inside my trunk. Furthermore, I possess a note intended for you. Hold on a second while I fetch it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Dear Miss Harcourt,” was what Miss Tabby had penned, “Maria and I found the news of your coming marriage extremely interesting. You have our finest wishes. Neither Maria nor I have ever taken a husband, yet we hold no bias against the matrimony of others. Our china dogs are being dispatched to you. My original plan was to bequeath them to you upon my death, since you appeared to hold a genuine fondness for them. However, Maria and I anticipate remaining above ground for a considerable time still (D.V.), which has led me to choose to bestow the dogs upon you during your youth. Surely it remains in your memory that Gog’s gaze is directed rightward and Magog’s leftward.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Only imagine those beautiful old dogs resting near the hearth in my dream house,” Nell remarked with delight. “I had not anticipated anything quite so wonderful.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: During that evening, activity buzzed through Grey Shutters as everyone readied for the next day, yet Nell quietly crept off into the dusk. On this final afternoon of her youth, she possessed a small journey to undertake, one that required her to be by herself. Making her way to the small Brierley cemetery beneath the shadow of poplars, she visited Obed’s grave, where she held a quiet rendezvous with eternal loves and bygone memories.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “How happy Obed would be tomorrow if he were present,” she murmured. “However, I feel he truly knows and is happy about it—in another place. I’ve read in some place that 'our dead are never dead until we have forgotten them.’ Obed will not ever be dead to me, because I am unable to ever forget him.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: Placing the flowers she had brought upon his grave, she made her way slowly down the long hill. The evening was gracious, abounding in delightful lights and shadows. Clouds of mackerel filled the western sky—tinted with crimson and amber, separated by long strips of apple-green sky. Farther off lay the shimmering glow of a sea at sunset, and the unceasing sound of many waters rose from the tawny beach. Surrounding her entirely, resting in the refined, lovely quiet of the countryside, were the hills, fields, and woods that she had known and cherished for so long.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “History repeats itself,” Hugh stated, coming alongside her when she went by the Carrow gate. “Nell, do you recall our initial journey down this hill—which was, in fact, our very first walk together anywhere?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “As dusk fell, I was returning from the grave of Obed—when you stepped through the gate; whereupon I set aside the pride I had held for years and addressed you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “And all heaven opened before me,” Hugh added. “From that point on I anticipated the next day. When I departed from you at your gate that evening and strolled home I was the most joyful youth on earth. Nell had forgiven me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “It seems to me that your burden of forgiveness was the greatest. I behaved as a miserable, unappreciative child—even following the moment when you truly rescued me on the pond that afternoon. In the beginning, how I detested that heavy weight of debt! The joy I have received is more than I merit.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: Hugh let out a laugh and squeezed more firmly the young hand wearing his band. A band of pearls formed Nell’s engagement ring. A diamond was something she had declined to wear.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Ever since learning that diamonds were not the beautiful purple I had imagined, I have never truly cared for them. They shall forever remind me of my past letdown.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “Yet the ancient tale holds that pearls signify tears,” Hugh had protested.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: “That does not frighten me. Furthermore, weeping can stem from joy just as easily as from grief. Indeed, my most joyful times occurred with tears filling my eyes—the moment Thirza informed me that I could remain at Grey Shutters—the moment Obed presented me with my first beautiful dress—the moment news reached me that you would pull through the fever. Therefore, bestow pearls upon me for our troth ring, Hugh, and I will gladly take the grief of existence alongside its happiness.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE LAND OF DREAMS AMONG
text: Yet on this evening, no thoughts of grief entered the minds of our lovers, who focused solely on happiness. Indeed, the next morning would bring their marriage, and the misty, purple coast of Seven Gulls Harbor held the home of dreams that was expecting them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: Upon opening her eyes on the morning she was to be married, Nell saw the sunlight glimmering through the window in the small porch gable while a breeze of September played about her curtains.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “It makes me so happy that the sun’s rays will fall upon me,” was her joyful thought.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: Nell remembered her initial morning waking inside that small porch room, as sunbeams slithered in toward her past the old Frost Maiden's drifting blossoms. That wakefulness had lacked joy, bringing alongside itself the preceding night's sharp letdown. Yet over the intervening time, years filled with joyful childhood daydreams and young womanly reveries had made the tiny chamber beloved and hallowed. Following every time she was away, she had returned to it with delight; beside its pane she had dropped to her knees during that night filled with sharp anguish when she thought Hugh was passing away, and beside it she had remained seated in silent bliss during the evening she became engaged. Numerous watchful nights of gladness along with a few of grief had occurred inside; and on this day she was required to abandon it eternally. From this point forward it would not belong to her; fifteen-year-old Lucy was destined to receive it once she departed. Neither did Nell desire a different outcome; the tiny chamber belonged sacredly to youth and maidenhood—to that former time slated to end on this day prior to the start of her story as a wife.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: Grey Shutters became a bustling and happy home during that morning. Isolde came early, accompanied by little Gideon and Small Nell Lucinda, so that she could assist. Robin and Lucy, who were the Grey Shutters twins, carried the babies away to the garden.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Make sure Small Nell Lucinda doesn’t ruin what she’s wearing,” Isolde cautioned with concern.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “You do not have to fear leaving Lucy in her care,” Thirza said. “That youngster possesses greater sense and caution than the majority of mothers I have encountered. In certain respects, she is truly remarkable. She bears little resemblance to the other reckless one I raised.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: Thirza offered a smile to Nell over her chicken salad. One could even imagine that the wild creature was her favorite, when all was said and done.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “The twin children are truly lovely,” Mrs. Agatha remarked, once she was certain they could no longer hear her. “Lucy shows such helpfulness and mature grace, while Robin is growing to be quite a clever lad. He has ceased being the dreadful little troublemaker he was in the past.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “I have never felt as bewildered in my entire life as I did during his initial six months with us,” Thirza admitted. “Following that period, I imagine I became accustomed to his presence. Recently, he has developed a keen interest in agriculture and desires my permission to attempt managing the farm in the coming year. I might allow it, since Mr. Pembroke does not believe he will wish to lease it for much longer, necessitating a different plan.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Well, Nell, the weather for your wedding is certainly lovely,” Isolde stated while pulling a large apron across her silk attire. “Even if you had ordered it from Eaton’s, you could not have gotten a better one.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: "In truth, that exact company, Eaton's, receives far too much money from this Island," declared Mrs. Sowerby crossly. Expressing her firm opinions regarding predatory department stores was a habit she indulged whenever possible. "Furthermore, the Brierley girls treat those catalogues like the Bible nowadays, and that is a fact. Rather than reading the Holy Scriptures on Sundays, they scrutinize those books instead."

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Indeed, for entertaining young ones, they are wonderful,” Isolde remarked. “The illustrations keep Gideon and Small Nell occupied for hours.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Without using Eaton’s catalogue, I entertained a total of ten children,” Mrs. Agatha stated sternly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “Come on, you two, do not fight about Eaton’s catalogue,” Nell said cheerfully. “You know, this is the most special day I have ever had. Because I am so glad, I wish for all other people to be glad as well.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: “I’m sure I hope your happiness will last, child,” sighed Mrs. Agatha. Indeed, she truly hoped for it and possessed faith in it, yet she held a fear that displaying one's joy with too much openness amounted to provoking Providence. For her own benefit, Nell needed to be moderated just a bit.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: Yet the bride who descended the old, homespun-carpeted staircase that September noon was joyful and lovely—the initial bride of Grey Shutters, slim and bright-eyed, wrapped in the mist of her bridal veil, holding an armful of roses. Hugh, who was awaiting her in the hallway beneath, gazed up at her with adoration in his eyes. She belonged to him finally, this elusive, long-pursued Nell, earned following years of steadfast waiting. It was toward him she was approaching in the gentle yield of a bride. Was he deserving of her? Would he be able to render her as joyful as he desired? Should he fail her—should he fall short of her ideal of manhood—then, as she extended her hand, their glances locked and every uncertainty was wiped out by a joyful confidence. They were meant for one another; and, regardless of what the future might bring them, that could never be changed. Their joy was entrusted to each other, and neither felt any fear.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: They were wed in the bright sunlight of the ancient orchard, surrounded by the affectionate and friendly faces of lifelong companions. Mr. Wace performed the marriage, and the Reverend Ez offered what Mrs. Agatha Sowerby later declared was the “most beautiful wedding prayer” that had ever met her ears. Although birds rarely sing during September, a songbird warbled sweetly from a concealed branch as Hugh and Nell spoke their immortal vows. Nell listened to it and felt a thrill; Hugh listened to it, feeling surprised only that every bird on earth had not broken into triumphant song; Cedric listened to it and subsequently composed a poem about it that became one of the most praised pieces in his initial collection of poetry; Belinda the Fourth listened to it and felt joyfully certain it boded good fortune for her beloved Miss Harcourt. That bird continued its song until the service reached its end, concluding with a single wild, happy little trill. The old gray-green dwelling surrounded by its enveloping orchards had never experienced a brighter, happier afternoon. Every traditional joke and witticism that must have served at marriage celebrations since the time of Eden was brought out, appearing just as fresh, clever, and amusing as though they had never previously been spoken. Mirth and happiness reigned supreme; and as Nell and Hugh departed to make the Delford train, driven by Cedric, the twins stood prepared with rice and worn shoes, which Belinda the Fourth and Mr. Pettifer assisted gallantly in tossing. Thirza remained at the gate, observing the carriage until it disappeared down the lengthy lane bounded by goldenrod. At its extremity, Nell turned to wave her final farewell. She had departed—Grey Shutters was no longer her residence; Thirza’s countenance appeared exceedingly gray and aged as she walked back toward the dwelling that Nell had supplied with illumination and vitality for fourteen years, even when she was away.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 THE FIRST BRIDE OF GREY SHUTTERS
text: However, Isolde along with her young children, the inhabitants of Echo Cottage, and the Waces remained behind so that the two elderly women would not feel lonely on their initial night; moreover, they managed to enjoy a calmly delightful small supper, remaining at the table for a extended period and discussing every single detail regarding the day. At the time they were seated there, Nell and Hugh were stepping off the train in Glen St. Agnes.

Dr. David Carrow had dispatched his buggy and horse so they would be met, and the boy who was the driver sneaked off while grinning sympathetically, abandoning them to the joy of riding by themselves toward the house that was now theirs amidst the glowing dusk.

Nell never lost the memory of how beautiful the sight was that suddenly appeared before them as they crested the hill in back of the village. Although her new residence was not yet visible, Seven Gulls Harbor stretched out in front of her resembling a massive, gleaming mirror colored in rose and silver. Way below, she observed where it opened, situated between the sand dune bar to one side and a sheer, tall, severe cliff of red sandstone to the other. Past the bar, the ocean rested in the lingering light, tranquil and solemn. Tucked into the cove where the sand dunes joined the edge of the harbor, the small fishing village appeared to be a huge opal through the haze. Above them, the sky resembled a gem-encrusted cup spilling forth the twilight; the sea’s irresistible tang made the air crisp, and the entire scene was filled with the delicate nuances of a coastal evening. Along the darkening harbor banks lined with firs, several faint sails drifted by. From the tower of a small white church situated on the opposite side, a bell tolled; the sound floated softly and dreamily over the water, mixing with the ocean’s moan. Against the bright northern sky, the massive rotating beam located on the channel cliff shone warm and golden, acting as a flickering, trembling star of optimistic promise. Distant along the horizon, the smoke from a passing steamer formed a wrinkled gray ribbon.
“Oh, gorgeous, gorgeous,” whispered Nell. “Seven Gulls will be a place I love, Hugh. Which one is our house?”

“That strip of birch stretching from the small cove conceals it, so we are unable to see it yet. It sits approximately two miles away from Glen St. Agnes, with a further mile separating it from the light-house. Nell, our neighbors will be few. Just one house stands close to ours, and the identity of its occupants is unknown to me. Will loneliness affect you while I am absent?”
“Not when I am accompanied by such light and beauty. Hugh, who resides in that house?”
“I am uncertain. Does it appear—precisely—that the residents would be compatible souls, Nell?”

The residence was a grand, solid structure, coated in a green so intense that it made the surrounding countryside appear utterly washed out in comparison. An orchard lay in the rear, and a well-maintained lawn stretched out front, yet a particular starkness hung over the place. Its orderliness might have been to blame for this effect; every part of the property—the dwelling, outbuildings, fruit trees, garden plots, grass, and driveway—was unsparingly tidy.

“It appears unlikely that a person possessing such preferences in paint could prove to be VERY kindred,” admitted Nell, “except if it happened by chance—similar to our blue hall. At the very least, I am convinced that no children reside there. The neatness surpasses even that of the old Copp place located on the Tory road, an achievement I never anticipated seeing matched.”

No one had been encountered by them on the damp, red road curving beside the harbor edge. However, right prior to reaching the birch belt concealing their house, a girl was spotted by Nell, who was guiding a herd of snow-white geese atop a velvety green hill to the right. Large, dispersed firs were growing on it. Through their trunks, one caught sight of yellow harvest fields, flashes of golden sand-hills, and portions of blue sea. The girl possessed height and was wearing a light blue print dress. She moved with a particular spring in her step and an upright posture. Just as Nell and Hugh were passing, she and her geese emerged from the gate located at the hill's base. Placing her hand on the gate latch, she stood still, gazing intently at them with a look that scarcely reached interest, yet did not sink to curiosity. For a brief instant, Nell felt that a concealed trace of enmity was also present in it. Yet it was the girl’s attractiveness that caused Nell to let out a small gasp—an attractiveness so striking that anywhere it would have drawn notice. Though she wore no hat, thick braids of shiny hair, having the shade of ripe wheat, were wound around her head like a crown; her eyes possessed a blue, starry quality; her frame, inside its simple print dress, was splendid; and her lips matched the redness of the cluster of blood-red poppies attached to her belt.
“Nell inquired in a soft tone, “Who was that girl we just walked by, Hugh?””
“I failed to spot any girl,” remarked Hugh, whose gaze was fixed entirely on his bride.
“At that gate, she was standing—no, avoid looking behind us. We are still being watched by her. A face so beautiful has never been seen by me.”
“I fail to recall meeting any particularly attractive young women during my time in this place. A few charming girls reside up at the Glen, though I doubt they would qualify as truly beautiful.”

“She is, indeed. You could not have looked at her, otherwise you would recall her. No one is capable of forgetting her. A face like hers has never been seen by me, save in artwork. As for her hair! Browning’s phrases 'cord of gold’ and 'gorgeous snake’ were brought to my mind by it!”
“It is likely that she is a guest staying in Seven Gulls, perhaps a person visiting from the large summer hotel across the harbor.”
“Dressed in a white apron, she was herding geese.”
“To entertain herself, she could act that way. Observe, Nell—that is where we live.”

Nell gazed and temporarily pushed the girl possessing the magnificent, indignant eyes from her mind. Seeing her upcoming dwelling for the first time brought joy to her sight and soul—its appearance so strongly resembled a large, cream-colored seashell cast up on the bay's edge. The lines of lofty Lombardy poplars descending its path appeared in grand, violet outlines against the heavens. Situated behind it, protecting its garden from the excessively sharp gusts of ocean breezes, stood a hazy forest of firs, wherein the gales could create every sort of uncanny and lingering melody. As with any forest, it appeared to hold and embrace mysteries within its depths,—mysteries that yield their allure solely to those who go inside and search with endurance. Externally, deep emerald branches preserve them unviolated against inquisitive or unconcerned glances.

Past the bar, the wild dances of the night winds were starting, while lights gemmed the fishing hamlet on the other side of the harbor when Nell and Hugh came up the poplar lane in their buggy. A flickering, warm glow from the fire poured into the twilight as the door of the small house swung open. Hugh hoisted Nell down from the vehicle and guided her into the garden, passing through the small gate set between the firs with ruddy tips, and continuing along the neat, red path until they reached the step made of sandstone.
“Welcome home,” he murmured, and holding hands, they crossed the doorway of their house of dreams.

“Old Doctor Dave” together with “Mrs. Doctor Dave” had traveled down to the small dwelling so that they could welcome the husband and wife. Doctor Dave was a large, merry, white-bearded aged man, whereas Mrs. Doctor was a neat, pink-cheeked, gray-haired small woman who immediately embraced Nell, both in reality and in spirit.

“My dear, seeing you brings me such joy. It must be that you are truly exhausted. A little evening meal is waiting for us, and some trout was carried up for you by Captain Saul. Where have you gone, Captain Saul? Ah, my guess is that he stepped outside to tend to the horse. Let us go to the upper floor so you can remove your coat.”

Bright, appreciative eyes glanced around Nell as she went up the stairs behind Mrs. Doctor Dave. The look of her new dwelling pleased her immensely. It appeared to possess Grey Shutters' atmosphere alongside the flavor belonging to her old traditions.

“It seems to me that Miss Elizabeth Russell and I would have been 'kindred spirits,'” she whispered once she was by herself in her room. Two windows were located inside it; the one in the dormer faced the lower harbor, the sand-bar, and the Seven Gulls lighthouse.
“A magical window giving onto the spray Of dangerous oceans in desolate realm of fays,”

recited Nell in a low voice. Looking out the gable window, one could see a small, harvest-colored valley intersected by a brook. Located a half-mile up this brook stood the solitary visible dwelling—an ancient, sprawling, gray structure encircled by enormous willows, with its windows peering through them into the dusk like timid, searching eyes. Nell pondered who resided there; as her closest neighbors, she hoped they would be pleasant. All at once, her thoughts turned to the lovely girl with the white geese.

“Hugh believed she was out of place here,” Nell reflected, “yet I am certain she fits. She possessed a quality that connected her to the ocean, the sky, and the port. Seven Gulls flows through her veins.”
As Nell reached the bottom of the stairs, Hugh stood in front of the fireplace, engaged in conversation with a man she did not know. Upon Nell’s entrance, both men turned toward her.
“Nell, meet Captain Garrick. Captain Garrick, I’d like you to meet my wife.”

Never before had Hugh spoken the words “my wife” to anyone except Nell, and the sheer pride of doing so almost made him burst. Extending a muscular hand toward Nell, the old captain exchanged smiles with her, establishing a friendship between them right then. One like-minded soul instantly recognized another.

“I am truly delighted to make your acquaintance, Mistress Carrow; and my wish is that your happiness equals that of the initial bride who arrived at this place. No finer wish could I offer you than THAT. However, the introduction given by your husband is not quite precise. My weekday title is 'Captain Saul' and, since you are bound to finish by using it, you may as well start by calling me that. You are undoubtedly a lovely little bride, Mistress Carrow. Gazing at you gives me a feeling as though I have only just gotten wedded myself.”
As the laughter died down, Mrs. Doctor Dave pressed Captain Saul to remain and join them for supper.

“I am very grateful to you. It will be a true pleasure, Mistress Doctor. Generally, I must consume my food by myself, accompanied only by the image of my hideous aged visage in an opposing mirror. I rarely get the opportunity to share a meal with a pair of such delightful, attractive women.”

The praise from Captain Saul might appear quite plain when written down, yet his delivery possessed a manner and expression of such polite, tender respect that the lady receiving it perceived she was receiving a royal homage in a grand manner.

An old man of high soul and simple mind, Captain Saul possessed everlasting youth within his heart and eyes. His tall and somewhat awkward form leaned forward slightly, but it still implied immense endurance and power; his hair was an iron-gray, thick mane that hung down to his shoulders, while his closely shaved face was bronzed and heavily furrowed; and his deep-set, exceptionally blue eyes would occasionally twinkle, occasionally dream, and at times gaze out toward the sea with a yearning search, like somebody hunting for a lost, precious object. Nell would discover on a future day the exact thing that Captain Saul was seeking.

Captain Saul was undeniably a plain-looking man. Beauty had not guided the shaping of his thin jaws, rough mouth, and broad forehead; furthermore, his frame and his inner self bore the visible scars of numerous trials and griefs he had endured; yet despite Nell initially viewing him as unattractive, she gave the matter no further thought, because his rough exterior was so completely illuminated and transformed by the light of his soul.

Cheerful spirits marked their assembly surrounding the evening meal table. Although the chill belonging to the September dusk was expelled by the hearth fire, sea gusts came in as they pleased through the unclosed dining room window. Encompassing the harbor alongside the expanse of muted, purple heights past it, the vista was splendid. Delights prepared by Mrs. Doctor piled the table, yet the large plate of sea trout served undeniably as the main attraction.

“I imagined they would be rather delicious following a journey,” Captain Saul remarked. “Mistress Carrow, these trout are as fresh as possible. A couple of hours back, the Glen Pond was where they were swimming.”
“Who is looking after the beacon this evening, Captain Saul?” Doctor Dave inquired.
“Nephew Hector. His understanding of it matches my own. Well, now, I am truly pleased that you invited me to remain for supper. My hunger is quite strong—I ate very little for dinner today.”
“I reckon you are nearly starving yourself much of the duration down at that lighthouse,” Mrs. Doctor Dave stated sternly. “You refuse to take the effort to cook a proper meal.”

“Oh, Mistress Doctor, indeed I do,” Captain Saul asserted. “Listen, my usual way of living is royal. Up at the Glen yesterday evening, two pounds of steak were bought by me to bring back. Today, my intention was to enjoy an extraordinarily fine dinner.”
“And the steak, what became of it?” Mrs. Doctor Dave inquired. “Was it lost by you on your journey back?”

“No.” Captain Saul appeared embarrassed. “Right at bedtime a pitiful, mean-tempered kind of dog showed up and requested a place to stay for the night. I suppose he was owned by one of the fishermen along the shore. I was unable to send the poor mongrel away—his foot was hurt. Consequently, I locked him inside the porch, gave him an old bag for a bed, and retired for the night. However, for some reason I was unable to rest. Upon reflecting on it, I somewhat recalled that the dog appeared starved.”
“And you arose and presented him with that steak—EVERY BIT OF that steak,” Mrs. Doctor Dave stated, expressing a sort of victorious scolding.

“Indeed, no other food was available for him,” Captain Saul remarked apologetically. “At least, nothing that would appeal to a dog. He devoured it in roughly two mouthfuls, so I suppose he truly was famished. For the remainder of the night, my slumber was excellent, though my noon meal ended up rather meager—essentially just potatoes with nothing to accompany them. As for the dog, he dashed back toward his own place earlier today. I guess he had no desire to be a vegetarian.”
“Imagine going hungry over an good-for-nothing hound!” Mrs. Doctor scoffed.

“Someone might consider him quite valuable, for all you know,” Captain Saul argued. “He failed to APPEAR to be worth much, yet a dog’s appearance can be deceiving. He could possess genuine inner beauty, just as I do. I must admit, the First Mate disapproved of him. His words were exceedingly harsh. Nevertheless, the First Mate holds a bias. A cat's view regarding a dog carries no weight. Regardless, I missed my meal, which makes this fine meal among this charming group truly enjoyable. Having wonderful neighbors is a wonderful blessing.”
“In the house nestled in the willows further up the brook, who resides there?” Nell inquired.
“Mrs. Rufus Vane,” Captain Saul stated—“and her husband,” he appended, as though he were offering a subsequent thought.
Nell beamed, forming an impression of Mrs. Rufus Vane based on how Captain Saul phrased it; clearly another Mrs. Agatha Sowerby.

“You haven’t got a lot of neighbors, Mistress Carrow,” Captain Saul continued. “On this side of the harbor, the settlement is very sparse. A majority of the land is owned by Mr. Stroud up yonder past the Glen, and he leases it for pasture. Now, the opposite side of the harbor is crowded with people—MacAllisters in particular. There is an entire settlement of MacAllisters where if you throw a stone, you are bound to strike one. I had a conversation with old Leon Blacquiere recently. He has spent the whole summer working on the harbor. 'Dey’re nearly all MacAllisters over thar,’ he said to me. 'Dare’s Neil MacAllister and Sandy MacAllister and William MacAllister and Hector MacAllister and Angus MacAllister—and I believe dare’s de Devil MacAllister.’”

“There are almost the same number of Kerrs and Crawfords,” Doctor Dave remarked, once the laughing had died down. “You see, Hugh, those of us living on this side of Seven Gulls share an ancient proverb—'From the conceit of the Kerrs, the pride of the MacAllisters, and the vainglory of the Crawfords, good Lord deliver us.’”

“However, a good deal of splendid folks are in their midst,” Captain Saul stated. “I went to sea beside William Crawford across a long stretch of years, and when it came to bravery, stamina, and honesty, nobody was his peer. People possess intelligence across there beyond Seven Gulls. Perhaps that reason explains why the inhabitants here are somewhat disposed to hassle them. It is peculiar, is it not, the way people appear to begrudge anybody coming into the world just a bit sharper than themselves.”
Doctor Dave, having engaged in a forty-year dispute with the individuals from over the harbor, chuckled and quieted down.
“What person resides in the bright emerald house roughly half a mile further along the road?” inquired Hugh.
A pleased grin spread across the face of Captain Saul.

“Miss Winifred Tolley. Because you are Presbyterians, she will probably come to visit you before long. She would not visit whatsoever if you happened to be Methodists. Methodists fill Winifred with a sacred dread.”
“She is quite a personality,” Doctor Dave laughed softly. “An exceptionally confirmed hater of men!”
“Unripe fruit?” asked Hugh, chuckling.

“No, ’tisn’t sour grapes,” replied Captain Saul in a serious manner. “Winifred had the ability to select anyone she wanted during her youth. Even now, the old widowers would jump the moment she uttered the word. It simply appears that she was born possessing a kind of persistent malice toward Methodists and men. Within Seven Gulls, hers is the most venomous tongue and the most compassionate heart. That woman turns up to assist in the gentlest manner whenever there is any difficulty. Another woman is never the subject of a cruel remark from her, and I suppose our thick old skins can endure it if she enjoys dressing down us poor scalawags of men.”
“Saul, Captain, she has only good things to say about you,” Mrs. Doctor remarked.
“Indeed, I fear that is the case. I really dislike it. It gives me the impression that there might be something rather unnatural concerning myself.”
“Captain Saul, who was the initial bride to arrive at this house?” inquired Nell, while they gathered by the hearth following their evening meal.
“Did she belong to the tale I’ve heard tied to this dwelling?” Hugh inquired. “I was told by someone that you could relate it, Captain Saul.”

“Indeed, yes, I am aware of it. I suppose I am the sole living inhabitant of Seven Gulls at present who is able to recall the schoolmaster’s bride as she appeared upon her arrival on the Island. Although she has been deceased these thirty years, she was a member of that class of women that one fails to ever erase from memory.”
“Narrate the tale to us,” requested Nell. “It is my desire to discover everything concerning the female inhabitants who resided in this dwelling prior to my arrival.”

“Well, only three have existed—Elizabeth Russell, along with Mrs. Ned Russell, and the schoolmaster’s bride. Elizabeth Russell was a pleasant, smart little thing, and Mrs. Ned was a pleasant woman, as well. However, they could never compare to the schoolmaster’s bride.

“John Tremayne was what the schoolmaster was named. During my sixteenth year, he arrived from the Old Country so he could instruct at the Glen's schoolhouse. He differed greatly from the typical castoffs who traveled to P.E.I. for teaching jobs back then. A majority of those men were smart, intoxicated wretches who imparted the three R’s to pupils while sober, yet thrashed them whenever they weren't. John Tremayne, on the other hand, was an attractive, splendid young man. My father provided him with lodging, and despite a decade separating our ages, he and I became close friends. A great deal of our time was spent reading, strolling, and conversing side by side. I suppose he was familiar with practically every poem ever composed, and as we walked beside the shore during the evenings, he would recite it to me. Father considered it a terrible misuse of hours, though he tolerated it to a degree, trusting that it might discourage my desire to head out to sea. Naturally, nothing was capable of accomplishing THAT—a line of seafaring people produced my mother, making the urge part of my nature. Even so, listening to John reading and declaiming gave me great pleasure. Although nearly six decades have passed, I remain able to recite vast stretches of verse that he taught me. Almost sixty years!”
For a short while, Captain Saul held his tongue, staring directly at the burning embers to search through the past. Afterwards, he uttered a sigh and continued with his tale.

“I recall encounters with him on the sand-hills one spring night. He appeared somewhat elevated—exactly as you appeared, Dr. Carrow, when you escorted Mistress Carrow inside this evening. The second I beheld you, I recalled him. Furthermore, he informed me that a sweetheart remained back home and that she was travelling out to join him. I was barely pleased at all, being an ill-conditioned young chunk of self-interest; I assumed he would not remain as strong a friend to me once she arrived. However, I possessed sufficient manners to conceal it from him. He shared every detail regarding her with me. Her name was Damaris Leigh, and she would have accompanied him out if not for her elderly uncle. He suffered from illness, and because he had cared for her following her parents' deaths, she refused to abandon him. Yet now he had passed away, and she was travelling out for the purpose of marrying John Tremayne. It was by no means a simple trip for a female in those times. You must remember that no steamers existed.
“‘At what time do you look for her?’ I ask.

“‘The 20th of June is when she departs on the Royal William,’ he states, ‘meaning mid-July ought to see her arrival. Carpenter Johnson must be put to work by me to construct a dwelling for her. Today brought her letter. Prior to unsealing it, I was aware it contained favorable tidings for me. A few evenings back, she appeared to me.’

“I was unable to comprehend him, and he subsequently clarified—even if my comprehension improved merely a fraction. He claimed to possess a gift—or a curse. Those were his exact terms, Mistress Carrow—a gift or a curse. Which one it was remained unknown to him. He mentioned that a great-great-grandmother belonging to him had possessed it, and she was burned as a witch because of it. He stated that peculiar spells—trances, I believe was the term he assigned to them—overcame him from time to time. Do such things exist, Doctor?”

“Certain individuals are undoubtedly prone to trances,” Hugh replied. “This issue falls more under the purview of psychical research rather than medicine. What characterized the trances experienced by this John Tremayne?”
“Like dreams,” the old Doctor remarked dubiously.
“He claimed he was able to perceive things inside them,” Captain Saul uttered deliberately.

“Remember, I am relating to you merely what HE stated—events that were occurring—events that were DESTINED to occur. He mentioned that they occasionally brought him solace and occasionally brought him dread. A quartette of nights prior to this, he had experienced one—entering it as he remained seated, watching the flames. Furthermore, he beheld an ancient chamber in England that was familiar to him, with Damaris Leigh inside it, extending her hands toward him while appearing joyful and pleased. Consequently, he understood that favorable tidings concerning her were coming to him.”
“A dream—a dream,” the aged Doctor sneered.

“Probably—probably,” agreed Captain Saul. “That’s what I remarked to him back then. Thinking that was a great deal more reassuring. I disliked the thought of him perceiving stuff of that nature—it felt truly strange.
“‘Negative,’ he states, ‘it was no dream of mine. However, our discussion on this matter ends here. Should you dwell on it too greatly, your friendship toward me will lessen.’”
“I informed him that nothing was capable of diminishing my friendship for him. He merely shook his head, however, and says, says he:

“‘Young man, I am aware. Previously, this has caused me to lose companions. I hold no grudge against them. At times, it makes me feel scarcely well-disposed toward my own self. That kind of ability possesses a touch of the divine—though whether it belongs to a benevolent or a malevolent deity, who can tell? And every one of us mortals recoils from coming into excessively intimate touch with a God or a devil.’
“Those were the words he used. I recall them just as if it happened yesterday, even if I was not entirely sure what he intended to say. What is your guess about what he REALLY intended, doctor?”
“I question whether he comprehended his own meaning,” Doctor Dave remarked crossly.

“It seems I comprehend,” Nell murmured. Lips pressed together and eyes gleaming, she paid attention in her customary manner. Captain Saul allowed himself an appreciative grin prior to continuing his tale.

“Well, shortly afterward every single person in the Glen and Seven Gulls was aware that the schoolmaster’s bride was arriving, and they were all delighted since he was held in such high esteem by them.
