And afterwards we establish ourselves happily in houses with eight rooms that appear to satisfy every wish of our hearts—for the reason that our prince is present. YOU ought to have truly possessed your palace, however—you possess such beauty. You MUST permit me to speak it—it simply must be spoken—I am almost exploding with awe. You are the most beautiful creature I have ever beheld, Mrs. Vane.”
“You must address me as Lorna if we are to be friends,” the other declared with a strange passion.
“Certainly I shall. Furthermore, I am called Nell by MY companions.”

“I guess my appearance is lovely,” Lorna continued, staring fiercely toward the ocean. “My loveliness is something I despise. My desire is that I had perpetually been as dark-skinned and ordinary as the darkest-skinned and most ordinary female in that fishing village across the way. So, how do you regard Miss Winifred?”
The sudden shift in topic precluded any additional disclosures.
“Isn’t Miss Winifred a darling?” Nell asked. “Last week, Hugh and I had an invitation to her home for a state tea. You know the phrase about groaning tables.”
“I think I remember coming across that phrase in newspaper write-ups about weddings,” Lorna said, with a smile.

“Indeed, Miss Winifred gave a groan—or, to be exact, a creak—without a doubt. It was beyond belief that she would prepare such a quantity of food for just two average folks. In my opinion, she possessed every sort of pie imaginable—save for lemon pie. According to her, she won the award for lemon pies at the Port Marlow Exhibition a decade prior and refrained from baking them ever since to avoid risking her standing for them.”
“Did you manage to consume a sufficient amount of pie to satisfy her?”

“I was not. Hugh captured her affections through eating—I will not reveal the exact amount. Her statement was that she had never met a man who failed to prefer pie over his Bible. Are you aware that I adore Miss Winifred?”
“I do as well,” Lorna remarked. “In all the world, she is my closest friend.”

Nell silently pondered why Miss Winifred had never brought up Mrs. Rufus Vane to her if that was the case. Miss Winifred had undoubtedly spoken openly regarding all the other people living in or around Seven Gulls.

“Is that not lovely?” Lorna inquired, following a short hush, as she indicated the stunning sight of a ray of sunshine streaming through a fissure in the cliff behind them, spanning a murky emerald basin at its bottom. “Were I to arrive at this spot—and witness only that single view—I should return satisfied.”

“The impacts of shadow and light right along these coasts are marvelous,” concurred Nell. “The harbor is visible from my small sewing room, and I perch by its window to satisfy my vision. Never during two consecutive minutes are the shadows and hues identical.”
“And you don't ever feel lonely?” Lorna inquired suddenly. “Not ever—when nobody else is with you?”

“No. I do not believe I have ever experienced true loneliness in my life,” Nell replied. “Even during times when I am by myself, I enjoy wonderful company—dreams, imaginations, and pretendings. I ENJOY being by myself occasionally, merely to reflect on things and TASTE them. However, I adore friendship—along with pleasant, cheerful little moments with others. Oh, WILL you not come visit me—frequently? Please. I think,” Nell added, laughing, “that you would care for me if you were acquainted with me.”

“I ponder whether YOU might find ME agreeable,” Lorna stated in earnest. A compliment was not what she was seeking. Her gaze swept over the sea, where crests of foam illuminated by the moon were starting to form like garlands, and darkness gathered within her eyes.

“I’m sure I would,” Nell said. “And please don’t consider me completely irresponsible simply because you caught me dancing on the beach as the sun was setting. I will undoubtedly become dignified eventually. You see, I haven’t been a wife for very long. I still feel like a girl, and occasionally even a child.”
“My marriage has lasted for twelve years,” Lorna remarked.
This was yet one more thing that was impossible to believe.
“Well, your age cannot possibly match mine!” cried Nell. “When your marriage took place, you had to be a mere youngster.”
“Sixteen was my age,” Lorna said, standing up and gathering the cap and jacket that were next to her. “My age is twenty-eight today. Well, returning is something I must do.”
“I have to go as well. It is likely that Hugh is at home now. However, I am extremely happy that the two of us visited the beach this evening and ran into one another.”

Lorna remained silent, which made Nell feel somewhat discouraged. Although she had extended a candid offer of amity, it was received with little grace, even if it had not been entirely rejected. Without speaking, they ascended the cliffs and traversed a pasture where the moonlight turned the soft, pale wild grasses into what resembled a creamy velvet rug. Upon arriving at the shore lane, Lorna turned around.
“This is my direction, Mrs. Carrow. You will visit me on occasion, will you not?”
It seemed to Nell that the invitation had been flung in her direction. Lorna Vane appeared to offer it with hesitation, in her view.
“I will attend if it is truly your desire,” she stated with a slight chilliness.
“Oh, I do—I do,” cried Lorna, her intensity breaking out as though it had shattered a limitation placed upon it.
“I will join you, in that case. Good-night—Lorna.”
“Have a good night, Mrs. Carrow.”
Lost in deep thought, Nell made her way back to the house and recounted her story to Hugh.
“Therefore, Mrs. Rufus Vane does not belong to the people who recognize Joseph?” Hugh asked in a playful manner.

“No—o—o, not precisely. Even so—it seems to me she WAS among their number at one time, though she has left or been forced into exile,” Nell remarked thoughtfully. “She undeniably differs greatly from the local women. One cannot converse regarding eggs and butter with HER. To imagine that I had been conceiving of her as another Mrs. Agatha Sowerby! Did you ever catch sight of Rufus Vane, Hugh?”
“No. While I have noticed a few individuals laboring in the farm's fields, I am unsure which one was Vane.”
“He was never spoken of by her. I am CERTAIN that happiness eludes her.”

“Based on what you are telling me, I imagine she got married prior to being mature enough to understand her own mind or feelings, only to discover when it was too late that she had erred. It happens to be a quite frequent tragedy, Nell.
“A woman of quality would have managed the situation as well as possible. It is obvious that Mrs. Vane allowed it to fill her with bitterness and resentment.”

“Let us withhold judgment until we are certain,” begged Nell. “Her situation is not so typical, I believe. Once you encounter her, Hugh, her allure will make sense to you. It exists completely distinct from her looks. My impression is that her personality is abundant, one a companion could step into like a realm; however, owing to some cause, she excludes everybody and locks her potential inside, preventing it from growing and flowering. Well, I have tried hard to describe her to myself from the moment I departed from her, and I have come as close as possible to doing so. Miss Winifred is the person I intend to question regarding her.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Indeed, two weeks back, the eighth infant was born,” Miss Winifred remarked, seated in a rocking chair in front of the hearth inside the tiny dwelling on a crisp afternoon in October. “A girl was born. Gideon lost his temper completely—claiming a boy was what he desired—though actually he had no wish for the child whatsoever. Had a boy arrived, he would have raged over it not being a girl. Their previous children consisted of four girls and three boys, which makes me think the gender of this newborn hardly mattered, yet naturally he was compelled to be disagreeable, as men always are. Outfitted in its lovely small garments, the infant is truly attractive. Dark eyes belong to it, along with the most charming, minuscule hands.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “I have to go look at it, as I simply adore infants,” Nell remarked, grinning inwardly at an idea far too precious and holy to express aloud.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “They are nice, I cannot deny,” Miss Winifred conceded. “However, take my word for it, certain people appear to possess a surplus beyond necessity. Eleven were born to my unfortunate cousin Flora up at the Glen, making her an absolute drudge! It was three years ago that her husband took his own life. Precisely what a man would do!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Why did he act in such a manner?” Nell inquired, feeling somewhat taken aback.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “He failed to have his own way about some matter, which led him to leap down the well. We are well rid of him! From birth, he was a bully. Naturally, the well was ruined by this. Poor Flora simply could not stand the idea of relying on it ever again! Consequently, she paid to have a new one constructed, incurring a terrible cost for water that turned out to be extremely hard. Had he been determined to drown, surely the harbor offered an abundance of water? A person of that sort exhausts my patience. During my time here, Seven Gulls has experienced merely two suicides. Frank Ainslie—who was Lorna Vane’s father—was the second one. On a side note, has Lorna come by to visit you yet?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “No, but I bumped into her on the beach a couple of evenings back and we struck up a conversation,” said Nell, suddenly listening intently.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: Miss Winifred gave a nod.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “I am happy, dearie. I had been hoping you would get together with her. How do you feel about her?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “She seemed extremely attractive to me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Oh, certainly. No person around Seven Gulls was ever capable of matching her beauty. Have you ever viewed her hair? It extends all the way down to her feet whenever she unbinds it. However, my question was how did she appeal to you?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “I feel that I might become quite fond of her should she allow it,” Nell stated unhurriedly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Yet she refused to allow you—she shoved you away and maintained her distance from you. Unfortunate Lorna! Knowing the nature of her past existence would leave you hardly astonished. That existence has been a tragedy—a tragedy!” Miss Winifred forcefully reiterated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “I would be glad if you could relate her whole story to me, provided you are able to do so while keeping any confidences intact.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Goodness, dear, all the folks in Seven Gulls are aware of poor Lorna’s tale. The EXTERNAL details aren't a secret at all. Only Lorna knows the INTERNAL truth, and she refuses to share her private thoughts with anyone. I suppose I’m pretty much the closest companion she possesses in the world, yet she has not spoken a single grievance to me. Have you ever laid eyes on Rufus Vane?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “No.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Well, I might just as well start from the very start and relate the entire story to you sequentially, which will enable you to comprehend it. As I stated previously, Frank Ainslie was Lorna’s father. He possessed intelligence and lacked ambition—in typical male fashion. Oh, he was blessed with an abundance of intellect—and a lot of benefit he derived from it! He commenced attending college, remaining there for a period of two years, after which his well-being collapsed. A tendency toward consumption existed throughout the Ainslie family. Consequently, Frank returned to his family home and initiated a farming career. He took as his wife Rose Kerr, who hailed from across the harbor. Rose held the reputation of being the most beautiful person in Seven Gulls—Lorna inherits her appearance from her mother, yet she possesses tenfold the energy and drive that Rose displayed, along with a vastly superior physique. Now, Nell, as you are aware, my position is consistently that we female folk should support one another. Heaven knows we are subjected to a sufficient amount of hardship from men, which is why I maintain that we should refrain from attacking each other, and rarely will you catch me disparaging a fellow woman. Nevertheless, I possessed little regard for Rose Kerr. To start with, trust ME, she was pampered, and she amounted to nothing more than an indolent, self-centered, complaining individual. Frank lacked any inclination toward labor, resulting in their being as impoverished as Job’s turkey. Impoverished! Trust ME, they subsisted on potatoes and point. A pair of children were born to them—Lorna and Julian. Lorna possessed the physical appearance of her mother alongside the intellect of her father, plus a quality inherited from neither parent. She inherited the traits of her Grandmother West—a magnificent elderly woman. During her childhood, Nell, she was the most intelligent, warm, and cheerful creature. All people held affection for her. She stood as the preferred child of her father, and she held immense affection for him in return. The two of them were 'chums,’ to use her own term. She proved incapable of perceiving any of his defects—and he TRULY was an appealing kind of man in particular respects.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Well, Lorna was twelve years old when the initial terrible event occurred. Little Julian was four years younger than her, and she adored him—and he TRULY was a sweet little fellow. Then he was killed one day—he fell from a large load of hay precisely as it entered the barn, and the wheel rolled directly over his tiny body, crushing his life out. And remember, Nell, Lorna witnessed it. Her eyes were on him from the loft. A single screech escaped her—the hired man claimed no sound in all his life had ever equaled it—he declared it would echo in his ears until driven out by Gabriel’s trump. Yet she never uttered another screech or wept over it afterward. From the loft she leaped onto the load and then from the load down to the floor, where she snatched up the little bleeding, warm, lifeless body, Nell—they were forced to tear it away from her before she’d release it. They summoned me—I cannot speak about it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: Drying the tears from her gentle brown eyes, Miss Winifred worked her needle in painful quiet for a little while.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Well,” she continued, “everything had ended—little Julian was laid to rest in the cemetery above the harbor, and when some time had passed, Lorna returned to her studies and her school. Julian’s name was never spoken by her—from then until now, I have not heard it pass her lips. I suppose that ancient pain continues to ache and burn occasionally; nevertheless she was merely a child, and time treats children very gently, Nell, dearie. Eventually her laughter returned—her laugh was the sweetest thing. It is rarely heard these days.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “I listened to it one evening recently,” stated Nell. “It REALLY IS a lovely laugh.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Following the passing of Julian, Frank Ainslie started a downward slide. Being frail, he suffered a heavy blow from it, since he truly adored the youth, even if, as I mentioned earlier, Lorna remained his preferred one. Becoming gloomy and despondent, he either lacked the ability or the desire to labor. Then, on a certain day when Lorna reached fourteen, he took his own life by hanging—specifically in the parlor, no less, Nell, directly in the center of the parlor suspended from the lamp hook attached to the ceiling. Was that not typical of a man? Furthermore, it coincided with his wedding anniversary. A pleasant, tasteful moment to select for such a deed, wouldn't you say? Naturally, that unfortunate Lorna ended up being the person who discovered him. She walked into the parlor during that morning, singing while carrying some new blooms for the vases, and at that spot she caught sight of her father suspended from the ceiling, possessing a face that was as black as coal. Believe ME, it was a terrible thing!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Oh, how awful!” Nell exclaimed, shivering. “That poor, unfortunate child!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Lorna refrained from weeping at the funeral of her father, just as she had not wept at Julian’s. Rose, on the other hand, shrieked and wailed enough for both of them, leaving Lorna fully occupied as she attempted to soothe and console her mother. Rose filled me with disgust, a feeling shared by all the others, yet Lorna never lost her composure. Her mother was someone she loved. Lorna possesses a loyal nature—in her view, her relatives were incapable of fault. Anyway, Frank Ainslie was laid to rest next to Julian, and a massive monument was erected for him by Rose. Take MY word for it, it exceeded the size of his character! At any rate, its cost surpassed what Rose was able to pay, given that the mortgage on the farm exceeded what the property was worth. Shortly afterward, however, Lorna’s elderly grandmother West passed away, leaving Lorna a modest sum of money—an amount sufficient to fund one year for her at Regent’s Academy. Lorna was determined to qualify as a teacher if possible, and subsequently earn the funds needed to put herself through Wexcombe College. Her father had cherished that very plan—he desired that she obtain what he had forfeited. Lorna overflowed with ambition, and her mind was packed with intelligence. She attended Regent’s, where she completed two years of studies in a single year to earn her First; upon returning home, she secured the position at the Glen school. She was filled with such joy, hope, vitality, and enthusiasm. Reflecting on her nature during those days compared to her present state makes me say—drat the men!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: Miss Winifred cut her thread away with a hostility that suggested she was slicing through the throat of humanity in a single blow, as if she were Nero.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Rufus Vane entered her life during that summer. His father, Abner Vane, managed a store at the Glen, yet Rufus inherited a nautical inclination from his mother; he was accustomed to sailing during the summer and working as a clerk in his father's store throughout the winter. He was a large, good-looking man, possessing a small, wicked soul. He continuously desired a thing until he obtained it, whereupon he ceased to desire it—precisely as a man does. Oh, he refrained from complaining about the weather whenever it was pleasant, and he was usually quite pleasant and amiable whenever all went well. However, he consumed a great deal of alcohol, and several unpleasant tales were recounted regarding him and a young woman down at the fishing village. He was not suitable for Lorna to wipe her feet upon, to put it plainly. Furthermore, he was a Methodist! Yet he was utterly crazy about her—due to her attractive appearance initially, and due to her refusal to speak to him subsequently. He swore he would possess her—and he obtained her!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “In what manner did he manage to accomplish this?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Oh, that was a truly wicked deed! Rose Ainslie will never have my forgiveness. You see, dearie, the mortgage on the farm belonging to the Ainslies was held by Abner Vane, with the interest remaining unpaid for a number of years, so Rufus went right to Mrs. Ainslie and declared that unless Lorna became his wife, he would persuade his father to foreclose on the property. Rose acted dreadfully—she swooned, cried, and begged Lorna to prevent her from being cast out of her dwelling. She claimed her heart would shatter if she had to depart from the place she had entered as a bride. I would not have held it against her for feeling terribly grieved about it—yet you would not have expected her to be self-centered enough to offer up her own kin on account of it, would you? Well, that is precisely what she was.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “And Lorna yielded—her love for her mother was so great that she would have performed any deed to spare her agony. She wedded Rufus Vane. At that moment, not one of us understood the reason. Only much later did I discover how her mother had nagged her into the match. Still, I was convinced that something was amiss, since I was aware of how repeatedly she had rejected him, and such a sudden reversal was out of character for Lorna. Furthermore, I was certain that Rufus Vane was not the sort of man Lorna could ever care for, regardless of his handsome appearance and lively manners. Naturally, there was no grand wedding, yet Rose requested that I attend their marriage. I attended, but I regretted going. I had observed Lorna’s expression during the funeral of her brother and during the funeral of her father—and at that moment, it felt to me as though I were witnessing it at her own funeral. Yet Rose was beaming like a basket of chips, believe ME!

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Lorna and Rufus established themselves on the Ainslie place—Rose was unable to endure being separated from her dear daughter!—and resided there during the winter. When spring arrived, Rose caught pneumonia and passed away—a year later than she should have! Lorna experienced quite a bit of heartbreak because of it. Isn’t it awful how certain unworthy people are cherished, whereas others who are much more deserving, one would imagine, never receive much love? Regarding Rufus, he had grown tired of peaceful domestic existence—exactly like a man. He wanted to pack up and leave. He traveled over to Nova Scotia so he could see his relatives—his father originated from Nova Scotia—and he sent a letter back to Lorna stating that Laurence Vane, his cousin, was embarking on a sea trip to Havana and he planned to go along. The ship's name was the Four Sisters and their absence was expected to last roughly nine weeks.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Lorna must have felt a sense of relief. However, she kept silent. Starting from her wedding day, her demeanor matched her current one—aloof and haughty, maintaining a wall between herself and all people save for me. Mark MY words, I refuse to BE pushed away! Despite all circumstances, I have simply held onto Lorna as tightly as I possibly could.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “According to her, you were her closest friend,” Nell stated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Was that what she did?” Miss Winifred cried out with great joy. “I am truly grateful to know that. There were times I questioned whether my presence was truly desired by her, given that she never allowed me to believe it was. Your effect in warming her up must have exceeded your expectations, or she would not have uttered even that much to you. Ah, what a miserable, sorrow-stricken girl! Whenever Rufus Vane comes into my sight, I am filled with a desire to plunge a knife right through his body.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: Miss Winifred dabbed her eyes a second time, and after easing her emotions with that violent desire, resumed her narrative.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Well, Lorna remained over on that side by herself. Before his departure, Rufus had sown the crop, and it was tended by old Abner. As the summer passed, the Four Sisters failed to return. An inquiry was made by the Nova Scotia Vanes, who discovered that the vessel had reached Havana, unloaded her freight, laden a new one, and departed bound for home; beyond that point, their discoveries ended completely. As time went on, folks started speaking of Rufus Vane as a deceased man. Nearly everybody was convinced of his death, even if nobody was sure, since sailors have reappeared here at the harbor following absences of many years. Lorna was certain he had not died—and her belief was correct. A terrible shame, as well! During the following summer, Captain Saul happened to be in Havana—which occurred prior to his retirement from nautical life, naturally. He decided to investigate a little—Captain Saul was forever interfering, as men so often are—and he began making inquiries in sailors’ boarding houses and similar establishments, attempting to learn any details regarding the crew belonging to the Four Sisters. It would have served him better to leave well enough alone, to my mind! Anyway, he visited a certain remote location, and there he discovered a person who he recognized immediately as Rufus Vane, despite the large beard he wore. Captain Saul had him shaved, leaving zero uncertainty—it was indeed Rufus Vane—physically, at any rate. His intellect was gone—and as far as a soul goes, I don't believe he ever possessed one!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “What had occurred with him?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “No one understands the exact truth about it. The boarding house owners could only state that roughly twelve months prior, they had discovered him slumped on their front steps one morning in a terrible state—with his head beaten nearly to a pulp. Their assumption was that he had been injured during a drunken brawl, which is probably accurate. They brought him inside, believing there was no chance he would survive. Yet he survived—and upon recovering, he was exactly like a child. He lacked memory, intellect, or the capacity to reason. Attempts were made to discover his identity, but they always failed. He was unable to state his own name—he could merely speak a handful of basic words. A letter was in his possession that started 'Dear Rufus’ and ended with 'Lorna,’ yet it lacked an address and had lost its envelope. They permitted him to remain—he was taught to perform some simple chores around the property—and that is where Captain Saul discovered him. He brought him back—a deed I have constantly called a unfortunate day's labor, even if I suppose no alternative existed for him. His hope was that upon returning home and viewing his previous environment and known faces, Rufus would regain his memory. However, it produced no result. He has remained at the residence up the brook from that time onward. He is simply like a child, neither more nor less. He exhibits bad-tempered periods at times, but he is usually merely blank, pleasant, and inoffensive. He tends to wander off if he is left unwatched. That represents the load Lorna has been forced to bear for eleven years—and entirely by herself. Old Abner Vane passed away shortly after the return of Rufus, whereupon it was discovered that he was nearly broke. Following the settlement of affairs, Lorna and Rufus were left with only the old Ainslie farm. Lorna leased it to John Ward, and that rental payment comprises her entire income. On occasion during the summer, she accommodates a lodger to assist her finances. Nevertheless, the majority of tourists favor the opposite shore of the harbor containing the hotels and vacation cottages. Lorna’s residence sits at too great a distance from the swimming beach. She has provided care for Rufus without leaving his side for eleven years—she is bound to that simpleton forever. And this follows every dream and expectation she formerly possessed! It is easy to envision her existence, Nell, dearie—given her attractiveness, animation, self-respect, and intelligence. It has been nothing short of a living death.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Poor, poor girl!” Nell repeated. She felt chided by her personal joy. When another individual was bound to be that wretched, what entitlement did she possess to experience such happiness?

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Would you explain to me precisely what Lorna stated and the way she behaved the evening you encountered her by the water?” Miss Winifred inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: Giving her full attention, she listened and indicated her approval with a nod.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “YOU believed she was formal and unemotional, Nell, my sweet, yet I am able to assure you that she warmed up remarkably for someone like her. She surely took a genuine liking to you. I am delighted. You might prove very helpful to her. It was a relief to learn that a newly married pair was moving into this dwelling, as I trusted it would bring Lorna some companionship; particularly if you were part of the group that understands Joseph. You WILL become her friend, won’t you, Nell, my sweet?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Indeed I will, if she’ll let me,” Nell said, showing all of her characteristic, sweet, and impulsive earnestness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “Regardless of whether she allows it, your duty is to be her friend,” Miss Winifred stated with determination. “If she acts aloof occasionally, ignore it—do not pay it any attention. Consider what her existence used to be—and currently is—and inevitably will remain, I assume, because individuals such as Rufus Vane never die, as far as I know. You ought to observe the weight he has gained following his return home. Formerly, he was quite thin. Simply FORCE her to accept your friendship—you possess the capability—you belong to the sort of people with that talent. However, you cannot afford to be easily offended. Furthermore, do not care if she appears reluctant to have you visit her house often. She understands that certain women dislike being in the presence of Rufus—they protest that he makes their skin crawl. Merely persuade her to visit this place as frequently as possible. Her opportunities to leave are limited—she is unable to abandon Rufus for extended periods, since Heaven only knows what he might perform—he would probably set the residence on fire. Her freedom occurs almost exclusively during nighttime, once he has retired to bed and drifted off to sleep. He consistently turns in at an early hour and rests deeply until the following day. That probably explains why you encountered her by the water. She frequently roams around that area.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “I will do everything I can for her,” said Nell. The fascination she felt for Lorna Vane, which had been lively from the moment she observed her herding her geese down the slope, grew a thousand times stronger because of Miss Winifred’s story. Her heart was drawn by an overpowering attraction to the girl’s attractiveness, grief, and solitude. Never before had she met someone of her kind; until now, her companions had been healthy, ordinary, cheerful girls resembling herself, whose youthfulness was darkened merely by ordinary human troubles and losses. Lorna Vane existed separately, an unhappy, moving embodiment of obstructed womanhood. Nell made up her mind to gain access to the realm of that isolated spirit and discover the fellowship it was so capable of bestowing, if not for the harsh bonds confining it within a dungeon not constructed by itself.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 THE STORY OF LORNA VANE
text: “And remember this, Nell, dearie,” Miss Winifred remarked, having not yet entirely unburdened her mind, “You ought not to suppose Lorna is an unbeliever since she scarcely ever attends church—or even that she belongs to the Methodists. Naturally, she cannot bring Rufus to church—not that he attended church very often during his finest days. But simply keep in mind that she remains a truly devoted Presbyterian in her soul, Nell, dearie.”

It was a chilly evening in October, with moon-drenched fog drifting across the harbor and winding like ribbons of silver through the seaward glens, when Lorna visited the house of dreams. Upon Hugh opening the door to her knock, she appeared to regret having come; however, Nell rushed past him, seized her, and pulled her inside.

“I’m very happy that you chose this evening to visit,” she remarked cheerfully. “A large batch of especially delicious fudge was prepared by me earlier today, and an assistant is needed to consume it alongside us—in front of the fireplace—as we share tales. Captain Saul might also make an appearance. Today belongs to him.”
“No. Captain Saul is across at home,” Lorna replied. “He—he forced me to come here,” she appended, with a touch of defiance.
“When I see him, I will express my gratitude to him for that,” Nell remarked, dragging comfortable armchairs in front of the hearth.
“Oh, I do not mean that coming was something I did not wish to do,” Lorna objected, her face reddening slightly. “I—I have had thoughts of visiting—however, leaving is not always simple for me.”

“Naturally, parting from Mr. Vane must prove difficult for you,” Nell remarked pragmatically. It was her conclusion that referring to Rufus Vane as a settled reality now and then would be ideal, preventing the topic from acquiring unnecessary grimness through avoidance. Her judgment proved correct, since Lorna’s restrained demeanor instantly disappeared. It was clear she had been speculating about the extent of Nell’s awareness regarding her living circumstances, feeling unburdened when no clarifications proved necessary. Permitting her hat and coat to be removed, she settled with a youthful cuddle into the large armchair near Magog. Her attire was attractive and meticulous, featuring her usual accent of color via a red geranium placed at her pale neck. The glowing hearth fire made her lovely hair shimmer like liquid gold. Radiant with gentle amusement and charm were her ocean-blue eyes. Temporarily, affected by the small dwelling of dreams, she reverted to being a girl—one oblivious to previous times and their acrimony. Surrounding her completely was the climate of numerous affections that had hallowed the small dwelling; enveloping her was the camaraderie of two robust, contented, youthful individuals belonging to her own era; experiencing the enchantment of her environment, she surrendered to it—Miss Winifred and Captain Saul could hardly have identified her; Nell struggled to accept that this lively girl, who conversed and paid attention with the intensity of a deprived spirit, was the same chilly, distant female she had encountered on the beach. Furthermore, Lorna’s eyes gazed with immense longing at the bookstands situated between the windows!

“The collection of books we own is quite small,” Nell remarked, “yet each volume within it serves as a FRIEND. Over time, in various places, we have gathered our books, always refusing to purchase any volume before reading it beforehand and determining that it originated from the lineage of Joseph.”
Lorna let out a laugh, a lovely sound that appeared to resemble every bit of joy that had reverberated within the tiny home during the bygone times.

“My father owned a small number of books, and I have them,” she remarked. “They have been read by me so often that I practically know them from memory. Books are rare for me to acquire. Though the Glen store contains a circulating library, the committee selecting books for Mr. Tibbs seems unaware of which ones belong to Joseph’s race, or maybe it does not matter to them. Because a book I truly enjoyed was such a rare find for me, I stopped procuring any.”
“I hope our bookshelves will be treated by you as your own,” Nell said.
“You are completely and genuinely invited to borrow any book from them.”
“A banquet of rich offerings is being placed prior to my eyes by you,” Lorna uttered with delight. Subsequently, the chime of ten upon the clock caused her to stand up, somewhat reluctantly.

“It is necessary for me to leave, as I failed to see how late it had gotten. Captain Saul frequently remarks that spending an hour does not require much time. However, I have remained for two—and oh, I truly have had a wonderful time,” she appended with candor.

“Come often,” said Nell and Hugh. Having gotten up, they were standing side by side within the radiance of the hearth. Lorna gazed upon them—young, full of hope, joyful, embodying everything that she lacked and would permanently lack. The brightness faded from her countenance and eyes; the young girl disappeared; it was the grieving, betrayed woman who replied to the offer nearly coldly and departed with a pathetic speed.
Nell observed her until she disappeared into the darkness of the cold and foggy night. Afterwards, she turned around deliberately toward the warmth of her own glowing hearthstone.

“Is she not beautiful, Hugh? I am captivated by her hair. It extends down to her feet, according to Miss Winifred. Opal Pettigrew possessed lovely hair—however, Lorna’s possesses LIFE—each individual strand is animate gold.”
“She is extremely lovely,” Hugh concurred, with such genuine warmth that Nell nearly preferred him to display a WEE bit less fervor.
“Hugh, if my hair was similar to Lorna’s, would it please you more?” she inquired yearningly.
“For all the world, I would not change the color of your hair to anything other than what it currently is,” Hugh declared, offering a couple of persuasive gestures to match.
Your hair wouldn't be golden—or any other shade, for that matter—if you were NELL”—
“Red,” Nell stated, her satisfaction dark.

“Indeed, red—so it adds warmth to that milk-white skin and those gleaming gray-green eyes you have. Golden hair would not fit you in any way Queen Nell—MY Queen Nell—queen of my heart and life and home.”
“In that case, Lorna’s can be admired by you as much as you wish,” Nell stated generously.

A week afterward, one night, Nell made up her mind to hurry across the meadows to the dwelling up the stream to pay a casual visit. The night was filled with a slate-colored mist that had slunk inside from the gulf, wrapped the port, packed the ravines and dales, and stuck weightily to the fall pastures. The ocean groaned and trembled through the haze. Nell observed Seven Gulls in a different light, discovering that it was uncanny, enigmatic, and intriguing; nevertheless, it likewise made her feel somewhat solitary. Hugh had gone and would not return before the next day, since he was present at a doctor's gathering in Port Marlow. Nell craved sixty minutes of companionship with a female companion. Captain Saul and Miss Winifred were both “good fellows” in their distinct manners; yet youth pined for youth.

“If Isolde or Cressy or Nonie or Mabel were able to drop in for a visit,” she remarked to herself, “it would be so wonderful! A GHOSTLY night like this is rare. Were that masking fog to be abruptly pulled away tonight, I am certain every vessel that ever departed Seven Gulls for its destruction would appear traveling up the harbor, carrying their drowned crews upon their decks. It strikes me as hiding countless secrets—as though I were encircled by the ghosts of former generations of Seven Gulls inhabitants staring at me from behind that gray screen. Should the beloved deceased women of this small home return to see it again, an evening precisely like this one is when they would arrive. Staying seated here much longer will cause me to spot one of them across from me in Hugh’s chair. Tonight, this location feels a bit uncanny. Even Gog and Magog seem to be perking up their ears so as to detect the strides of invisible visitors. Before my own imagination terrifies me, just as it did in the past regarding the Whispering Wood, I will rush over to visit Lorna. I shall leave my house of dreams behind so it can greet its former residents. They will receive my goodwill and welcome from my fire—prior to my return they will have departed, and my home shall belong to me again. I feel certain it is meeting with history tonight.”

Although she smiled slightly at her own imagination, Nell felt a chilling feeling along her backbone as she blew a kiss to Gog and Magog, stepping into the mist while carrying a few recent magazines beneath her arm to give to Lorna.

“Lorna is crazy about books and magazines,” Miss Winifred had mentioned to her, “and she scarcely ever gets a look at one. Buying them or paying for subscriptions is beyond her means. Her poverty is truly pitiful, Nell. How she manages to subsist at all on the meager rent that the farm yields is a mystery to me. She does not ever drop a single hint complaining about her lack of money, but I am well aware of what she endures. It has been a burden to her for her entire life. In the days when she was unencumbered and full of ambition, it did not bother her, but it must be painful now, believe ME. It makes me happy that she appeared so cheerful and lively on the night she was over at your place. Captain Saul informed me that he was forced to actually place her coat and cap on her and shove her out the doorway. Do not delay too much before visiting her, either. Should you take too long, she will assume it stems from your dislike of looking at Rufus, causing her to retreat right back into her shell. Rufus is a huge, gentle baby, yet that absurd grin and laugh of his do agitate the nerves of certain folks. Fortunately for me, I am not troubled by nerves. My liking for Rufus Vane is greater now than it ever was during the time he possessed his proper faculties—although the Lord is aware that is not saying much. One day during housecleaning season I was down at her place giving Lorna a little help, and I happened to be frying doughnuts. Rufus was hovering about hoping to catch one, as he always does, when suddenly he grabbed a boiling hot one that I had only just scooped out and flipped it onto the nape of my neck as I was stooping down. After that, he chuckled and chuckled. Believe ME, Nell, I needed every bit of God’s grace in my heart to refrain from simply grabbing that pot of sizzling fat and dumping it right over his head.”

Nell chuckled about the anger of Miss Winifred while she hurried through the blackness. Laughter, however, fit poorly with such a night. By the time she arrived at the residence amidst the willows, she was quite solemn. All was extremely quiet. Because the forward section of the dwelling appeared unlit and abandoned, Nell stole around to the side entrance, which led from the veranda into a small sitting room. At that spot, she paused without making a sound.

The door had been left unclosed. Past it, Lorna Vane was sitting inside the faintly illuminated space, her head resting on her arms which were stretched across the table. She was crying terribly—her low, intense, gasping sobs sounding as though an inner torment was attempting to rip its way free from her soul. Next to her sat an aged black dog, who had placed his nose upon her lap, his large canine eyes completely filled with silent, pleading compassion and loyalty. Nell stepped backward in alarm. It seemed to her that she must not intrude upon such sorrow. Her own heart pained with a compassion she could not express. Entering at this moment would mean permanently closing the door on any potential aid or companionship. A certain intuition alerted Nell that the haughty, resentful girl would fail to ever pardon anyone who caught her unawares in such a helpless state of hopelessness.

Stealthily leaving the veranda, Nell made her path through the yard. On the other side, voices echoed in the darkness, accompanied by the faint radiance of a light. Reaching the gate, she encountered two men—Captain Saul carrying a lantern, and a companion who she realized could only be Rufus Vane—a large individual, severely overweight, possessing a wide, circular, florid face, and expressionless eyes. Despite the dim illumination, Nell formed the feeling that his eyes possessed an extraordinary quality.

“Mistress Carrow, is that you?” Captain Saul inquired. “Come, come, walking around by yourself on such a night isn't right. Getting lost in this fog is all too easy. Wait right here until Rufus is safely through the door, and then I will return to guide you across the fields with my light. Dr. Carrow must not return to discover you tumbled right off Cape Leforce because of the fog. It happened to a woman once, four decades back.
“So you went across to visit Lorna,” he remarked, once he returned to her side.
“I remained outside,” Nell stated, before describing the things she had witnessed. A sigh escaped Captain Saul.

“Unfortunate, unfortunate, young girl! She rarely weeps, Mistress Carrow—she possesses too much courage for that. She has to be hurting terribly whenever she actually weeps. Such a night is difficult for miserable females who carry griefs. It has a quality that somewhat resurrects everything we have endured—or dreaded.”
“It is completely haunted,” Nell remarked, shuddering. “I crossed over for that very reason—my wish was to hold a living person’s hand and listen to a living person’s voice.”

“A multitude of INHUMAN presences appear to be lurking around this evening. My very own beloved home was packed with them as well. In fact, they pushed me right out. Thus, I escaped to this spot seeking company among my own species.”

“However, Mistress Carrow, it was correct of you to refrain from entering. Lorna would have disapproved. She would have objected to me entering alongside Rufus, which I would have carried out had I not encountered you. I retained Rufus by my side throughout the entire day. I maintain him in my company as frequently as possible in order to assist Lorna somewhat.”
“Does he not have a strange look in his eyes?” Nell inquired.

“Did you observe that? Indeed, one eye is blue while the other is hazel—a trait inherited from his father. The Vane family possesses that distinct characteristic. It was precisely how I identified him as Rufus Vane upon initially spotting him down in Cuby. Had it not been for the appearance of his eyes, his beard and weight might have prevented me from recognizing him. I suppose you are aware that I was the one who discovered him and escorted him back home. Miss Winifred continually maintains that I ought not to have done so, yet I am unable to concur with her view. Doing so was the RIGHT action—making it the sole option available. I possess no doubts whatsoever regarding THAT. Nevertheless, my aging heart grieves for Lorna. At merely twenty-eight years old, she has endured far greater grief than the majority of women experience over the course of eighty years.”

For a short time, their walk continued without a word. Before long, Nell remarked, “Are you aware, Captain Saul, that carrying a lantern during a walk is something I never enjoy? The oddest sensation always comes over me that a loop of sneaky, malevolent beings encompasses me just beyond the light's reach, right past its dark perimeter, observing me with inimical eyes from the gloom. Since I was a child, I have experienced that emotion. Why should that be? Such a feeling never comes over me when the dark actually encompasses me—when I am totally surrounded by it—I do not feel at all afraid.”

“I share a similar sentiment,” Captain Saul conceded. “My belief is that the dark acts as a companion when it surrounds us tightly. However, when we kind of shove it back—severing our connection to it, in a manner of speaking, through the glow of a lantern—it turns into an adversary. Still, the mist is dispersing.
“If you pay attention, a clever west wind is picking up. By the time you reach home, the stars will have appeared.”
The pair had gone; and upon Nell’s return to her house of dreams, the hearth still held glowing red embers, while every haunting presence had departed.

The brilliant hues that had shone for weeks beside the margins of Seven Gulls Harbor had dissolved into the muted gray-blue of late autumn hills. Numerous days arrived in which mist-laden rain obscured the fields and shores, or where they trembled in the chill of a doleful wind from the sea—as well as nights filled with storm and tempest, during which Nell would occasionally wake to offer prayers that no vessel was striving along the formidable north coast, because under such conditions not even the immense, steadfast beacon revolving fearlessly amid the dark could succeed in steering it to a secure refuge.

“In November I sometimes feel as if spring could never come again,” she sighed, lamenting the utter ugliness of her frozen and messily ruined flower-plots. The cheerful small garden of the schoolmaster’s bride was a somewhat dismal spot at present, and the Lombardies and birches were under bare poles, in the words of Captain Saul. Yet the fir-forest in back of the small house remained perpetually green and steadfast; and even during November and December gentle days occurred featuring sunlight and violet hazes, when the harbor leaped and gleamed as cheerfully as in the middle of summer, and the gulf was so mildly blue and delicate that the tempest and the fierce wind appeared merely to be elements of a ancient dream.

Numerous autumn evenings were spent by Nell and Hugh at the lighthouse. A cheery place it remained at all times. Hints of sunshine appeared to be hiding everywhere around it, even on occasions when the sea was lifeless and gray while the east wind sang in a minor key. This was possibly due to the First Mate constantly strutting through it adorned in gold. The sun was scarcely missed because he was so big and radiant, and the laughter together with the conversation taking place beside Captain Saul’s fireplace was pleasantly accompanied by his booming purrs. On topics exceeding the understanding of cat or king, Captain Saul and Hugh engaged in numerous lengthy discussions and elevated discourse.

“I enjoy reflecting upon every type of issue, even if I am unable to resolve them,” Captain Saul stated. “It was my father's belief that we ought to refrain from discussing matters beyond our comprehension, yet if we followed that rule, doctor, our topics of discourse would be exceptionally scarce. I suppose the gods frequently chuckle upon listening to us, but it is of no consequence provided we keep in mind that we are merely human and refrain from imagining that we are actually divine entities ourselves, possessing knowledge of right and wrong. I suppose our discussions will not cause much injury to us or to anybody else, so let us attempt another go at the origin, purpose, and destination tonight, doctor.”

Nell either paid attention or drifted into thought as the others “whacked.” On occasion, Lorna accompanied them to the lighthouse, where she and Nell strolled the coast during the strange dusk, or remained perched on the boulders beneath the lighthouse structure until nightfall forced them to return to the cozy driftwood fire. At that point, Captain Saul would make tea for them and recount
“stories about the earth and ocean, and whatever could happen to the vast, overlooked realm beyond.”

Lorna appeared to forever take great pleasure in those lighthouse revelries, flowering for the duration into swift humor and lovely laughter, or silence with shining eyes. The discourse possessed a particular zest and flavor while Lorna was there that was absent during her nonattendance. She appeared to stimulate brilliance in everyone else even when she refrained from speaking. Captain Saul narrated his tales with greater skill, Hugh proved swifter in debate and quick retorts, and Nell sensed small spurts and streams of whim and creativity welling up to her lips beneath the sway of Lorna’s persona.

“Far removed from Seven Gulls, that girl came into the world destined to head intellectual and social spheres,” she remarked to Hugh while they strolled toward their house one evening. “Here she is simply wasted—wasted.”

“Didn’t you hear Captain Saul and me the other evening as we were talking about that matter in a general way? It was our reassuring deduction that the Creator likely understood how to manage His universe just as effectively as we do, and that, in the end, 'wasted’ lives do not exist, unless a person deliberately throws away and ruins his own life—a thing Lorna Vane definitely has not done. Furthermore, certain folks could consider that a Wexcombe B.A., who was starting to be recognized by editors, was 'wasted’ by becoming the spouse of a hardworking country doctor in the small town of Seven Gulls.”
“Hugh!”
“Now, had Cyril Lisle been the man you wed,” Hugh went on without pity, “'a leader in social and intellectual circles far away from Seven Gulls' is what YOU might have become.”
“Hugh CARROW!”
“You ARE aware that he had your affection once, Nell.”

“Hugh, that is cruel—'pisen mean, just as all the men are,’ to quote Miss Winifred. I was NEVER in love with him. It was merely my imagination. You are aware of that. You KNOW that I would prefer being your wife within our house of dreams and fulfillment to being a queen inside a palace.”

Hugh did not respond verbally; nevertheless, I fear they both failed to think of poor Lorna as she hurried alone through the fields toward a dwelling that was far from being a palace or the realization of a dream.

At their backs, the rising moon began to transform the dark, melancholy sea. Across the harbor, where her illumination had not yet arrived, the distant shoreline appeared shadowy and evocative, full of faint coves, deep darkness, and sparkling lights.

“In what way the home lights beam through the night!” exclaimed Nell. “The harbor’s line of them resembles a necklace. And see what a glitter shines up at the Glen! Oh, see, Hugh; ours is right there. Leaving it lit makes me so happy. Returning to a pitch-black home is something I detest. OUR homelight, Hugh! Is it not wonderful to behold?”

“Nell—girl—it is merely a single dwelling among the countless millions on earth, yet it is ours—OURS—our guiding light in 'a naughty world.’ Once a man possesses a home containing a beloved, tiny, red-haired wife, what additional thing could he possibly request from life?”
“Well, ONE additional request might come from him,” Nell softly murmured with joy. “Oh, Hugh, I feel as though waiting until springtime is simply IMPOSSIBLE for me.”

Initially, Hugh and Nell discussed traveling back to Brierley for Christmas, yet in the end, remaining in Seven Gulls was their choice. “It is my wish that the initial Christmas we share as a married couple takes place within our personal dwelling,” Nell declared.

Thus it happened that Thirza, accompanied by Mrs. Agatha Sowerby and the twins, arrived at Seven Gulls to spend Christmas. The countenance Thirza possessed resembled that of a female who had sailed all the way around the world. Never previously had she traveled as far as sixty miles from her home; furthermore, she had never partaken of Christmas dinner at any location other than Grey Shutters.

A huge plum pudding had been baked by Mrs. Agatha and brought along by her. Mrs. Agatha could not be persuaded by anything that a Christmas plum pudding could be made correctly by a college graduate of the younger generation; nevertheless, the house of Nell received her praise.

“Nell manages a home well,” she remarked to Thirza inside the guest bedroom on the evening they reached the house. “My inspection covered both her bread box and her garbage bucket. My assessment of a housekeeper relies on those two things every time, that is my method. The pail holds nothing except proper waste, while the bread box lacks any dry crusts. Naturally, your guidance shaped her early on—yet her education continued at college later. The presence of my tobacco stripe quilt on this bed caught my attention, alongside your large circular braided rug placed in front of her parlor fireplace. Those touches make me feel completely comfortable.”

Nell experienced all the joy she could have hoped for during her initial Christmas in her personal home. Brightness and fine weather marked the day; Christmas Eve had brought the initial thin layer of snow, bestowing beauty upon the world, while the open harbor continued to sparkle.
Dinner was attended by Captain Saul and Miss Winifred. Though Lorna and Rufus received an invitation, Lorna declined, stating that they invariably spent Christmas at her Uncle Isaac West’s.

“She prefers it that way,” Miss Winifred said to Nell. “Bringing Rufus around unfamiliar people is something she cannot endure. For Lorna, Christmas is consistently a difficult period. Her father and she were accustomed to celebrating it greatly.”

Miss Winifred and Mrs. Agatha failed to form a particularly strong liking for one another. “Two suns hold not their courses in one sphere.” Yet no conflict arose between them, because Mrs. Agatha remained in the kitchen aiding Nell and Thirza as they prepared dinner, leaving Hugh responsible for entertaining Captain Saul and Miss Winifred—or, more accurately, leaving him to be entertained by the pair, since a conversation between two such longtime companions and rivals was certainly never uninteresting.

“It’s been a long time since this place hosted a Christmas dinner, Mistress Carrow,” Captain Saul remarked. “Miss Russell consistently visited her town friends when Christmas came. However, I attended the initial Christmas dinner that this house ever saw—and it was prepared by the schoolmaster’s bride. Sixty years ago today that took place, Mistress Carrow—on a day quite similar to this one—with merely sufficient snow for whitening the hills, while the harbor matched June in its blueness. Being just a boy, I had never received a dinner invitation previously, and my shyness kept me from eating a full portion. I’ve completely recovered from THAT.”
“The majority of men do,” replied Miss Winifred, stitching with great intensity. Miss Winifred refused to allow her hands to be inactive, even though it was Christmas.

Infants arrive with no regard for festive occasions, and an impending birth was anticipated in a destitute home at Glen St. Agnes. Miss Winifred had dispatched a generous meal to that dwelling for its numerous children, intending thereby to consume her own feast with a peaceful mind.
“Well, you know, through his stomach is the way to a man’s heart, Winifred,” Captain Saul explained.

“I believe you—when he HAS a heart,” Miss Winifred retorted. “I suppose that’s the reason so many women kill themselves cooking—just like poor Amelia Baxter did. She passed away last Christmas morning, and she remarked that it was the first Christmas since she got married that she didn’t have to cook a huge, twenty-plate dinner. It must have been a truly pleasant change for her. Well, she’s been dead for a year, so you’ll soon hear about Horace Baxter taking notice.”

“I was told he was already paying attention,” Captain Saul remarked, giving Hugh a wink. “Did he not visit your home on a recent Sunday, dressed in his dark funeral suit and wearing a starched collar?”

“No, he was not. And he does not need to come either. I might have had him a long time back when he was fresh. I do not desire any second-hand goods, believe ME. Regarding Horace Baxter, he was facing financial troubles a year ago last summer, and he asked the Lord for aid; and when his wife passed away and he received her life insurance he stated he believed it answered his prayer. Was that not just like a man?”
“Is there actual evidence that those were his words, Winifred?”

“I have the word of the Methodist minister on it—if THAT constitutes proof. Robert Baxter also recounted the identical story to me, though I concede THAT does not amount to evidence. Telling the truth is not something Robert Baxter is frequently known to do.”
“Now, now, Winifred, I believe he usually speaks truthfully, yet his views shift with such frequency that it occasionally appears as though he were lying.”

“Believe ME, it frequently seems that way. However, you can rely on one male to justify another. Robert Baxter is someone I cannot tolerate. Simply because 'Behold the bridegroom cometh’ was being performed by the Presbyterian choir as an offering selection when he and Margaret proceeded down the aisle the Sabbath following their wedding, he converted to a Methodist. Arriving tardy meant he got what he deserved! He consistently maintained that the choir deliberately performed it to offend him, as though his significance was that great. Nevertheless, that household constantly viewed themselves as far more crucial than they actually were. Eliphalet, his brother, fancied that Satan was perpetually beside him—yet I was never convinced Satan expended that degree of effort on him.”

“I—don’t—know,” Captain Saul remarked reflectively. “Eliphalet Baxter’s existence was overly solitary—he did not possess so much as a cat or dog for humanizing companionship. If a person stays isolated, he is extremely prone to associate with the devil—unless God is his companion. I suppose he must select the company he wishes to maintain. Should the devil have constantly remained at Life Baxter’s side, it was undoubtedly because Life preferred his presence.”
“Resembling a man,” Miss Winifred uttered, then became quiet once more while working on an intricate set of tucks, before Captain Saul intentionally provoked her anew by casually observing:
“I went up to the Methodist church on the previous Sunday morning.”
“It would have been better if you had stayed home and read your Bible,” Miss Winifred retorted.

“Now then, Winifred, I see no injury in attending the Methodist church if there is no sermon at yours. For seventy-six years I have been a Presbyterian, so my theology is hardly going to weigh anchor at this advanced stage.”
“A poor precedent is being established by this,” Miss Winifred remarked with severity.

“Furthermore,” evil Captain Saul kept on, “I desired to listen to some fine singing. A fine choir belongs to the Methodists; and it cannot be denied by you, Winifred, that terrible singing has plagued our church ever since the choir experienced the split.”
“Supposing the vocal performance is lacking? Their efforts are sincere, and the Almighty perceives no distinction between the call of a crow and the song of a nightingale.”
“Now, now, Winifred,” Captain Saul uttered gently, “my faith in the Lord’s musical judgment is higher than THAT.”
“What brought about the disturbance in our choir?” inquired Hugh, who was struggling to contain his laughter.

“It originated with the new church, three years back,” Captain Saul replied. “We experienced a terrible period regarding that church's construction—disagreed about the matter of a new location. A mere two hundred yards separated the two locations, yet you would imagine a thousand lay between them given how bitter the dispute became. We were divided into three groups—a first desired the east location, a second preferred the south, and a third stuck to the former one. The battle occurred in bed and at board, and in church and at market. Every old scandal from three generations was pulled from its grave and exposed. It caused three engagements to be broken off. And those meetings held to attempt a resolution! Winifred, will you ever recall the one where old Luther Burns stood and gave an address? HE stated his opinions forcibly.”

“Be frank, Captain. You are saying he flew into a rage and blasted every single one of them. And they had it coming—they were totally incompetent. Yet what else could come from a group of men? Twenty-seven sessions were conducted by that building committee, and as the twenty-seventh concluded, their progress toward a church was no further along than at the start—actually, it was less, because during a sudden push to speed up the process, they had proceeded to knock the previous church down, leaving us stranded without any church and forced to hold services in the hall.”
“The Methodists offered us their church, Winifred.”

“Had us women not simply stepped up and taken control,” Miss Winifred continued, paying no mind to Captain Saul, “the church at Glen St. Agnes still would not be constructed. We declared that WE intended to possess a church, even if the men intended to dispute until the end of time, and that we had grown weary of serving as a source of amusement for the Methodists. Following a SINGLE meeting, we chose a committee and solicited pledges. And we secured them. Whenever any man attempted to give us backtalk, we reminded him that they had attempted to construct a church for two years, meaning our turn had arrived. You can take MY word for it that we silenced them completely, and our church stood completed in six months. Naturally, once it became clear to the men that our resolve was firm, they ceased their arguing and began working, in typical male fashion, the moment they realized they must either do so or forfeit their leadership. Indeed, women are forbidden from preaching or serving as elders; nevertheless, they are capable of constructing churches and raising the funds required for them.”
“Women are permitted to preach among the Methodists,” Captain Saul said.
The look Miss Winifred directed at him was a glare.
“I did not state that the Methodists lacked common sense, Captain. My point is, I question whether they possess a great deal of religion.”
“I take it that you support female suffrage, Miss Winifred,” Hugh remarked.

“Believe ME, I’m not eager for the right to vote,” Miss Winifred stated with contempt. “I understand the reality of tidying up the mess men leave behind. However, one of these days, as soon as the men recognize they have plunged the world into a predicament beyond their power to fix, they will happily grant us the vote and shift their burdens onto our shoulders. That is THEIR plan. Oh, it is a blessing that women possess patience, believe ME!”
“How about Job?” Captain Saul proposed.

“Job! Discovering a patient person was so unusual that when a real one was found, people made sure he would be remembered,” Miss Winifred countered in triumph. “Either way, that quality is not attached to the name. Old Job Taylor across the harbor was the most impatient man ever brought into the world.”

“Well, as you are aware, he endured a great deal of hardship, Winifred. Her own behavior is indefensible, even by you. The remark made about her by old William MacAllister during her burial remains fresh in my mind, 'There’s nae doot she was a Chreestian wumman, but she had the de’il’s own temper.’”

“I guess she WAS making an effort,” Miss Winifred conceded with hesitation, “however, that was no excuse for Job’s remark upon her death. The day she was buried, he traveled back from the cemetery alongside my father. He kept entirely silent until they approached home. At that point, he let out a deep sigh and stated, 'You may not believe it, Stephen, but this is the happiest day of my life!’ Is that not typical of a man?”
“I guess the late Mrs. Job rendered his existence rather difficult,” Captain Saul pondered.

“Well, decency exists, doesn't it? Though a man may be secretly glad that his wife has died, he doesn't have to announce it to the entire world. And regardless of whether it was a happy day, Job Taylor remarried quickly, as you may have observed. His second spouse knew how to handle him. She certainly made him toe the line! Her initial action was forcing him to bestir himself and erect a gravestone for the original Mrs. Job—and she ensured space remained on it for her name too. She remarked that no one would compel Job to erect a marker for HER.”
“Apropos of Taylors, doctor, what is the word on Mrs. Penrose Taylor over at the Glen?” inquired Captain Saul.
“Although she must labor excessively, her condition is gradually improving,” Hugh answered.

“Her spouse also puts in long hours—breeding champion swine,” Miss Winifred remarked. “His exquisite pigs have made him famous. The pride he takes in his pigs far surpasses the pride he feels for his offspring. However, it must be admitted that his pigs achieve absolute perfection, whereas his offspring are fairly useless. The mother he chose for them was a bad choice, and he deprived her of nourishment during her pregnancies and their upbringing. The richest cream was given to his pigs, while his offspring were left with the watery milk.”

“Winifred, although it causes me pain, there are occasions where I must concur with you,” Captain Saul stated. “You have described Penrose Taylor’s nature precisely. Whenever I look at his unfortunate, pitied children, denied every single thing a child deserves, it poisons my own food and drink for many days following.”
Answering Nell’s gesture, Hugh walked into the kitchen. After closing the door, Nell delivered a marital reprimand to him.
“Hugh, Miss Winifred must no longer be baited by you and Captain Saul. Oh, you have been heard by me—and it simply will not be permitted by me.”
‘Nell, Miss Winifred is having a wonderful time. You are aware that she is.’

“Oh, it does not matter. The pair of you do not have to encourage her in that manner. The meal can be served now, and, Hugh, do NOT permit Mrs. Agatha to cut up the geese. I am aware that she intends to volunteer for the task since she doubts your ability to perform it correctly. Prove to her that you are capable.”

“It is something I should manage, given that I have spent the last month examining A-B-C-D carving diagrams,” Hugh stated. “Just refrain from speaking to me during the process, Nell, because should those letters be forced from my mind, my situation will be even more difficult than yours used to be in those past geometry lessons whenever the instructor altered them.”

The geese were carved beautifully by Hugh, a fact even Mrs. Agatha was forced to acknowledge. Everybody partook of them with great pleasure. Radiant with housewifely pride, Nell saw her initial Christmas dinner turn out to be a resounding success. The banquet was both joyful and lengthy, and upon its conclusion, they assembled near the warmth of the red hearth flame, where Captain Saul recounted stories to them until the red sun dipped low above Seven Gulls Harbor, and the Lombardies cast their long blue shadows over the lane's snow.

“I need to be returning to the lighthouse,” he eventually stated. “I will barely have sufficient time to travel back on foot prior to sunset. I appreciate the lovely Christmas, Mistress Carrow. Have Master Robin come down to the lighthouse one evening before his departure for home.
“Those stone gods are what I want to see,” Robin said eagerly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: The people of Grey Shutters departed for home following Christmas, Thirza having made a binding promise to come back for four weeks during the spring season. Additional snow arrived prior to New Year’s, freezing the harbor completely, yet past the pale, trapped fields, the gulf remained open. A bright, freezing, glaring winter day marked the final day of the old year, striking us with its radiance and forcing us to admire it while failing to win our affection. The sky appeared keen and blue; the snow diamonds glinted relentlessly; the naked trees stood unclad and unashamed, possessing a sort of bold charm; the hills launched attacking spears of crystal. The shadows themselves were precise, rigid, and well-defined, defying the nature of true shadows. Every attractive thing appeared tenfold more attractive and less appealing within the blinding brilliance; every unsightly thing appeared tenfold more unsightly, with all things falling into the category of either attractive or unsightly. No gentle merging, charitable dimness, or subtle haze existed within that probing shine. The firs alone retained their distinct character—since the fir serves as the tree of secrets and gloom, never surrendering to the intrusion of harsh light.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: At last, the day started to recognize her own aging. Thereafter, a particular gloominess settled upon her beauty, dulling it even as it grew more profound; rigid points and shining tips softened into gentle bends and seductive glints. Soft grays and pinks covered the white harbor; amethyst hues stole over the distant hills.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “The departing year is making a lovely exit,” Nell remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: Lorna, Hugh, and she were traveling toward the Seven Gulls Point, having arranged with Captain Saul to observe the New Year's arrival at the lighthouse. Below the horizon the sun had gone, while Venus, magnificent and gilded, rested in the southwestern heavens, having approached her earthly sibling as closely as she can. Nell and Hugh beheld for the very first time the silhouette created by that luminous night star, a delicate, enigmatic shadow that remains invisible unless exposed by pale snow, and even then solely through indirect sight, disappearing the moment one looks at it straight on.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “It resembles the phantom of a shade, doesn’t it?” Nell murmured. “You notice it so clearly hovering beside you while looking forward; yet the moment you turn around to face it—it disappears.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “It has been told to me that the shadow of Venus is visible merely a single time in one's existence, and that the greatest blessing of your existence will arrive within twelve months of beholding it,” Lorna remarked. Yet her words were uttered with a certain sternness; perchance she believed that not even the shadow of Venus was capable of delivering a life's blessing to her. Nell gave a smile in the gentle dusk; she experienced no doubt regarding the nature of the pledge made to her by the mysterious shadow.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: Ambrose Kerr was discovered by them at the lighthouse. Nell initially experienced a desire to be angry about how this long-haired and long-bearded oddity had barged into the accustomed small group. However, it was not long before Ambrose Kerr demonstrated that he had a rightful right to belong among the inhabitants of Joseph's home. Being a clever, sharp, and widely read individual, he equaled Captain Saul himself when it came to the skill of sharing an entertaining tale. Every one of them felt pleased after he consented to join them in seeing the old year through to its end.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: Having traveled down to pass New Year’s alongside his great-uncle, Captain Saul’s young nephew Joe had drifted off to sleep upon the couch, where the First Mate lay asleep at his feet, rolled into a large sphere of gold.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “Isn’t he a sweet small man?” Captain Saul remarked in a gloating manner. “Watching a tiny child sleeping is something I truly cherish, Mistress Carrow. I consider it to be the most gorgeous vision on earth. Spending a night down here is something Joe really loves, since he gets to share my bed. Being forced to share a bed with his two brothers at home is something he dislikes. 'Why am I forbidden from sleeping with father, Uncle Saul?’ he inquires. 'In the Bible, every person slept alongside their fathers.’ Regarding the inquiries he makes, even the clergyman could not provide answers. I am utterly overwhelmed by them. 'Uncle Saul, who would I be if I wasn't ME?’ along with, 'Uncle Saul, what would occur should God perish?’ Prior to drifting off to sleep this evening, he aimed those two questions right at me. Concerning his fancy, it drifts far beyond all limits. He creates the most extraordinary tales—only for his mother to confine him inside the closet on account of his story-telling. Yet he takes a seat and invents a new story, keeping it prepared to tell her upon his release. Tonight when he arrived down here, he possessed one for me. 'Uncle Saul,’ he utters, as grave as a grave marker, 'I experienced an ’venture today in the Glen.’ 'Indeed, what occurred?’ I ask, anticipating a rather shocking tale, though I was in no manner ready for the actual account I received. 'A wolf crossed my path in the street,’ he states, 'an ’normous wolf featuring a giant, red mouf alongside TERRIBLY long teeth, Uncle Saul.’ 'I was unaware of any wolves existing up at the Glen,’ I say. 'Oh, he traveled there from a great distance away,’ Joe claims, 'and I believed he intended to devour me, Uncle Saul.’ 'Did it frighten you?’ I ask. 'No, because a large gun was in my possession,’ Joe replies, 'and I gunned the wolf down until he was dead, Uncle Saul,—entirely dead—after which he ascended into heaven and snapped his teeth at God,’ he asserts. Truly, I was completely astonished, Mistress Carrow.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: By the fire of driftwood, the hours unfolded in joyful laughter. Captain Saul recounted stories, while Ambrose Kerr delivered old Scotch ballads with an excellent tenor voice; ultimately, Captain Saul retrieved his antique brown fiddle off the wall and commenced playing. His fiddling abilities were fairly decent and enjoyed by everyone except the First Mate, who leaped off the sofa like he was shot, uttered a loud cry of objection, and escaped frantically up the stairs.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “It is impossible to develop a musical ear in that cat under any circumstances,” Captain Saul remarked. “His stays are too brief for him to acquire a taste for it. The moment the organist started playing after we had the organ installed in the Glen church, old Elder Richards leaped from his chair and hurried down the aisle and out the church door with extreme speed. Because it made me think so powerfully of the First Mate bolting the instant I start playing the fiddle, I came closer to bursting into laughter in church than I ever have at any other time.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: The lively melodies that Captain Saul performed were so contagious that before long, Ambrose Kerr experienced a twitching in his feet. During his younger years, he had been a famous dancer. Soon he leaped to his feet and extended his hands toward Lorna. She reacted right away. With marvellous, rhythmic elegance, they twirled repeatedly around the room illuminated by the fire. Lorna danced as if moved by a higher power; she appeared to be filled and dominated by the music's untamed, delightful freedom. In mesmerized awe, Nell observed her. Never before had she witnessed her in this state. Every bit of her character's natural depth, vividness, and attractiveness appeared to unbind itself, spilling over in her flushed cheek, shining eye, and fluidity of movement. The sight was not ruined even by the appearance of Ambrose Kerr, who possessed a lengthy beard and hair. Quite the opposite, it appeared to improve the scene. Ambrose Kerr resembled a Viking from ancient times, engaged in a dance alongside a blue-eyed, golden-haired daughter from the Northland.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
