text: “That was the finest dancing I have ever witnessed, though I have viewed a fair share throughout my life,” announced Captain Saul, as his weary hand finally relinquished the bow. Lorna collapsed onto her seat, filled with laughter and out of breath.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “I love dancing,” she whispered to Nell. “I have not taken part in a dance since turning sixteen—and yet I adore it. The melody appears to course through my blood like quicksilver, causing me to lose all memory of everything—everything—save for the joy of moving in rhythm with it. I feel no floor below my feet, no walls around my body, no roof above my head—I am drifting among the stars.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: Captain Saul placed his fiddle back on its hook, which was next to a sizeable frame holding a collection of banknotes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “Do you know anyone else who has the means to decorate his walls with banknotes instead of pictures?” he inquired. “A score of ten-dollar bills are right there, worthless compared to the glass covering them. Those are former Bank of St. Brendan’s Island banknotes. I possessed them when the bank went under, so I got ’em encased in frames and displayed, partly to serve as a caution against trusting banks, and partly to impart a truly lavish, wealthy sensation to me. Hey there, Matey, there is no need to be frightened. It is safe for you to return now. The tunes and merrymaking have concluded for this evening. Only one more hour remains for the old year to remain among us. I have watched seventy-six New Years arrive across that gulf over there, Mistress Carrow.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “A hundred of them will come into view,” remarked Ambrose Kerr.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: A shake of his head came from Captain Saul.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “No; and I have no desire to—or at any rate, I believe I don’t. As we advance in age, death becomes more welcoming. Even so, none of us actually desires to pass away, Ambrose. That was a true statement from Tennyson. Consider old Mrs. Wallace over at the Glen. Throughout her existence, that poor woman has endured immense hardship, and nearly all her loved ones are gone. She constantly claims she will welcome the end when it arrives, having no wish to remain in this vale of tears any longer. Yet whenever illness strikes her, what a commotion ensues! Physicians brought from town, a specialized nurse, and a quantity of medicine sufficient to destroy a dog. While life might indeed be a vale of tears, I suppose certain people find pleasure in crying.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: Sitting near the hearth, they passed the final hour of the old year in silence. Saul, the Captain, stood up and unlatched the door a short while prior to midnight.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “The New Year must be let in by us,” he said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: A splendid blue night reigned outdoors. The gulf was adorned with a shimmering strand of lunar light. Within the establishment, the harbor glittered like a pearl-paved street. Prior to the door, they waited in attendance—Captain Saul possessing his mature, complete expertise, Ambrose Kerr amidst his energetic yet vacant middle age, Hugh and Nell bearing their cherished recollections and delicate aspirations, Lorna burdened by her history of deprived years and her bleak destiny. Twelve was chimed by the clock situated upon the small shelf over the hearth.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 16 NEW YEAR’S EVE AT THE LIGHT
text: “Welcome, New Year,” said Captain Saul, making a deep bow as the final chime faded. “I wish you all the finest year you have ever known, mates. It is my belief that anything the New Year delivers to us will be the finest the Great Captain provides for us—and one way or another every one of us will reach a safe haven.”

Cold weather began intensely following New Year’s Day. Large, pale banks piled up around the small dwelling, and fronds of ice blanketed its glass panes. The ice in the harbor became firmer and denser, to the point that the residents of Seven Gulls commenced their customary winter journeys across it. The secure routes were marked with evergreen branches by a kindly Government, and both day and night the cheerful ringing of the sleigh-bells echoed across the frozen surface. When the moon shone at night, Nell listened to them inside her dwelling of fantasy as if they were magical bells. The gulf turned to ice, and the beam from the Seven Gulls light ceased to shine. Throughout the period in which shipping was halted, Captain Saul’s position required no work.

“My companion, the First Mate, and I have no duties until spring other than staying warm and entertaining ourselves. In the past, the lighthouse keeper routinely relocated to the Glen during the winter months; however, my preference is to remain at the Point. At the Glen, there is a risk that the First Mate could ingest poison or be attacked by dogs. Admittedly, it is somewhat solitary without the light or the water to keep us company, yet provided our friends visit us frequently, we will manage until the season passes.”

Captain Saul owned an ice boat, and with him, Hugh and Nell and Lorna enjoyed numerous wild, glorious spins across the smooth harbor ice. Nell and Lorna also went on long snowshoe tramps together, traversing the fields, crossing the harbor following storms, or trekking through the woods past the Glen. In their walks and their chats by the fireside, they proved to be very good comrades. Both had something to offer the other—both considered life richer because of friendly sharing of thought and friendly silence; both gazed across the white fields separating their homes with a pleasant awareness that a friend was on the other side. Yet, regardless of all this, Nell sensed that a barrier constantly stood between Lorna and herself—a constraint that was never entirely gone.

“I have no idea why it is impossible for me to draw nearer to her,” Nell remarked to Captain Saul one night. “My affection for her is so great—my admiration for her is so deep—it is my DESIRE to welcome her fully into my heart and slip directly into hers. Yet I am utterly unable to pass the boundary.”

“Mistress Carrow, your whole life has contained too much happiness,” Captain Saul remarked in a reflective manner. “That, I believe, explains the inability of you and Lorna to achieve true closeness in your spirits. Her history of grief and hardship forms the obstacle that separates you both. She bears no blame for it, nor do you; yet it remains, impassable to either of you.”

“Prior to my arrival at Grey Shutters, my early years were not particularly joyful,” stated Nell, as she looked quietly through the window toward the quiet, gloomy, lifeless elegance created by the shadows of bare trees casting themselves upon the snow in the light of the moon.

“Perhaps that isn't so—nevertheless, it merely amounted to the customary misery of a youngster lacking somebody to care for them adequately. No TRAGEDY has occurred throughout your existence, Mistress Carrow. Conversely, nearly ALL of poor Lorna’s has consisted of tragedy. I suppose she senses, even if she is scarcely aware of the feeling, that a huge portion of her existence lies beyond your ability to access or comprehend—consequently forcing her to prevent you from reaching it—keeping you at a distance, as it were, to avoid being injured by you. You are aware that whenever we possess a tender spot on ourselves, we flinch away from anybody touching it or coming close. In my opinion, this applies to our spirits just as much as our physical forms. Lorna’s spirit has to be almost raw—so it is hardly surprising that she keeps it concealed.”

“Were that truly everything, Captain Saul, it wouldn’t bother me. It would make sense to me. Yet at certain moments—not continuously, but from time to time—I am nearly forced to think that Lorna doesn’t—doesn’t care for me. On occasion I catch an expression in her eyes that appears to reveal bitterness and aversion—it vanishes so fast—yet I have witnessed it, I am certain of that. And Captain Saul, it causes me pain. Being disliked is not something I am accustomed to—and I have striven so earnestly to gain Lorna’s affection.”

“You have earned it, Mistress Carrow. Do not entertain any silly idea that Lorna does not care for you. Were that the case, she would not interact with you at all, let alone be as friendly with you as she is. I am too familiar with Lorna Vane not to be certain of it.”

“The initial occasion I ever beheld her, herding her geese down the slope on the date I arrived at Seven Gulls, she gazed at me with that identical look,” Nell insisted. “I sensed it, even while I was marveling at her loveliness. She gazed at me with resentment—she truly did, Captain Saul.”

“Mistress Carrow, the ill feeling had to be over a different matter, and you merely received a portion of it since you chanced to walk by. Lorna TRULY has gloomy moods once in a while, the poor girl. Knowing what she is forced to endure, I am unable to fault her. The reason it is allowed is beyond me. Though the doctor and I have held many conversations regarding where evil comes from, we still have not fully uncovered everything about it. Life contains a great deal of incomprehensible matters, does it not, Mistress Carrow? At times events appear to turn out very fittingly, just as it happened for you and the doctor. On the other hand, everything appears to turn completely topsy-turvy. Take Lorna, who is so bright and lovely that one would consider her destined to be a queen, but she is confined over there instead, deprived of nearly every single thing a woman would treasure, possessing no future beyond serving Rufus Vane her entire existence. Mind you, however, Mistress Carrow, I venture to say she would select her present existence, modest as it may be, instead of the existence she endured alongside Rufus prior to his departure. THAT topic is a matter an awkward old sailor’s speech should not touch upon. You have given Lorna great assistance, though—she has become an altered person since your arrival at Seven Gulls. We who are her longtime friends observe the change in her, which you are unable to see. Miss Winifred and I were discussing the matter recently, and it represents one of the extremely few issues where we hold identical views. Therefore, simply discard any notion that she harbors dislike toward you.”

Nell could scarcely ignore it entirely, because there were certainly moments when she sensed, through an intuition that reason could not defeat, that Lorna nursed a strange, unexplainable bitterness toward her. Sometimes, this hidden awareness spoiled the joy of their friendship; other times it was nearly out of mind; yet Nell was constantly aware that the concealed spike remained, ready to pierce her whenever. She received a harsh wound from it the day she informed Lorna about what she anticipated the spring would yield for the little house of dreams. Lorna stared at her with harsh, resentful, hostile eyes.

“So you are to have THAT, too,” she uttered, her voice strangled. Then, not saying another word, she swung around and walked over the fields toward home. Nell was profoundly pained; at that instant, it seemed to her that she could never care for Lorna again. However, when Lorna visited a couple of nights afterward, she behaved in such an agreeable, warm, candid, amusing, and engaging manner that Nell was captivated into pardoning and forgetting. Nevertheless, she did not ever speak of her cherished wish to Lorna again, and Lorna also never brought it up. Even so, one night, when late winter was waiting to hear the call of spring, she walked over to the small house to have a twilight conversation; and as she departed, she deposited a little, white box upon the table. Nell discovered it once she had departed and unsealed it in astonishment. Inside it lay a minuscule white gown of superb craftsmanship—fine embroidery, amazing tucks, pure beauty. Each stitch throughout it had been done by hand, and the small lace ruffles located at the collar and cuffs consisted of genuine Valenciennes. Resting upon it was a card—“with Lorna’s love.”
“She must have spent so many hours working on it,” Nell said. “Plus, the fabric probably cost a lot more than her budget actually allowed. She is so sweet to do this.”
Yet Lorna proved sharp and brief upon receiving Nell’s gratitude, causing the latter to feel once more turned inward.

Lorna’s present was not the only one inside the small home. Miss Winifred had temporarily stopped making clothes for eighth infants who were neither desired nor welcomed, turning instead to stitching for a first child who was eagerly awaited and whose reception would be all that could be wished. A pair of extraordinary garments arrived from Cressida Hale and Isolde Duckett, one from each; while Mrs. Agatha Sowerby dispatched a few, where fine fabrics and sturdy needlework replaced lace and decorative borders. Nell personally crafted a great deal of them, untouched by any mechanical device, devoting to their creation the most joyful moments of that joyful winter.

The small house had no visitor more regular or cherished than Captain Saul. Nell’s affection for the pure-hearted, genuine old mariner grew with each passing day. He possessed the invigorating quality of an ocean wind and the fascination of an old historical text. Listening to his tales never bored her, while his peculiar observations and notes gave her endless pleasure. Captain Saul belonged to that exceptional and captivating group of individuals who “never speak but they say something.” Within his nature, the essence of human compassion and the cunning of the snake blended in captivating measure.
No circumstance appeared capable of unsettling Captain Saul or dampening his spirits in the slightest degree.

“I’ve sort of acquired a pattern of enj’ying things,” he stated one time, after Nell had made a remark about his constant good humor. “It’s become so persistent that I think I even enj’y the unpleasant things. It’s wonderful entertainment believing they are unable to endure. 'Old rheumatiz,’ says I, whenever it clutches me severely, 'you’ve GOT to cease aching eventually. The harsher you are the quicker you’ll cease, perhaps. I am destined to overcome you eventually, either inside the body or outside of the body.’”
Beside the fire at the lighthouse one evening, Captain Saul’s “life-book” was seen by Nell. Requiring no persuasion to display it, he handed it to her to read with pride.

“I composed it for little Joe to inherit,” he remarked. “The thought of all my deeds and sights being entirely forgotten once I embark on my final voyage displeases me. As for Joe, he will keep it in mind and recount the tales to his offspring.”

The volume was bound in aged leather and contained the log of his travels and exploits. Nell considered what a wealth of material it might offer a writer. A valuable insight was contained in each sentence. By itself, the work possessed no artistic value; the captivating narrative ability of Captain Saul deserted him whenever he took up a pen; his famous stories were reduced to roughly scribbled outlines, and he suffered from terribly flawed spelling and grammar. Nevertheless, Nell believed that if an individual with true talent were given that plain account of a courageous, daring existence—interpreting the understated text to uncover the stories of hazards bravely confronted and obligations courageously fulfilled—an extraordinary tale could be crafted from its pages. Deep humor and intense sorrow were both concealed within Captain Saul’s “life-book,” awaiting the skill of a gifted storyteller to evoke the amusement, sorrow, and dread of a vast audience.
Nell mentioned a portion of this to Hugh while the two of them walked toward home.
“Why do you not give it a shot on your own, Nell?”
Nell gave a shake of her head.

“No. Only I wish it were possible for me. But my talent does not encompass it. Hugh, you are aware of my specialty—the imaginative, the whimsical, the attractive. One ought to possess a command of a forceful yet delicate manner of expression, be a sharp psychologist, a natural humorist, and a natural tragedian in order to compose Captain Saul’s biography as it ought to be done. An unusual blend of talents is required. Were Cedric older, he might manage it. In any case, my intention is to request that he travel here next summer to be introduced to Captain Saul.”

“Travel to this coast,” Nell penned in a letter to Cedric. “I fear that Nora, the Golden Lady, or the Twin Sailors cannot be located here by you; nevertheless, a single aged mariner who is able to share marvelous tales will be found by you.”
Cedric, nevertheless, replied in writing, expressing his regret that he would be unable to make the visit that year. His plans involved traveling overseas to pursue two years of study.
“Upon my return, my beloved Teacher, I shall visit Seven Gulls,” was his written message.
“However, in the time that passes, Captain Saul ages,” Nell remarked mournfully, “and no person exists to record the story of his life.”
The March suns caused the harbor ice to turn black and decay; blue waters and a breezy, white-crested gulf returned in April; and the light of Seven Gulls once more adorned the twilights like jewels.

“It brings me such joy to view it again,” Nell remarked, during the initial night that it returned. “During the entire winter, I felt its absence deeply. Without its presence, the sky to the northwest has appeared empty and desolate.”

Extremely young, golden-green foliage imparted a softness to the countryside. Over the trees past the Glen hung a haze of emerald. During the early morning, enchanted vapors filled the glens facing the sea.

Energetic breezes blew back and forth, carrying the spray of salty foam upon their breath. Resembling an attractive, flirty female, the ocean giggled, sparkled, groomed itself, and enticed. Schools of herring gathered, causing the fishing community to rouse itself into activity. White sails heading toward the channel filled the harbor with vitality. Vessels started journeying out to sea and returning back again.
“During a spring day such as this,” Nell remarked, “I am certain of the precise feeling my soul will experience on the morning of resurrection.”

“Occasionally during spring, I kind of get the impression that I could have turned into a poet had I been trained early,” Captain Saul observed. “I discover that I am reviewing ancient rhymes and lines I listened to the schoolmaster declaiming six decades back. During different seasons, they do not bother me. At present, I feel driven to go forth onto the stones or the meadows or the sea and recite them aloud.”

It was during that afternoon that Captain Saul arrived, delivering to Nell some sweet-grass he had gathered while wandering across the sand dunes, along with a quantity of shells intended for her garden.

“It’s becoming truly rare beside this beach these days,” he remarked. “During my childhood there was an abundance of it. However, nowadays you will merely discover a patch occasionally—and at no time when you are searching for it. You simply must chance upon it—you are strolling across the sand dunes, not at all considering sweet-grass—and suddenly a sweet fragrance fills the atmosphere—and the grass is right beneath your steps. I prefer the scent of sweet-grass. It constantly brings my mother to my mind.”
“Was she attached to it?” Nell inquired.

“Not as far as I am aware. I am not sure she ever encountered any sweet-grass. Rather, it is owing to its sort of maternal fragrance—not excessively youthful, you see—something rather mature, healthy, and reliable—exactly like a mother. The schoolmaster’s bride perpetually stored it in her handkerchief drawer. You could place that small bundle with your own, Mistress Carrow. Store-bought perfumes are not to my liking—yet a hint of sweet-grass fits in any place a lady inhabits.”

Nell had felt no great excitement about the prospect of bordering her flower beds using quahog shells; as an embellishment, they failed to attract her initially. However, she refused to wound Captain Saul’s emotions under any circumstances; consequently, she feigned an appreciation she initially lacked, expressing warm gratitude to him. Then, after Captain Saul had boastfully bordered each bed using a ring formed from the large, milk-white shells, Nell discovered, much to her astonishment, that the result pleased her. Upon a lawn in town, or even higher up at the Glen, such things would have felt out of place, yet right here, within the traditional, ocean-bordered garden belonging to the small house of dreams, they BELONGED.
“They TRULY appear lovely,” she remarked with genuine feeling.

“Cowhawks were constantly encircling her flowerbeds, the schoolmaster’s bride’s,” Captain Saul remarked. “Flowers were her true specialty. Her mere LOOK—and touch—LIKE THAT—made them grow at a wild pace. Certain people possess that talent—and I believe you possess it as well, Mistress Carrow.”

“Oh, I am not sure—yet I adore my garden, and working in it brings me great joy. To putter around with green, growing vegetation, observing daily to witness the precious, fresh shoots emerge, feels like assisting in creation, in my opinion. At this moment my garden resembles faith—the evidence of things unseen. But wait a little.”

“Observing those small, shriveled brown seeds and contemplating the rainbows inside them never fails to astonish me,” Captain Saul stated. “As I reflect upon those seeds, believing that our souls will endure in different realms becomes not in the least bit difficult for me. Had you not witnessed the wonder yourself, you could scarcely accept that vitality existed within those minuscule objects—some no larger than specks of dust—to say nothing of fragrance and hue, could you?”

Nell, who was reckoning her remaining days like the silver beads of a rosary, had become unable to make the long journey to the lighthouse or along the Glen road. Nevertheless, Captain Saul and Miss Winifred visited the small house frequently. The delight of Hugh’s and Nell’s lives was Miss Winifred. Following each visit, her remarks caused them to laugh uproariously. Great amusement was provided to anyone listening whenever she and Captain Saul chanced to be at the small house together. A battle of words occurred between them, wherein she launched attacks and he maintained a defense. Nell on one occasion chided the Captain because he baited Miss Winifred.

“Oh, I truly delight in getting her started, Mistress Carrow,” laughed the shameless offender. “Nothing in my existence brings me more entertainment. That tongue she possesses could scorch a rock. And both you and that youthful rascal of a physician derive just as much pleasure from hearing her as I do.”

Captain Saul arrived on a different evening so that he could give Nell a handful of mayflowers. The moist, fragrant air of a spring evening by the sea filled the garden. A white mist like milk lingered at the border of the ocean, touched by the light of a new moon, while stars shone with silver joy above the Glen. The bell from the church on the opposite side of the harbor rang with a dreamy sweetness. Through the twilight, that rich ringing drifted until it combined with the sea's gentle spring murmur. The night's enchantment received its final, perfecting element from Captain Saul’s mayflowers.
“I haven’t noticed any this spring, and I’ve missed them,” said Nell, pressing her face into them.

“They cannot be located near Seven Gulls, but solely within the barrens back behind the Glen up there. I made a short journey today unto the Land-of-nothing-to-do, and searched these out on your behalf. I suppose they are the final ones you will behold this spring, because they are almost finished.”
“You are so considerate and generous, Captain Saul. No one beside you—not even Hugh”—shaking her head toward him—“recalled my constant spring yearning for mayflowers.”

“Furthermore, I had an additional task—I wished to bring a meal of trout back over there to Mr. Stroud. He enjoys one now and then, and doing this is the sole way I can repay him for a favor he previously did me. Remaining there the entire afternoon, I conversed with him. He enjoys conversing with me, despite the fact that he is a very educated man whereas I am merely an uneducated old sailor, since he belongs to that class of people who MUST converse or else suffer misery, and he discovers that listeners are rare in this area. The people of The Glen keep their distance from him owing to their belief that he is an infidel. He is not quite that far gone—I suppose few men are—yet he could be described as a heretic. Heretics are evil, but they are extremely interesting. It is simply that they have become somewhat lost while searching for God, laboring under the belief that He is difficult to locate—which He never is. I suppose most of them stumble their way to Him eventually. I do not suppose that hearing Mr. Stroud’s reasoning is apt to cause me great injury. Mind you, my belief remains what I was taught from childhood to believe. It prevents a great deal of trouble—and beneath everything, God is good. The problem concerning Mr. Stroud is his being just a bit TOO smart. He believes he must act according to his smartness, and that finding a novel path to reach heaven is cleverer than following the ancient route that ordinary, uneducated people travel. However, he will arrive there eventually without doubt, and at that point he will mock his own foolishness.”
“Mr. Stroud started out as a Methodist,” declared Miss Winifred, implying that moving from there to heresy was not a large step for him.
“Winifred, do you know,” Captain Saul remarked with seriousness, “I’ve frequently considered that were I not a Presbyterian, I would belong to the Methodists.”

“Oh, all right,” Miss Winifred admitted, “if being a Presbyterian wasn't what you were, the rest wouldn't be of much importance. Talking about false doctrine brings to my mind, doctor—I returned the volume you borrowed me—that Natural Law in the Spiritual World—I only managed about a third. Sense is something I can read, and nonsense is something I can read, but neither description fits that work.”
“It IS viewed as somewhat heretical by certain people,” Hugh conceded, “however I mentioned that to you prior to your taking it, Miss Winifred.”

“Oh, I wouldn’t have cared about it being heretical. Wickedness is something I can endure, whereas foolishness is something I cannot,” Miss Winifred remarked placidly, giving off the impression that nothing more could possibly be uttered regarding Natural Law.

“On the topic of books, A Mad Love finally finished two weeks back,” Captain Saul observed thoughtfully. “One hundred and three chapters were in it. Once their wedding happened the book ceased immediately, meaning I suppose there were no more troubles for them. Isn’t it truly lovely that things happen like that in books at least, even though nowhere else is that the case?”
“Novels are something I never read,” Miss Winifred remarked. “Captain Saul, have you heard any news about Geordie Russell’s condition today?”
“Yes, I stopped by to visit him as I was heading home. He is recovering well—though he remains mired in a mess of problems, as always, poor chap.
“Granted, he makes the majority of it for his own consumption, yet I imagine that hardly renders it simpler to endure.”
“Miss Winifred remarked that he was a terrible pessimist.”
“Well, no, he isn’t precisely a pessimist, Winifred. He merely just does not ever discover a single thing that satisfies him.”
“And does that not make one a pessimist?”
“No, no. A pessimist is someone who does not ever anticipate discovering something that pleases him. Geordie has not reached THAT point yet.”
“You’d discover a favorable word for Satan himself, Saul Garrick.”
“Well, the tale of the elderly woman who called him persistent has reached your ears. However, Winifred, I possess no favorable words regarding the devil,” no.
“Have you any belief in him whatsoever?” inquired Miss Winifred with gravity.
“In what way can you inquire about that, Winifred, given your knowledge of my strong Presbyterian faith? In what manner would a Presbyterian manage if there were no devil?”
“DO you?” Miss Winifred persisted.
SAUL, the Captain, was abruptly overcome by a serious demeanor.

“I put my faith in what a minister I once listened to termed 'a mighty and malignant and INTELLIGENT power of evil working in the universe,’” he declared with gravity. “I certainly do THAT, Winifred. You may label it the devil, or the 'principle of evil,’ or the Old Scratch, or whichever title pleases you. It EXISTS, and every single infidel and heretic on earth is unable to reason it out of existence, just as they are unable to reason God out of existence. It exists, and it is at work. However, mark my words, Winifred, I am convinced that it will ultimately be defeated.”

“I certainly wish it to be the case,” Miss Winifred remarked with little optimism. “Yet regarding the devil, I feel certain he currently controls Barney Booth. Did you learn about Barney’s most recent behavior?”
“No, what was it?”

“Because he claims the men gazed at her with excessive admiration during her initial time wearing it to church, he went ahead and destroyed his wife’s brand-new, brown broadcloth suit, which set her back twenty-five dollars in Port Marlow. Isn’t that just how a man behaves?”
“Mistress Booth IS very attractive, and brown suits her,” Captain Saul said thoughtfully.

“Does that justify him shoving her new suit inside the kitchen stove? Barney Booth is an envious idiot, and he renders his wife’s existence unhappy. She has wept the entire week over her suit. Oh, Nell, I wish I possessed your writing ability, believe ME. Wouldn’t I criticize a few of the men around here!”

“Every one of those Booths is a bit peculiar,” Captain Saul remarked. “Barney appeared to be the most rational among them until he took a wife, at which point this strange possessive tendency surfaced in his character. As for his brother Daniel, he was perpetually strange.”

“He threw fits every couple of days or thereabouts and refused to leave his bed,” Miss Winifred remarked with delight. “All the farm chores fell on his wife until his fit passed. People sent her notes of sympathy after his death; had I composed a message, it would have offered congratulations instead. Old Abram Booth, their father, was a vile old drunkard. At his wife’s burial, he was intoxicated, staggering around and hiccuping 'I didn’t dri—i—i—nk much but I feel a—a—awfully que—e—e—r.’ Upon his approaching me, I poked him hard in the back using my umbrella, which brought him to his senses until the casket was removed from the home. Yesterday was supposed to be young Johnny Booth’s wedding day, yet the ceremony could not happen since he went and caught the mumps. Is that not just like a man?”
“Poor guy, in what way was he able to avoid contracting the mumps?”

“Were I Kate Sterns, trust ME, I would not be feeling sorry for him. While I am uncertain how he could have avoided catching the mumps, I am CERTAIN that the wedding feast was fully made and that every bit of food will go bad prior to his recovery. What a loss! His time to have the mumps was during his childhood.”
“Come along, Winifred, aren't you being a bit unreasonable, do you think?”

Without deigning to answer, Miss Winifred addressed Tabitha Pratt instead, a stern-visaged, good-natured aged unwed woman from the Glen, who had been employed for a few weeks as a general servant at the small residence. Having gone to the Glen to visit an ill person, Tabitha had only recently come back.
“In what state is poor old Aunt Mandy this evening?” inquired Miss Winifred.
A sigh escaped Tabitha.
“Extremely ill—extremely ill, Winifred. I fear that she will shortly be in heaven, poor creature!”
“Oh, certainly, things aren't quite that terrible!” Miss Winifred cried out in a sympathetic manner.
Captain Saul and Hugh exchanged glances. After that, they abruptly stood up and departed.
“There are moments,” Captain Saul remarked, amid fits, “in which refraining from laughter would be a sin. Those two fine ladies!”

At the start of June, during a time when the sand hills displayed a grand splendor of pink wild roses and apple blossoms enveloped the Glen, Thirza came to the little house along with a black horsehair trunk decorated with brass nails, a chest that had rested untouched in the Grey Shutters garret for fifty years. Tabitha Pratt had spent her few weeks' stay at the little house growing to adore “young Mrs. Doctor,” her name for Nell, with an unreasoning devotion, causing her to view Thirza with a somewhat envious suspicion initially. However, because Thirza refrained from meddling with affairs in the kitchen and displayed no wish to hinder Tabitha's care of young Mrs. Doctor, the loyal servant made peace with her being there, informing her friends in the Glen that Miss Abernethy was a splendid old woman who understood her place.

One night, while the clear vessel of the sky held a crimson brilliance, and the robins were serenading the gilded dusk with joyful songs for the evening stars, an abrupt disturbance occurred in the little house of dreams. Phone calls went out to the Glen, Doctor Dave along with a nurse wearing a white cap arrived in a hurry, Thirza walked back and forth along the garden paths lined with quahog shells, whispering prayers through her clenched lips, and Tabitha remained in the kitchen, her ears stuffed with cotton wool and her apron pulled over her head.
Lorna, who observed the small dwelling up the stream from inside the house, noticed that each of its windows was illuminated, which kept her awake throughout the night.
The night in June was brief, yet to the ones waiting and watching, it felt like forever.

“Oh, will it NEVER end?” Thirza asked; after that, observing the somber expressions of the nurse and Doctor Dave, she did not venture to ask any further questions. Imagine if Nell—yet Thirza was unable to imagine such a thing.

“Never say,” declared Tabitha with ferocity, responding to the torment visible in Thirza’s eyes, “that God would act with such cruelty as to rob us of that sweet lamb when each of us holds her so dear.”
“He has taken other ones who were loved just as much,” Thirza said in a raspy voice.

However, as day broke, the ascending sun tore asunder the fog suspended above the shoal and converted it into rainbows, bringing happiness to the small dwelling. Nell had survived, and a tiny, pale female babe, possessing the large eyes of her mother, reposed next to her. Hugh, whose visage appeared ashen and drawn on account of the night’s suffering, descended to inform Thirza and Tabitha.
“Thank God,” Thirza shuddered.
Rising to her feet, Tabitha removed the cotton wool from her ears.

“Time for breakfast now,” she stated in a brisk manner. “It is my belief that some food and drink will be welcomed by us all. Instruct young Mrs. Doctor to be entirely free of concern—Tabitha is taking charge. Instruct her to occupy her thoughts solely with her infant.”

Hugh offered a somewhat melancholic smile as he departed. Nell, whose pallid countenance was drained by its initiation into suffering, and whose eyes shone with the sacred fervor of maternity, required no prompting to consider her infant. No other thought occupied her mind. Over the course of several hours, she experienced a delight of such unique and refined quality that she pondered whether the heavenly angels might be jealous of her.

“Little Joyce,” she whispered, as Thirza entered to look at the infant. “If she turned out to be a girl, that was the name we intended to give her. There were numerous people after whom we wished to name her; because choosing among them was impossible, we settled on Joyce—shortened, we can refer to her as Joy—Joy—it is so fitting. Oh, Thirza, I believed my previous state was happiness. I realize now that I merely experienced a delightful dream of being happy. THIS is real.”
“Nell, you must not speak—hold off until your strength returns,” Thirza said in a warning tone.
“You are aware of how difficult I find it NOT to speak,” Nell smiled.

Initially she was too feeble and too joyous to perceive that Hugh and the nurse appeared solemn and Thirza appeared grief-stricken. Afterward, as imperceptibly, and chillily, and pitilessly as a sea-fog drifting toward the shore, dread slithered into her heart. For what reason was Hugh not more joyful? For what reason refused he to speak regarding the infant? For what reason refused they to allow her to keep it beside her following that initial divine—joyous hour? Was—was anything amiss?
“Hugh,” Nell entreated in a whisper, “is the baby—doing fine—or not? Speak to me—speak to me.”

Hugh took a great deal of time to turn around; after that, he leaned over Nell and peered into her eyes. Outside the door, listening in terror, Thirza caught a sorrowful, despairing groan, and she ran away to the kitchen where Tabitha was crying.

“Oh, that unfortunate dear—that unfortunate dear! How is it possible for her to endure this, Miss Abernethy? It will be her death, I fear. That baby was all she anticipated and prepared for, bringing her such joy and hope. Is there really no way to help at all, Miss Abernethy?”
“I regret that is not the case, Tabitha. Hugh states that all hope is gone. From the very beginning, he was aware the small creature could not survive.”

“And that child is so adorable,” wept Tabitha. “Never before have I beheld a newborn so pale—normally they are reddish or yellowish. Furthermore, its large eyes unclosed just like a baby several months along. That tiny, tiny creature! Oh, that tragic, youthful Mrs. Doctor!”

When the sun went down, the tiny spirit that had arrived at dawn departed, causing deep grief. Miss Winifred received the small, pale girl from the nurse’s well-meaning yet unfamiliar hands, and she clothed the minuscule, waxy body in the lovely gown Lorna had crafted for the baby. Lorna had requested that she perform this task. Afterwards, she carried the child back and placed it next to the pathetic, crushed, weeping mother.
“The Lord gave and the Lord took back, dearie,” weeping herself, she said. “Blessed be the Lord’s name.”
Afterward she departed, leaving Nell and Hugh by themselves alongside their deceased.

On the following day, a velvet casket, lined with apple-blossoms by Lorna, received the small white Joy, who was then carried to the church’s graveyard on the opposite side of the harbor. Every tiny, lovingly made garment was packed away by Miss Winifred and Thirza, along with the ruffled basket that had been decorated with frills and lace to hold downy-headed, dimpled limbs. There little Joy would never rest, having obtained a narrower, colder bed instead.
“This has proved a terrible letdown for me,” Miss Winifred uttered with a sigh. “I’ve anticipated this child—and I really wished it would be a girl, as well.”
“I can only be glad that Nell did not die,” Thirza said, trembling as she remembered those dark hours when the girl she held dear was hovering on the brink of death.
“Her heart is broken, poor, poor lamb!” said Tabitha.
“I ENVY Nell,” Lorna uttered with sudden fierceness, “and even if she had died, I’d still envy her! For one beautiful day, she was a mother. For THAT, I’d give my life gladly!”
“Lorna, my dear, I would avoid speaking in that manner,” Miss Winifred remarked with disapproval. She worried that Miss Abernethy, in her dignity, would view Lorna as utterly dreadful.

The recovery of Nell took a considerable length of time, rendered painful to her owing to numerous causes. She was deeply irritated by the brightness and warmth of the Seven Gulls realm; nevertheless, during periods of heavy rainfall, her mind conjured images of the water striking relentlessly against that tiny burial plot on the far side of the harbor; and whenever gusts swept about the rooflines, she detected mournful tones within them that she had not previously perceived.

Sympathetic visitors also caused her pain through the good-intentioned cliches they used in an attempt to cloak the starkness of loss. A note sent by Cressy Hale served as another painful blow. Having received news about the child being born, but being unaware that it had died, Cressy sent Nell a letter filled with joyous congratulations that caused her immense suffering.

“Had my infant been with me, I could have shared a joyous laugh about it,” she wept to Thirza. “Yet lacking my child, it feels like nothing short of mindless malice—even as I recognize that Cressy would never willingly cause me pain. Oh, Thirza, I fail to understand how I can EVER regain happiness—EVERY single thing will cause me sorrow for as long as I live.”
“You will be aided by time,” stated Thirza, who was torn apart by compassion yet lacked the ability to convey it except through time-honored clichés.

“It does not appear JUST,” Nell stated in defiance. “Infants come into the world and exist in places where they are unwelcome—where they face neglect—where they are denied any opportunity. I would have adored my child immensely—and nurtured it with such gentleness—and striven to afford her all possibilities for a righteous life. Even so, I was forbidden from retaining her.”
“It was the Lord’s desire, Nell,” Thirza uttered, powerless when facing the mystery of existence—the reason behind unearned suffering. “And young Joy is in a finer place.”

“I can’t believe THAT,” Nell exclaimed with bitterness. Upon observing Thirza’s shocked expression, she continued with passion, “Why ought she to be brought into the world—why ought any person to be brought into the world—if her death makes her better off? I DON’T hold the belief that dying at birth is preferable for a baby over living out its full existence—and loving as well as being loved—and experiencing joy alongside suffering—and completing its duties—and forming a character that endows it with an eternal personality. Furthermore, what makes you certain it aligned with God’s will? It might have simply been an obstruction of His design caused by the Power of Evil. One cannot expect us to accept THAT with resignation.”

“Oh, Nell, do not speak in that manner,” Thirza stated, truly frightened that Nell might be wading into perilous and profound depths. “Understanding is beyond us—yet our faith must remain intact—it is ESSENTIAL to believe that everything happens for the best. I realize it is difficult for you to hold that view at present. Nevertheless, strive to show courage—on account of Hugh. Your condition causes him great anxiety. Your recovery of strength is not progressing as rapidly as it ought to.”

“Oh, I am aware of how extremely self-centered I have been,” Nell uttered with a sigh. “My affection for Hugh is stronger than it has ever been—and I desire to go on living because of him. Yet I feel as though a portion of my being remains interred in that small cemetery by the harbor—and the pain is so intense that I am terrified of existing.”
“Always, the pain will not be this intense, Nell.”
“The idea that the pain might cease at times causes me greater distress than anything else, Thirza.”

“Indeed, I am aware of that, as I have experienced the same feeling regarding different matters. Nevertheless, every one of us holds you dear, Nell. Daily visits have been made by Captain Saul to inquire after your condition—while Mrs. Vane constantly frequents the area—and the majority of her hours, it seems to me, are spent by Miss Tolley preparing delicious food for you. This is not particularly to Tabitha’s liking. Her belief is that her own culinary skills equal those of Miss Tolley.”

“Dearest Tabitha! Oh, Thirza, everyone has shown such fondness and goodness and beauty toward me. I am not without gratitude—and maybe—once this dreadful pain subsides even slightly—I will discover that I am able to continue my life.”

It proved possible for Nell to continue her existence; eventually, a day arrived in which one of Miss Winifred’s remarks caused her to smile once more. Yet contained within that smile was a quality that had previously never existed in Nell’s smile, one that would henceforth remain a permanent part of it.

Hugh brought her down to Seven Gulls Point on the initial day she could manage a drive, leaving her at that location while he made the row across the channel to visit a patient located at the fishing village. Across the dunes and the harbor, a buoyant wind was racing, churning the water up into white-caps and sweeping over the sandshore using lengthy rows of silvery breakers.

“It makes me truly proud to have you back here, Mistress Carrow,” Captain Saul stated. “Have a seat—have a seat. I’m afraid this place is dreadfully dusty today—yet one doesn't need to gaze at dust when such scenery is right there to be seen, does one?”
“The dust doesn’t bother me,” Nell stated, “however, Hugh insists that I remain outdoors. I believe I will head down to those rocks and sit.”
“Do you want someone with you, or do you prefer to be by yourself?”

“Should you be referring to your own presence when you speak of company, I would far prefer it to being by myself,” Nell said, offering a smile. A sigh followed her words. Being by herself had never bothered her in the past. At present, it filled her with dread. These days, whenever she found herself on her own, a terrible sense of isolation consumed her.

“In this pleasant small location, you are protected from the wind,” Captain Saul remarked upon their arrival at the rocks. “This is a place where I frequently sit. Simply sitting and dreaming here is wonderful.”
“Oh—dreams,” Nell let out a sigh. “Captain Saul, I am unable to dream now—dreams are behind me.”

“Oh, no, you’re not, Mistress Carrow—oh, no, you’re not,” Captain Saul remarked thoughtfully. “I understand your current feelings—however, provided you remain alive, joy will return to you, and before you realize it, dreaming will resume—we must express gratitude to the Lord for that! Without the dreams we have, interring us might as well happen. In what way could we endure existence were it not for our immortality dream? Furthermore, Mistress Carrow, that specific dream is CERTAIN to be realized. Some day, your little Joyce will be seen by you again.”

“However, my baby will no longer be mine,” Nell uttered, her lips quivering. “Oh, it is possible she will turn out to be, in the words of Longfellow, 'a fair maiden clothed with celestial grace’—yet she is going to be an unfamiliar person to me.”
“I think God is going to handle things better than THAT,” Captain Saul remarked.
The pair remained quiet for a brief moment. After that, Captain Saul spoke in a very soft voice:
“Mistress Carrow, can I speak to you regarding lost Margaret?”
“Naturally,” Nell softly replied. Though she lacked knowledge of who “lost Margaret” might be, she sensed she was about to be told the story of Captain Saul’s romantic past.
“I’ve frequently wished to speak to you regarding her,” Captain Saul continued.

“Do you know why, Mistress Carrow? It’s because I desire someone to recall and hold her in their thoughts occasionally once I have passed away. I cannot endure the thought that every living person will forget her name. And currently, I am the sole person who still remembers lost Margaret.”

Captain Saul subsequently recounted the tale—a ancient, long-lost narrative, because more than fifty years had elapsed since Margaret had dozed off one afternoon inside her father’s dory and floated—or at least that was the assumption, since her ultimate destiny was never definitely determined—away from the channel, past the bar, to meet her end in the dark thundersquall that had arisen so abruptly on that distant summer afternoon. Yet for Captain Saul, those fifty years seemed like nothing more than yesterday when it has gone.

“Following that event, I spent months pacing the coastline,” he uttered sorrowfully, “hoping to locate her beloved, darling small corpse; yet the ocean failed to return her to me. However, I will locate her eventually, Mistress Carrow—I will locate her eventually. She waits for me. I would like to describe to you precisely how she appeared, yet I am unable to do so. Over the sandbar at dawn, I have observed a delicate, silver fog that resembled her—and on other occasions, I have noticed a white birch tree in those woods back there that reminded me of her. She possessed light, brown locks and a small, fair, lovely visage, alongside long, thin fingers similar to yours, Mistress Carrow, though darker, because she was raised on the coast. At times, I awaken during the night to the ocean summoning me as it used to, and it feels as though missing Margaret were shouting within it. Furthermore, during a tempest when the swells weep and groan, I detect her weeping in their midst. And whenever they giggle on a bright afternoon, it is HER giggle—missing Margaret’s lovely, playful, small giggle. I lost her to the ocean, yet eventually I will locate her. Mistress Carrow. It is impossible for it to separate us eternally.”
“It pleases me that you shared information regarding her with me,” Nell remarked. “I frequently pondered the reason you resided by yourself for your entire existence.”

“I could never love another person. Lost Margaret carried my heart away with her—out there,” declared the elderly lover, who had remained devoted for half a century to the sweetheart he lost to the sea. “You will not care if I speak of her frequently, will you, Mistress Carrow? I find joy in it—since the sorrow vanished from her recollection many years back and simply gave its benediction instead. I am certain you will always remember her, Mistress Carrow. And should the coming years, as I trust they will, grant more young ones to your household, I desire your word that you will recount to THEM the tale of lost Margaret, ensuring her memory does not perish among humanity.”
“Nell,” Lorna uttered, suddenly interrupting a brief lull, “you have no idea how DELIGHTFUL it feels to sit beside you once more—busy at work—and chatting—and sharing quiet moments.”

In Nell’s garden beside the brook, they sat amidst the blue-eyed grasses. Past them, the sparkling water crooned, while dappled shadows were cast over them by the birches, and roses were in bloom along the walks. As the sun started to sink low, the air grew filled with a tapestry of music. A single melody came from the wind in the firs at the back of the house, a different one from the waves upon the bar, and yet another from the far-off bell of the church beside which the tiny, white lady slept. Even though it presently invoked sad thoughts, Nell was fond of that bell.
Her gaze turned attentively to Lorna, who had tossed aside her needlework and uttered her thoughts with a degree of freedom that was highly uncommon for her.

“During that dreadful evening while you were so sick,” Lorna continued, “it occurred to me repeatedly that maybe we would not share any additional conversations, strolls, or WORKS side by side. Then I understood precisely what your companionship had grown to signify to me—exactly what YOU signified—and what an unpleasant little monster I had been.”
“Lorna! Lorna! Calling my friends names is something I never permit anyone to do.”

“That is accurate. What you described is precisely what I am—a despicable small creature. Nell, I HAVE to share something with you. I imagine it will cause you to look down on me, yet I HAVE to admit it. Nell, during certain moments throughout this previous winter and spring, I actually HATED you.”
“I KNEW it,” Nell remarked serenely.
“Did you KNOW it?”
“Indeed, I observed it within your eyes.”
“And still you continued to like me and remain my friend.”
“Indeed, you merely despised me at times, Lorna. In the intervals, I believe your affection was mine.”

“I most assuredly did. Yet that additional dreadful sensation remained constantly present, ruining things, deep within me. I suppressed it—on occasion I did not remember it—yet on other occasions it would rise higher and overcome me. My hatred for you stemmed from my ENVY toward you—oh, at intervals I was utterly consumed with envy of you. You possessed a sweet tiny house—plus affection—plus joy—plus cheerful visions—all the things I desired—yet lacked entirely—and could not possibly attain. Oh, could not possibly attain! THAT served as the source of the pain. I would not have felt envy toward you, provided I possessed any EXPECTATION that my existence would at any point change. Yet I lacked that—I lacked that—and it appeared UNJUST. It caused me to feel defiant—and it inflicted pain on me—and for that reason I detested you at times. Oh, I felt such deep embarrassment about it—I am perishing from embarrassment at present—yet I failed to defeat it.

“During that evening, when I feared you might not survive—I believed I would face retribution for my evil—and my love for you was so strong at that moment. Nell, Nell, since my mother passed away, I had not possessed anything to love, save for the old dog belonging to Rufus—and having no object of affection is terribly awful—existence is incredibly EMPTY—and NOTHING exceeds the misery of emptiness—and my love for you could have been so great—and that awful event had ruined it—”
Lorna shook and became nearly unintelligible as her intense feelings overwhelmed her.
“Please, Lorna,” begged Nell, “oh, please refrain. I comprehend—let’s not speak about it further.”

“I must—I must. Upon learning that your life was saved, I swore to inform you the moment you recovered—that I would cease taking your friendship and company while hiding how little I deserved them. And I have felt such dread—that it might make you despise me.”
“There is no need for you to worry about that, Lorna.”

“Oh, I’m so glad—so glad, Nell.” To stop her brown, work-hardened hands from trembling, Lorna pressed them firmly together. “But now that I’ve started, I want to tell you everything. I don’t suppose you recall when I first laid eyes on you—it wasn't during that night on the beach—”

“No, that occurred the evening Hugh and I arrived back. You were guiding your geese down the slope. I certainly DO recall it! In my eyes, you were incredibly beautiful—for weeks afterward, I yearned to learn who you were.”

“I recognised who YOU were, even though I had never set eyes on either of you previously. News had reached me about the new doctor and his bride who were moving into Miss Russell’s small house. I—I despised you at that precise instant, Nell.”
“I sensed the bitterness in your gaze—subsequently I was uncertain—I believed I had to be wrong—since WHY ought that to be?”

“It was on account of you appearing so cheerful. Oh, now you will concur with me that I TRULY am a spiteful creature—hating a different female simply due to her joy,—and when her joy did not rob me of a thing! That reason accounts for why I did not ever pay you a visit. I was fully aware that I should visit—even the modest traditions of Seven Gulls required it. However, I was unable to. I was accustomed to observing you out of my window—I was able to glimpse you and your spouse walking slowly around your garden during the evening—or you rushing down the poplar lane so as to meet him. And I was pained by it. Even so, in a different manner, I desired to cross over. My feeling was that, were I not this unhappy, I could have been fond of you and discovered within you something I have not ever possessed during my existence—a close, GENUINE friend belonging to my own age group. And after that, do you recall that evening by the shore? You feared that I might deem you out of your mind. You surely believed that I was.”
“No, yet I was unable to comprehend you, Lorna. You pulled me close at one instance—and then you repelled me the next.”

“My spirits were very low that night. My day had been difficult. Rufus was exceedingly—exceedingly troublesome to handle on that occasion. Usually his disposition is rather pleasant and he is simple to manage, as you are aware, Nell. However, on certain days he is extremely different. My heart was so weary—the moment he fell asleep, I fled to the coast. That was my sole sanctuary. I remained there pondering the way my poor father had taken his own life, and asking myself if I might be forced to do the same eventually. Oh, black thoughts completely filled my heart! And just then you arrived, dancing beside the cove like a happy, carefree child. At that moment, I—I despised you to a greater degree than I ever have since. Even so, I longed for your comradeship. One emotion ruled me one instant; the opposite emotion ruled me the next. Upon returning home that evening, I wept from embarrassment over the opinion you must hold of me. Still, it has continuously been the exact same way whenever I visited this place. On occasion I would feel joyful and take pleasure in my call. Yet on different occasions that terrible emotion would ruin everything. There were moments when every single thing concerning you and your home caused me pain. You possessed such a quantity of lovely small items that were out of my reach. Would you believe—it is absurd—yet I felt a particular malice toward those porcelain dogs belonging to you. There were moments when I desired to grab Gog and Magog and smash their saucy black snouts against one another! Oh, you grin, Nell—yet it was not at all amusing to me. I used to come to this place and observe you and Hugh with your literature and your blossoms, and your domestic treasures, and your small private family humors—with your affection for one another evident in every glance and statement, even if you were unaware of it—and I would return home to—you are aware of what I returned home to! Oh, Nell, I do not think I am envious and resentful naturally. Throughout my girlhood I was without numerous items that my classmates possessed, yet I never minded—I never resented them because of it. Nevertheless, I appear to have become so malicious—”

“Lorna, my darling, do not accuse yourself any longer. You possess NO hatred or jealousy or envy. It is possible that the existence you are forced to lead has twisted you slightly—however, a spirit that was not as splendid and honorable as yours would have been destroyed by it. My reason for allowing you to confess all of this to me is my belief that speaking of it and cleansing your spirit will benefit you. However, cease accusing yourself now.”

“Indeed, I will not. It was simply my desire that you understand my true self. Nell, the most terrible moment of all occurred when you shared your dearest wish for the springtime with me. My conduct at that moment is something I will never pardon myself for. My remorse was accompanied by weeping. Furthermore, it is TRUE that I embedded numerous affectionate and fond thoughts of you within the small garment I crafted. However, I should have realized that whatever I created was destined to become merely a burial garment eventually.”
“Now, Lorna, that IS morbid and bitter—cast those ideas aside.

“It made me so happy when you carried over that tiny dress; and given that I was forced to part with little Joyce, I find comfort in knowing that she was clothed in the very garment you crafted for her at the moment you permitted yourself to care for me.”

“Nell, do you know, I think I will always care for you from now on. I do not believe I will ever experience that terrible feeling toward you any more. Discussing everything fully appears to have removed it, in a way. It is so odd—and I considered it so genuine and severe. It resembles unlocking a dark room's door to reveal a terrifying beast you thought was inside—and once the illumination pours in, your creature proves to be merely a shade, disappearing as the brightness arrives. It will never separate us again.”
“No, Lorna, we have become true friends now, and it makes me extremely happy.”

“I trust you will not misinterpret me should I add another thought. Nell, I suffered deep sorrow in my innermost heart when your baby was taken from you; and had it been possible to preserve her life for you by severing one of my hands, I would gladly have performed the act. Nevertheless, your grief has drawn us nearer to one another. The perfection of your happiness no longer stands as an obstacle. Oh, do not misinterpret me, my dearest—I am NOT joyful that your happiness has ceased to be complete—I can speak those words in all honesty; yet because it has changed, the chasm separating us is no longer so vast.”

“I REALLY comprehend that as well, Lorna. Now, we will simply seal away the past and erase whatever was disagreeable within it. Everything is about to change. Both of us belong to the race of Joseph now. I believe you have been remarkable—remarkable. And, Lorna, I am unable to refrain from trusting that life still holds something favorable and lovely in store for you.”
Lorna gave a shake of her head.

“No,” she uttered listlessly. “There is no hope at all. Rufus will not ever improve—and should he actually regain his memory—oh, Nell, things would turn out worse, still worse, than what we have at present. You are unable to comprehend this, you joyful bride. Nell, did Miss Winifred at any time inform you about the way I arrived at marrying Rufus?”
“Yes.”

“It makes me happy—I wished for you to be aware—yet I was unable to speak about it had you been unaware. Nell, it appears to me as though life has held bitterness ever since I reached twelve. Prior to then my childhood was full of happiness. Our poverty was great—nevertheless it bothered us not. Father possessed such splendor—he was extraordinarily intelligent, affectionate, and understanding. We had been close companions for as long as my memory extends. Furthermore, mother had such sweetness. Her beauty was truly immense. I resemble her, though my beauty falls short of hers.”
“According to Miss Winifred, you are much more beautiful.”

“She is wrong—or biased. I believe my own body IS superior—mother was frail and stooped from strenuous labor—yet her face resembled that of an angel. I would simply gaze up at her with devotion. Every one of us adored her,—father and Julian and I.”

It was recalled by Nell that a contrasting idea regarding Lorna’s mother had been conveyed to her by Miss Winifred. Yet, was the clearer sight not possessed by love? Even so, forcing her daughter into a marriage with Rufus Vane was indeed selfish on the part of Rose Ainslie.
“Julian was my brother,” Lorna continued. “Oh, I cannot express how much I loved him. And his life was taken in a cruel way. Do you know in what manner?”
“Yes.”

“Nell, his tiny face was visible to me when he was run over by the wheel. On his back, he fell. Nell—Nell—it is present to my mind right now. My eyes will never stop seeing it. Nell, my sole plea to heaven is for the erasure of that memory from my mind. O my God!”
“Lorna, do not mention it. I am aware of the tale—avoid delving into particulars that merely torment your mind to no purpose. It SHALL be erased.”
It took a moment of effort before Lorna recovered some degree of composure.
“Afterward, my father’s physical condition deteriorated and his spirits sank—he lost his mental equilibrium—have you also been told all of those details?”
“Yes.”

“Following that, mother was the sole reason I had left to go on living. However, my ambition was immense. My intention was to work as a teacher and pay my own tuition through college. My plan was to scale the utmost heights—oh, I shall refrain from discussing that as well. It serves no purpose. What transpired is known to you. I was unable to bear the sight of my precious, grief-stricken mother, who had spent her entire existence in toil, being evicted from her residence. Naturally, I possessed the ability to make a sufficient living for the two of us. Nevertheless, mother was INCAPABLE of departing from her home. It was there that she arrived as a bride—and her affection for father was so deep—and every one of her memories resided in that place. Still, Nell, whenever I reflect on the fact that I rendered her final year joyful, I feel no regret regarding my actions. Concerning Rufus—my sentiment toward him at the time of our marriage was not hatred—I merely harbored toward him the same unconcerned, pleasant regard I held for the majority of my fellow students. It was to my knowledge that he consumed alcohol to some degree—yet the tale regarding the young woman down at the fishing cove had never reached my ears. Had I known it, marrying him would have been IMPOSSIBLE for me, even for the sake of my mother. Subsequently—I TRULY came to despise him—however, mother remained unaware. Her life ended—and at that point I found myself completely solitary. My age was merely seventeen and I found myself completely solitary. Rufus had departed aboard the Four Sisters. My wish was that his presence at home would not occur very frequently in the future. A passion for the sea had continuously run in his veins. No other expectation remained for me. Indeed, Captain Saul carried him back home, as is known to you—and there remains nothing further to state. The truth about me is now clear to you, Nell—the most terrible aspects of me—every obstacle has been removed. And is it still your desire to be my friend?”
Nell gazed upward amidst the birch trees toward a half moon, resembling a white paper lantern, as it descended into the sunset's gulf. Her expression was exceedingly sweet.

“I am your friend and you are mine, forever,” she said. “A friend like I have never possessed until now. I have possessed numerous cherished and adored friends—yet there exists a certain quality in you, Lorna, which I failed to discover in any other person. You possess greater abundance to provide me from that wealthy essence of yours, and I possess greater abundance to yield to you than I possessed during my heedless youth. We are two women—and friends for eternity.”
Hand in hand, they shared a smile as tears welled up in both the blue eyes and the gray.
Hugh demanded that Tabitha ought to remain employed at the small dwelling throughout the summer months. At the outset, Nell objected.

“Being in this place with merely you and me is wonderful, Hugh. Having another person around ruins it somewhat. Although Tabitha is a lovely person, she remains a stranger. Performing the chores in this house will not harm me.”

“You have to follow what your doctor recommends,” Hugh said. “A well-known adage states that wives of shoemakers walk without shoes and wives of doctors pass away early. I refuse to let that happen in my home. Tabitha stays with you until your stride regains its former bounce, and the slight depressions in your cheeks flesh out.”

“Just relax now, Mrs. Doctor, my dear,” Tabitha stated as she entered suddenly. “Enjoy yourself and refrain from stressing over the kitchen supplies. The steering is in Tabitha’s hands. Owning a dog is pointless if you bark yourself. Each morning, I will bring breakfast up to your room.”

“You certainly are not,” Nell chuckled. “It seems disgraceful to me, as it does to Miss Winifred, when a healthy woman has her morning meal in bed, which nearly excuses whatever outrageous things men might do.”

“Oh, Winifred!” Tabitha uttered, showing boundless scorn. “Mrs. Doctor, dear, I believe your judgment is too good for you to pay attention to the words of Winifred Tolley. Even though she has remained unmarried, I fail to understand why it is necessary for her to constantly criticize men. An old maid I may be, yet you do not catch ME speaking ill of men. They suit me fine. Had the opportunity arisen, I would gladly have wed one. Mrs. Doctor, dear, isn't it peculiar that not a single man ever proposed marriage to me? Although I lack exceptional beauty, my appearance matches that of the majority of wives around us. Yet no man ever courted me. Why do you imagine that was?”
“It could be predestination,” Nell offered, displaying a eerie gravity.
Tabitha gave a nod.

“I have frequently held that same opinion, Mrs. Doctor, dear, which provides immense solace. Should the Almighty have ordained it for His own sagacious reasons, I care not that no one desires me. Yet at times, Mrs. Doctor, dear, uncertainty enters my mind, causing me to question whether the Old Scratch might be primarily responsible instead. Under THOSE circumstances, I am unable to accept my fate. Nevertheless,” Tabitha continued with renewed cheer, “an opportunity for me to wed may still arise. My thoughts frequently return to the ancient stanza my aunt was accustomed to reciting:
No goose ever existed that was so gray that, sooner or later, some honest gander did not come along and take her to be his mate!

A woman can never truly be certain she will avoid marriage until she is in her grave, Mrs. Doctor, dear, and in the meantime I shall bake a batch of cherry pies. I have observed that the doctor prefers them, and I REALLY enjoy preparing food for a man who values his meals.”
Arriving that afternoon, Miss Winifred was slightly out of breath when she paid a visit.

“The world or the devil do not concern me greatly, though the flesh TRULY causes me trouble,” she confessed. “Nell, my dear, you constantly appear as cool as a cucumber. Is that cherry pie I smell? Should that be the case, invite me to remain for tea. Not a single cherry pie has passed my lips this summer. Those Gilman boys, scamps from the Glen, have taken every one of my cherries.”

“Come, come, Winifred,” protested Captain Saul, who was sitting in a corner of the living room absorbed in a sea novel, “it isn’t right to speak like that regarding those two unfortunate, motherless Gilman boys, unless you possess positive evidence. Simply because their father lacks honesty doesn’t justify labeling them as thieves. Your cherries were probably taken by the robins instead. Their numbers are turrible high this year.”
“Robins!” Miss Winifred declared with contempt. “Humph! Believe ME, they are two-legged robins!”
“Indeed, the majority of the Seven Gulls robins ARE built according to that design,” Captain Saul remarked with seriousness.
For a moment, Miss Winifred gazed at him. Afterwards, reclining in her rocking chair, she chuckled heartily for a long time.

“Indeed, you HAVE bested me this time, Saul Garrick, I must confess. Observe his delight, Nell, my love, smirking like a Chessy-cat. Regarding those robins’ legs if robins possess huge, exposed, sun-browned legs, featuring torn pants dangling from them, like the ones I spotted high in my cherry tree a week ago one morning at dawn, then I will apologize to the Gilman boys. When I reached the ground, they had vanished. Their swift departure was a mystery to me, but Captain Saul has clarified the matter. Naturally, they flew off.”
Captain Saul chuckled and departed, sorrowfully turning down an offer to remain for the evening meal and enjoy some cherry pie.

“I am going to visit Lorna to inquire whether she would accept a paying guest,” Miss Winifred continued. “Yesterday, a letter reached me from a Mrs. Daly living in Toronto, who stayed as a boarder with me briefly two years past. She requested that I accommodate a friend of hers during the summer. Adrian Treleaven is his name, and he works as a journalist, and it appears he is the grandson of the schoolmaster by whom this house was erected. The eldest daughter of John Tremayne was wedded to an Ontario resident called Treleaven, and he is her child. He wishes to view the ancient homestead where his grandparents resided. A severe attack of typhoid afflicted him during the spring from which he has not fully recovered, so he was instructed by his physician to go to the ocean. Going to the hotel does not appeal to him—a peaceful domestic environment is all he desires. Taking him in is impossible for me, because I must be absent throughout August. My appointment as a delegate to the W.F.M.S. conference in Portmaris has occurred and I am attending it. Whether Lorna will care to take the trouble of accommodating him is also unknown to me, but no other option exists. Should she be unable to accept him, he will be obliged to go across the harbor.”

“After you have watched her return and assist us in consuming our cherry pies,” Nell said. “Have Lorna and Rufus come as well, if they are able. And you are traveling to Portmaris, then? You are going to have such a lovely time. I need to hand you a note for an acquaintance of mine who lives there—Mrs. Ezra Hale.”

“Mrs. Thomas Holt was persuaded by me to accompany me,” Miss Winifred stated self-satisfiedly. “In MY opinion, a brief vacation for her is overdue. Her labor has nearly driven her into the grave. A beautiful job of crocheting can be done by Tom Holt, yet providing for his household is beyond him. The time he rises never appears early enough for accomplishing any labor, whereas rising early for a fishing trip is something I observe he manages without fail. Is that not typical of a man?”

Nell beamed. She had gotten used to heavily discounting Miss Winifred’s views regarding the men of Seven Gulls. If she did not, she would have been forced to view them as the most irredeemable collection of scoundrels and good-for-nothings anywhere, whose spouses were absolute slaves and sufferers. For instance, she recognized this specific Tom Holt as a gentle husband, a deeply cherished father, and an outstanding neighbor. Though he leaned toward laziness, preferring the fishing into which he was born over the agriculture he was not, and possessed an inoffensive quirk for doing fancy work, no one except Miss Winifred appeared to resent him for it. His spouse was a “hustler,” who took pride in hustling; his household derived a cozy livelihood from their land; and his sturdy sons and daughters, having received their mother’s vigor, were all well on their way to succeeding in life. Within Glen St. Agnes, no family was contented beyond the Holts’.
Miss Winifred came back from the house up the brook, feeling satisfied.

“Lorna is taking him,” she declared. “The opportunity was seized by her eagerly. To pay for shingling her house’s roof this autumn, she needed to earn a bit of money, though the means had eluded her. Captain Saul will likely be exceedingly intrigued upon learning that a grandson belonging to the Selwyns is arriving at this place. A message from Lorna for you was to state that she craved cherry pie, yet tea was impossible since her turkeys required searching out by her. Wandered off, they have. However, she mentioned that should a slice remain, you ought to place it inside the pantry so she could hurry over during the cat’s light, when prowling is appropriate, to retrieve it. What comfort my heart experienced, Nell, dearie, upon listening to Lorna dispatching such a message to you, chuckling in her former manner from long past, is unknown to you.
“She has altered considerably of late. Her laughter and jesting resemble those of a young girl, and based on what she says, I deduce she visits this place quite frequently.”

“Each day—otherwise I go to her house,” Nell stated. “Without Lorna, I am unsure how I would manage, particularly at this moment with Hugh being extremely occupied. He is rarely at the house save for a couple of hours during the early morning. Truly, he is exhausting himself with work. A great number of the residents from across the harbor request his services at present.”

“It would be preferable for them to remain satisfied with their own physician,” Miss Winifred remarked. “However, I certainly cannot fault them, given that he is a Methodist. Since the time Dr. Carrow successfully treated Mrs. Allonby, people hold the opinion that he possesses the ability to resurrect the dead. In my view, Dr. Dave exhibits a touch of envy—in typical male fashion. His belief is that Dr. Carrow relies excessively on modern ideas! 'Well,’ I remarked to him, 'a modern idea was precisely what spared Rhoda Allonby. Had YOU been caring for her, she would be dead, marked by a gravestone declaring that it pleased the Almighty to remove her.’ Ah, I truly enjoy expressing my thoughts openly to Dr. Dave! Having ruled the Glen for many years, he believes his forgotten knowledge exceeds everything others have ever learned. On the subject of physicians, I desire that Dr. Carrow would visit and examine the boil located on the neck of Rufus Vane. Lorna’s ability is no longer sufficient to handle it. I certainly cannot comprehend why Rufus Vane must begin developing boils—as though he failed to cause adequate difficulty without them!”
“Rufus has developed a real liking for me, you know,” Nell stated. “He trails behind me such as a dog would, and when I pay attention to him, he smiles like a happy child.”
“Are you made unsettling by it?”
“By no means. Poor Rufus Vane is actually quite to my liking. Somehow, he appears so pathetic and engaging.”

“Trust ME, you would not consider him to be very attractive if you were to see him on the days he is ill-tempered. However, I am happy that he does not bother you—it makes things so much better for Lorna. Her duties will increase once her boarder arrives. My hope is that he proves to be a respectable person. You will likely find him appealing—his profession is writing.”

“I am curious as to why it is so widely assumed that two people will find each other immensely compatible simply because they are both writers,” Nell remarked, somewhat contemptuously. “No one would anticipate that a pair of blacksmiths would draw each other irresistibly for the sole reason that both shared the same trade.”

Even so, she awaited the arrival of Adrian Treleaven with a delightful feeling of anticipation. Should he turn out to be young and agreeable, he could become an exceedingly welcome enhancement to the social life of Seven Gulls. The door of the small residence was perpetually unlatched for those belonging to the lineage of Joseph.
A certain evening, Miss Winifred made a phone call down to Nell.

“That author chap has just gotten in. My plan is to chauffeur him over to where you are, which will allow you to direct him across to Lorna’s house. Taking that path cuts down the distance compared to taking the alternate route, plus I am in an extreme rush. Over at the Glen, the Coyle baby went and tumbled headfirst into a bucket filled with boiling water, ending up almost scalded to death, so my presence is requested immediately—to grow a fresh layer of skin on the infant, I imagine. Mrs. Coyle acts so negligently all the time, only to anticipate that everyone else will fix her errors. This won't bother you, will it, sweetheart? The luggage he brought can be brought down the next day.”
“All right,” Nell stated. “How would you describe him, Miss Winifred?”

“Once I bring him out, you will observe his exterior nature. Regarding his interior self, that is known solely to the Lord who created him. I refuse to speak anything further, because all the receivers throughout the Glen are out of order.”

“Miss Winifred clearly cannot discover many flaws in the appearance of Mr. Treleaven, or despite the receivers she would discover them,” Nell remarked. “Consequently, Tabitha, I infer that Mr. Treleaven is good-looking rather than the reverse.”
