“Indeed, Mrs. Doctor, my dear, observing a handsome male brings me great pleasure,” Tabitha admitted openly. “Should I prepare a bit of food for him? A strawberry pie is available that is exceptionally tender.”

“No, Lorna expects him and already prepared his supper. Furthermore, I desire that strawberry pie for my own poor husband. He will not arrive home until a late hour, so set aside the pie and a glass of milk for him, Tabitha.”

“I certainly shall, Mrs. Doctor, dear. Tabitha is in control. Indeed, offering pie to your own people is preferable to giving it to unfamiliar folk, who might merely be trying to consume everything, and the doctor himself is as handsome an individual as one frequently encounters.”

Upon the arrival of Adrian Treleaven, Nell privately acknowledged, while Miss Winifred escorted him inside, that he was truly quite “well-looking”. He possessed a tall, broad-shouldered frame, complemented by dense brown hair, a sharp nose and chin, alongside expansive, luminous dark-gray eyes.

“Did you observe his teeth and his ears as well, Mrs. Doctor, dear?” Tabitha asked subsequently. “His ears have the most pleasing shape I have ever seen on any man. I am particular regarding ears. In my youth, I was terrified that I would be forced to wed a man possessing ears that resembled flaps. However, there was no reason for my anxiety, because I was never given an opportunity with a man having any type of ears.”

Although Nell failed to observe Adrian Treleaven’s ears, his teeth became visible to her when his lips separated in a candid, amiable smile. When he was not smiling, his countenance appeared somewhat sorrowful and distracted, resembling the somber, enigmatic protagonist of Nell’s former fantasies; however, laughter, wit, and attractiveness illuminated his features when he grinned. Indeed, externally, just as Miss Winifred remarked, Adrian Treleaven was a most attractive man.

“You cannot realize how delighted I am to be here, Mrs. Carrow,” he said, casting his gaze about with enthusiastic, curious eyes. “I have a strange sensation of returning home. As you know, my mother was born here and passed her youth here. She was accustomed to speak to me at great length about her former home. I am as familiar with its layout as with that of the place where I resided, and, naturally, she recounted to me the tale of the dwelling’s construction, along with my grandfather’s desperate vigil for the Royal William. I had assumed that a home so ancient would have disappeared long ago, otherwise I would have traveled to view it prior to now.”

“Along this bewitched shoreline, ancient homes fail to disappear with ease,” Nell stated with a smile. “A ‘land where all things always seem the same’ is what this place is—or almost always, anyway. The residence of John Tremayne has barely undergone any alterations, and right now, the rose-bushes that were planted by your grandfather for his bride are flowering outdoors.”
“That idea connects me to those people! With your permission, I need to check out the entire location before long.”

“You will always be welcome to visit us,” Nell pledged. “And are you aware that the former sea captain running the Seven Gulls lighthouse was acquainted with John Tremayne and his bride when he was young? He recounted their history to me on the evening I arrived at this place—the old house's third bride.”
“Is that even conceivable? This truly CONSTITUTES a find. I have to track him down.”

“It will not be hard; every one of us is an old friend of Captain Saul. His eagerness to meet you will match your own desire to meet him. In his mind, your grandmother glimmers like a star. However, it seems to me that Mrs. Vane awaits your arrival. I am going to point out our 'cross-lots’ path to you.”

Nell accompanied him to the home up the stream, crossing a pasture that held a snow-like whiteness from its daisies. A group of individuals in a boat sang far on the other side of the harbor. The audio floated across the water resembling soft, celestial melodies carried by the breeze over a sea beneath the stars. The large light shone and signaled. Adrian Treleaven surveyed his surroundings with contentment.

“So Seven Gulls is finally here,” he remarked. “Mother praised it so much, yet I was not expecting to encounter such immense beauty. The colors are so striking, the landscape so stunning, and the overall charm so delightful! My strength will surely return to me like a horse’s before long. Furthermore, if beauty serves as a spark for inspiration, this location will undoubtedly enable me to commence writing my major Canadian novel.”
“It hasn’t been started by you yet?” Nell inquired.

“Ah me, no. The correct core concept for it has always eluded me. It hides past my reach—it entices—and signals—and withdraws—I nearly hold it and it vanishes. It may be that surrounded by such tranquility and beauty, I will manage to seize it. I am told by Miss Tolley that you are a writer.”

“Oh, I write small pieces for young people. Since my marriage, I haven’t accomplished a great deal. Furthermore—a grand Canadian novel is not something I plan to attempt,” Nell chuckled. “Such a task is far past my abilities.”
Adrian Treleaven was also laughing.

“I suppose it surpasses my ability too. Even so, I intend to make an attempt at it eventually, provided I can find the time. An individual who works for a newspaper rarely gets an opportunity for that type of work. I have composed quite a few short stories for various magazines, yet I have lacked the free time that appears required to produce a book. However, given a three-month period of freedom, I should begin—if I were merely able to obtain the required theme for it—the SOUL of the work.”

A thought flashed across Nell’s mind so abruptly that it caused her to leap. Nevertheless, she kept it to herself, because the Vane residence had been reached. Just as they came into the yard, Lorna emerged onto the porch via the side entryway, squinting into the darkness to spot her anticipated visitor. The illuminated doorway cast a bath of golden radiance directly upon the spot where she paused. A simple outfit made of inexpensive, cream-colored cotton voile was what she had on, accompanied by her customary belt of crimson. Lorna was never seen lacking her splash of crimson. She had explained to Nell that contentment eluded her unless a spark of red adorned her somewhere, even if it was merely a single blossom. For Nell, this consistently appeared to signify Lorna’s vibrant, restrained character, which was refused any outlet except through that vivid flash. The neckline of Lorna’s dress was slightly lowered, and its sleeves were short. Ivory-colored marble seemed to shimmer in the form of her arms. Set against the illumination, every lovely contour of her figure stood out in gentle shadow. The light caused her hair to glisten like fire. Past her stretched a violet sky, blooming with stars above the harbor.
Nell listened as her partner let out a sharp breath. The shock and wonder filling his features remained visible to her, despite the gathering gloom.
“Which person is that stunning individual?” he inquired.
“Mrs. Vane is that lady,” Nell remarked. “She possesses great beauty, doesn’t she?”

“I—I have never witnessed anyone quite like her,” he replied, somewhat bewilderedly. “I was not ready—I had not anticipated—good lord, a person DOES NOT anticipate a goddess as a landlady! Really, were she dressed in a sea-purple robe, holding a string of amethysts within her hair, she would truly be a genuine sea-queen. And she accepts boarders!”

“All goddesses still have to survive,” Nell remarked. “Besides, Lorna is no goddess. She is simply an exceptionally lovely woman, every bit as human as we are. Has Miss Tolley informed you concerning Mr. Vane?”

“Yes,—he is lacking in his intellect, or some such thing, is he not? However, she mentioned nothing concerning Mrs. Vane, so I assumed she would be the typical bustling rural homemaker who accommodates guests to make a decent living.”

“Indeed, Lorna is engaged in that very action,” Nell stated sharply. “Furthermore, the situation is not entirely enjoyable for her, either. I trust Rufus will not bother you. Should he do so, kindly refrain from showing it to Lorna. Her feelings would be terribly injured. He is merely an oversized infant, and on occasion a somewhat vexing one.”
“Oh, I will not pay attention to him. I do not think I will spend much time inside the dwelling anyway, save to eat. Even so, what a pity the whole situation is! She must have a difficult existence.”
“That is correct. Nevertheless, she dislikes being felt sorry for.”

Lorna had returned inside the residence, and she now encountered them at the main entrance. She welcomed Adrian Treleaven with chilly politeness, informing him in a matter-of-fact voice that his chamber and his evening meal had been prepared for his arrival. Rufus, wearing a delighted smirk, shuffled up the stairs carrying the traveling bag, and Adrian Treleaven was settled as a resident of the ancient dwelling amid the willows.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “A small brown cocoon of an idea is in my possession, one that might perhaps grow into a grand moth of realization,” Nell remarked to Hugh upon her arrival at the house. He had come back sooner than she anticipated, and was relishing a piece of Tabitha’s cherry pie. Tabitha was waiting nearby, resembling a somewhat severe yet kindly protective angel, deriving just as much joy from seeing Hugh consume the pie as he experienced while consuming it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: When the next evening arrived, Adrian Treleaven brought a message from Lorna to Nell; after spending the hours of sunset in the garden, they took the small vessel Hugh had prepared for summer trips out on the harbor for a sail under the moon. Their liking for Adrian was immense, and they experienced that sense of long acquaintance that marks the kinship of the house of Joseph. “He is as nice as his ears, Mrs. Doctor, dear,” Tabitha remarked after his departure. He had informed Tabitha that her strawberry shortcake surpassed anything he had previously eaten, winning over Tabitha’s impressionable heart for eternity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “There is a way about him,” she mused while tidying away the remains of the meal. “That he remains unmarried is truly strange, because a person of his sort could win anyone just by asking. Well, perhaps he resembles me and has hitherto failed to encounter his proper match.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: As she cleaned the dishes from the evening meal, Tabitha truly became rather imaginative in her thoughts.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: When two nights had passed, Nell brought Adrian Treleaven along to Seven Gulls Point so he could be introduced to Captain Saul. The western wind was turning the clover fields pale beside the harbor shore, while Captain Saul had put one of his most splendid sunsets on display. He had only recently come back from a voyage across the harbor.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “It fell to me to visit Henry Pollack and inform him that his end was near. No one else possessed the courage to break the news. A terrible reaction was anticipated from him, given his desperate determination to survive and his extensive preparations for the autumn. It was his wife's belief that he should be informed and that I was the most suitable person to impart the truth about his fatal condition. Henry and I share a long friendship—we crewed the Gray Gull together over many years. So, I traveled there and took a chair beside Henry’s mattress, and I spoke to him, saying I, directly and without fuss, because when news must be shared it is best delivered immediately, saying I, 'Mate, I reckon you’ve got your sailing orders this time,’ I was trembling somewhat internally, since delivering news of impending death to someone completely unaware of it is a fearful duty. Yet to my amazement, Mistress Carrow, Henry gazes at me, his shriveled face featuring those luminous, ancient dark eyes, and he speaks, saying he, 'Tell me something I don’t know, Saul Garrick, if you want to give me information. I’ve known THAT for a week.’ Speechless from shock, I watched as Henry gave a quiet laugh. 'To see you coming in here,’ saying he, 'with your face as solemn as a tombstone and sitting down there with your hands clasped over your stomach, and passing me out a blue-mouldy old item of news like that! It’d make a cat laugh, Saul Garrick,’ saying he. 'Who told you?’ saying I, foolishly. 'Nobody,’ saying he. 'A week ago Tuesday night I was lying here awake—and I jest knew. I’d suspicioned it before, but then I KNEW. I’ve been keeping up for the wife’s sake. And I’d LIKE to have got that barn built, for Eben’ll never get it right. But anyhow, now that you’ve eased your mind, Saul, put on a smile and tell me something interesting,’ Indeed, that was the situation. Everyone had been terrified of informing him, yet he was aware the whole duration. It is remarkable how nature cares for us, isn't it, and reveals what we ought to understand when the moment arrives? Have I ever related the story to you concerning the time Henry caught a fish hook in his nose, Mistress Carrow?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “No.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Well, he and I shared a laugh about it today. Almost thirty years ago, it took place. A group of us, including him and me, went out mackerel fishing one day. The day was wonderful—a school of mackerel that large was something I had never seen in the gulf—and as everyone grew excited, Henry became very reckless and managed to plunge a fish hook straight through a side of his nose. Well, that was his situation; a barb was on one end and a large lead piece was on the other, meaning pulling it out was impossible. Taking him to shore right away was our wish, but Henry showed pluck; he declared he’d be jiggered if he’d abandon such a school for anything less than lockjaw; after that he continued fishing, pulling them in rapidly while groaning in between. Eventually the school moved on and we returned with a full catch; acquiring a file, I started trying to file through the hook. My intention was to be as gentle as possible, but hearing Henry was an experience you should have had—actually, you shouldn't have either. It was fortunate that no ladies were present. Swearing was not Henry's habit, but over time he had heard a few such expressions along the coast, and retrieving them all from his memory, he launched them at me. Ultimately he announced that he was unable to bear it and that I lacked any feelings of sympathy. Therefore we harnessed the horse and I took him in a wagon to a physician in Port Marlow, a distance of thirty-five miles—in those times there were none closer—while that confounded hook remained dangling from his nose. Upon our arrival, old Dr. Crabb simply picked up a file and filed the hook in the exact same manner I had attempted, except he did not care in the least about being gentle!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: Seeing his longtime companion once again had brought back numerous memories for Captain Saul, who was currently immersed in a flood of past experiences.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Today, Henry was inquiring whether I recalled when Alexander MacAllister’s boat was blessed by old Father Chiniquy. It is another strange story—and completely true. I was aboard the boat myself. One morning at dawn, him and I went out in the boat belonging to Alexander MacAllister. Additionally, a French boy was in the boat—naturally a Catholic. As you are aware, old Father Chiniquy had become a Protestant, meaning the Catholics did not care for him much. Anyway, we remained out in the gulf under the scorching sun until midday, without getting a single bite. When we landed, old Father Chiniquy needed to depart, so in his courteous manner he stated, 'I’m very sorry I cannot go out with you dis afternoon, Mr. MacAllister, but I leave you my blessing. You will catch a t’ousand dis afternoon. 'Well, our catch was not a thousand, yet we retrieved precisely nine hundred and ninety-nine—the largest haul for a little boat across the entire north shore during that summer. Strange, wasn't it? Alexander MacAllister asked Andrew Peters, 'Well, and what do you think of Father Chiniquy now?’ 'Vell,’ Andrew grumbled, 'I t’ink de old devil has got a blessing left yet.’ Goodness, how Henry laughed about that today!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Have you any idea who Mr. Treleaven is, Captain Saul?” Nell inquired, observing that Captain Saul’s stream of memories had temporarily dried up. “I would like you to make a guess.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: A shake of his head came from Captain Saul.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “I was never skilled at making guesses, Mistress Carrow, but even so, upon entering I reflected, ‘Where did I previously encounter those eyes?’—because I TRULY have encountered them.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Recall a September morning from a long time in the past,” Nell said quietly. “Picture a vessel coming into the harbor—a vessel anticipated for a long period and given up on. Picture the day when the Royal William arrived and the initial glimpse you caught of the schoolmaster’s bride.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: Captain Saul leaped to his feet.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Those are Damaris Tremayne’s eyes,” he nearly yelled. “You cannot be her son—it must be that you are her—”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Grandson; indeed, my mother was Alice Tremayne.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: Captain Saul plunged downward toward Adrian Treleaven and gripped his hand once more.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “The child of Alice Tremayne! My goodness, you are truly welcome! On numerous occasions I have pondered where the schoolmaster’s progeny resided. I was aware that not one remained on the Island. Alice—Alice—the initial infant who came into the world inside that tiny dwelling. Never did a newborn deliver such happiness! A hundred times I bounced her on my knee. It was off my lap that she managed her very first solitary steps. Clearly I recall her mother's countenance gazing at her—and almost sixty years have passed since then. Does she still draw breath?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “No, my mother passed away while I was still just a young boy.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Oh, it feels wrong for me to still be alive to learn of that,” Captain Saul sighed. “However, seeing you fills my heart with joy. For a brief moment, it has restored my youth. You have not yet learned how great a blessing THAT is. Mistress Carrow present possesses the ability—she accomplishes it for me fairly frequently.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: When he found out that Adrian Treleaven was a person he referred to as a “real writing man,” Captain Saul became even more thrilled. He looked upon him as though he were a higher order of person. Captain Saul was aware of Nell’s writing, yet he had never given much weight to the matter. It was Captain Saul’s view that women were charming beings who should be granted the right to vote along with whatever else they desired, bless their hearts; nevertheless, he lacked faith in their ability to write.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Jest take a look at A Mad Love,” he was prone to object. “That was written by a woman and jest look at the result—it has one hundred and three chapters even though ten would have sufficed to tell everything. Knowing when to stop is something a writing woman never manages; there lies the issue. Knowing when to stop is the p’int of good writing.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Captain Saul, Mr. Treleaven wishes to listen to a few of your tales,” Nell remarked. “Relate to him the story concerning the captain who lost his mind and believed he was the Flying Dutchman.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: Captain Saul’s finest tale was this one. Horror and humor were blended within it, and even though Nell had listened to it a number of times, she chuckled just as warmly and shuddered just as terrifyingly over it as Mr. Treleaven did. Subsequent stories came next, because Captain Saul possessed a group of listeners completely to his liking. He recounted how a steamer had collided with his vessel; how Malay pirates had boarded him; how his vessel had caught fire; how he aided a political prisoner in escaping from a South African republic; how he had been shipwrecked one autumn on the Magdalens and remained stuck there for the winter; how a tiger had escaped on shipboard; how his crew had mutinied and left him marooned on a desolate island—Captain Saul narrated these and numerous other stories, whether tragic, humorous, or bizarre. His audience felt and comprehended all of them—the sea’s mystery, the charm of distant territories, the attraction of adventure, and the world’s laughter. Resting his head on his hand while the First Mate purred upon his knee, Adrian Treleaven listened, his shining eyes fixed on Captain Saul’s rough, expressive face.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Will you not allow Mr. Treleaven to inspect your life-book, Captain Saul?” Nell inquired, after Captain Saul ultimately announced that the telling of tales had to cease for the moment.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Oh, THAT isn't something he wants to be bothered by,” Captain Saul objected, though he was secretly longing to display it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Captain Garrick, nothing would please me more than viewing it,” Adrian stated. “It will be well worth the sight if it possesses even half the wonder of your stories.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: Captain Saul, feigning unwillingness, pulled his life-book from his ancient chest and passed it over to Adrian.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “It is my guess that you will not want to struggle for very long with my old handwriting. My education was quite limited,” he remarked in a casual tone. “I merely penned that piece to entertain my nephew Joe. He has a constant desire for tales. He arrives here yesterday and tells me, in a somewhat reproachful manner, while I was hoisting a codfish weighing twenty pounds out of my vessel, 'Uncle Saul, ain’t a codfish a dumb animal?’ You see, I had been explaining to him that he ought to be truly gentle with dumb animals, and never cause them any harm. I escaped the difficult situation by claiming that a codfish was sufficiently dumb but was not an animal, yet Joe failed to appear convinced, and I lacked satisfaction myself. A person must exercise extreme caution regarding what they impart to those little youngsters. THEY are capable of seeing right through you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: As he spoke, Captain Saul kept a side-glance on Adrian Treleaven, who was scrutinizing the life-book; and when he noticed soon after that his visitor was engrossed in what he was reading, he faced his cupboard with a smile and set about brewing tea. Adrian Treleaven parted from the life-book—showing the same unwillingness that a miser displays when forced away from his fortune—only as long as it took to consume his tea, after which he eagerly went back to reading.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Oh, you can bring that item back to your house if you wish,” remarked Captain Saul, pretending that the “thing” was not the item he held most dear. “I am required to head below and draw my vessel a little higher along the skids. A gust is approaching. Were you paying attention to the heavens this evening?

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “When mares’ tails and mackerel skies appear, grand vessels must reduce the canvas they wear.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: The proposal regarding the life-book was accepted with pleasure by Adrian Treleaven. As they were returning home, the tale of lost Margaret was recounted to him by Nell.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “That aged captain is a marvelous old man,” he remarked. “What an existence he has had! Indeed, that person experienced a greater number of adventures during a single week of his existence than the majority of us experience over a whole life. Do you truly believe that his stories are entirely genuine?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL
text: “Indeed I do. Captain Saul is undoubtedly incapable of lying; furthermore, the local inhabitants all confirm that events occurred precisely as he describes. Numerous former crew members of his were once living to verify his story. He remains a rare survivor of the traditional St. Brendan’s Island sea-captains, a group that has nearly vanished.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: The following morning, Adrian Treleaven arrived at the small dwelling, intensely thrilled. “Mrs. Carrow, a truly marvellous book—it is completely marvellous. Should I be allowed to possess it and draw upon its contents for a work, I am convinced I could create the most outstanding novel of the year from it. Is it likely Captain Saul would permit me to perform this?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “Allow you! I am certain he would be thrilled,” Nell exclaimed. “I confess that this was precisely my intention when I brought you below yesterday evening. Captain Saul has constantly desired to find someone who could compose his life-book correctly for him.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “Would you accompany me to the Point tonight, Mrs. Carrow? I will personally inquire of him regarding that life-book, yet I desire that you inform him that the tale of lost Margaret was imparted to me by you, and inquire whether he would permit me to employ it as a romantic thread to interweave the life-book’s stories into a unified whole.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: Adrian Treleaven’s revelation of his proposal made Captain Saul feel unprecedentedly thrilled. His long-held ambition would finally come to fruition, allowing his “life-book” to be presented to the public. Additionally, he felt delighted about incorporating the tale of the vanished Margaret into its pages.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “Her name won't be forgotten because of it,” he murmured with longing.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “It’s for that reason I desire to have it inserted.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “We shall work together,” Adrian exclaimed with joy. “The soul will be provided by you and the body by me. Oh, Captain Saul, a renowned book will be authored by the two of us. And our labor will commence immediately.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “And to imagine that the schoolmaster’s grandson is going to write my book!” Captain Saul cried out. “Boy, I held your grandfather as my closest companion. To my mind, he was without equal. Now I understand the reason for my lengthy wait. The writing had to hold off until the proper person arrived. You BELONG in this place—the spirit of this ancient north shore resides within you—you are the sole person who COULD write it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: They agreed to assign the small chamber adjoining the lighthouse's living room to Adrian as a workroom. Because Adrian lacked knowledge regarding numerous aspects of maritime and gulf traditions, it was essential for Captain Saul to remain close by while he composed to provide advice.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: Work on the volume commenced for him on the following morning, a task to which he devoted his entire being. Regarding Captain Saul, the summer brought him great joy. The small chamber where Adrian laboured was viewed by him as a holy place. While Adrian discussed every detail with Captain Saul, the written pages were kept hidden from his sight.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “It is necessary for you to hold off until publication,” he remarked. “After that, you will receive everything together in its finest condition.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: He drew unreservedly from the riches of his personal history. He pondered and fantasised about the departed Margaret to the point where she gained a vibrant presence for him and inhabited his writing. With the book’s advancement, it completely consumed him, driving him to labor upon it with intense excitement. He permitted Nell and Lorna to peruse the text and offer feedback; furthermore, the final chapter of the volume, which reviewers subsequently saw fit to label idyllic, was based on an idea provided by Lorna.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: Nell wrapped her arms around herself in sheer joy because her scheme had worked so well.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “The moment I set eyes on Adrian Treleaven, I realized he was the ideal person for the task,” she remarked to Hugh. “His countenance revealed both humor and passion, which, combined with his skill for expression, provided precisely what was required to write a book of that nature. In the words of Mrs. Agatha, he was foreordained for the role.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: Adrian Treleaven engaged in writing during the morning hours. The afternoon period was usually occupied by a cheerful excursion alongside the Carrows. Lorna frequently joined them as well, because Captain Saul regularly assumed responsibility for Rufus so that she could be liberated. They navigated boats across the harbor and along the trio of lovely rivers that emptied into it; they held clambakes upon the bar as well as mussel-bakes over the rocks; they gathered strawberries among the sand-dunes; they embarked on cod-fishing trips accompanied by Captain Saul; they targeted plover within the coastal pastures and wild ducks inside the cove—or rather, the male members of the party did. During the evening hours they wandered through the low-lying, daisied, coastal pastures beneath a golden moon, or else they gathered inside the living room of the small house where the chill of the ocean wind frequently made a driftwood fire welcome, discussing the endless topics that joyful, enthusiastic, intelligent youth are capable of discovering to converse about.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: From the exact date she had confessed to Nell, Lorna had transformed into a completely different person. Not a hint remained of her former distance and reticence, nor any trace of her previous rancor. The youth she had been denied appeared to return to her alongside her mature womanhood; she opened up like a blossom of fire and fragrance; during the twilight gatherings of that magical summer, no one laughed more easily or possessed a sharper wit than she did. Whenever she was absent, everyone sensed that their time together was missing a delightful essence. Her inner soul had awakened, illuminating her beauty in the manner of a rose-colored light glowing through a perfect alabaster urn. At times, the sheer brilliance of her presence seemed to make Nell’s eyes throb. Regarding Adrian Treleaven, the "Margaret" in his manuscript—despite possessing the gentle brown locks and pixie-like features of the actual young woman who had disappeared such a long time back, "pillowed where lost Atlantis sleeps"—carried the character of Lorna Vane, just as it unfolded before him throughout those blissful times at Seven Gulls Harbor.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: Taken as a whole, it proved to be an unforgettably grand summer—the sort of season that rarely occurs in anyone's existence, yet bequeaths a wealth of lovely recollections upon its departure—a summer that, through a happy blending of pleasant weather, pleasant companions, and pleasant activities, approaches perfection as closely as anything possibly can in this life.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “It’s too good to endure,” Nell remarked softly to herself, uttering a small sigh, on that day in September when a particular chill in the breeze and a particular hue of vivid blue across the gulf water indicated that autumn was right at hand.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: That night, Adrian Treleaven informed them that his book was completed and his holiday had to conclude.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: “There is still quite a lot of work for me to perform on it—editing, trimming, and the like,” he remarked, “however, it is essentially finished. The final line was composed by me earlier today. Should I manage to locate a publisher, its release will likely occur during the upcoming summer or autumn.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 25 THE WRITING OF THE BOOK
text: Adrian felt fairly certain about securing a publisher. It was clear to him that his creation was a great book—one destined for remarkable success—a work that would endure. He was aware of the fame and fortune it would earn him; yet, upon finishing its final line, he rested his head against the manuscript and remained in that position for a while. Nor were his reflections centered on the fine accomplishment he had achieved.

“I am extremely sorry that Hugh is not here,” Nell remarked. “A grave mishap befell Wace Lyons at the Glen, forcing him to leave. His return is unlikely to occur before a very late hour. Nevertheless, he instructed me that he would head up to your place sufficiently early tomorrow morning so that he could catch you prior to your departure. It is deeply frustrating. A delightful little gathering for your final evening in this place had been arranged by Tabitha and me.”

Next to the garden stream, upon the small wooden bench that Hugh had constructed, she was seated. Positioned in front of her, Adrian Treleaven leaned against the yellow birch's bronze trunk. A distinct pallor was upon him, and his face displayed the evidence of the previous night spent without sleep. Looking upward toward him, Nell pondered whether, despite everything, he had gained the vigor from his summer that it ought to have given him. Was his labor on his book excessive? It occurred to her that he had not appeared healthy for a week.

Adrian spoke with deliberation, “Having the doctor absent makes me somewhat pleased. Mrs. Carrow, my intention was to meet with you privately. If I do not disclose something to someone, it feels as though it will push me to insanity. For seven days, I have attempted to confront it directly—yet I am unable to do so. You possess my trust, I am certain—plus, comprehension will come to you. Understanding is constant in a woman whose eyes resemble yours. You belong to those individuals who naturally draw confidences from others. Lorna is loved by me, Mrs. Carrow. LOVED! A word that faint hardly seems sufficient!”

The restrained intensity of his speech caused his voice to crack without warning. Turning his head aside, he concealed his countenance upon his arm. His entire body trembled. Pale and horrified, Nell remained sitting as she watched him. Such a possibility had never crossed her mind! Yet—why had it never occurred to her? The situation appeared natural and unavoidable now. Her former inability to see it amazed her. Nevertheless—such occurrences were unheard of in Seven Gulls. Beyond these borders, mankind's desires might ignore societal rules and statutes—yet certainly not HERE. During a period of ten years, Lorna had occasionally taken in summer visitors, and no such event had ever transpired. Still, those guests might not have resembled Adrian Treleaven; furthermore, the vibrant, ALIVE Lorna of the present season was distinct from the distant, moody young woman of previous times. Oh, THIS ought to have been anticipated by someone! What kept Miss Winifred from foreseeing it? Miss Winifred was consistently prompt to raise a warning regarding men. An irrational anger toward Miss Winifred arose within Nell. Subsequently, she uttered a faint quiet sigh. Regardless of who bore the fault, the damage had been inflicted. And what about Lorna? Nell experienced the deepest worry on Lorna's account.
“Is Lorna aware of this, Mr. Treleaven?” she inquired softly.

“No—no,—provided she hasn't deduced it. You certainly cannot believe I would act as enough of a cad and scoundrel to inform her, Mrs. Carrow. I was unable to prevent myself from loving her—that is everything—and my agony exceeds what I am capable of bearing.”

“Is SHE concerned?” inquired Nell. As soon as the words were spoken, a sense that the question ought to have been withheld came over her. With an excessively enthusiastic denial, Adrian Treleaven responded to it.
“No—no, certainly not. However, if she were available, I could cause her to feel affection—I am certain I could.”
“Though she truly cares, he is aware of it,” was the thought that crossed Nell's mind. Speaking aloud, her voice carried both empathy and firmness:
“Yet her freedom is absent, Mr. Treleaven. And departing quietly while abandoning her to her own existence remains the sole action available to you.”

“I understand—I understand,” Adrian uttered with a groan. Sitting on the bank of grass, he gazed gloomily down at the amber-colored water below. “I understand there is no alternative—no alternative except uttering formally, 'Good-bye, Mrs. Vane. Thank you for all your kindness to me this summer,’ in the exact manner I would have spoken it to the comely, energetic, sharp-sighted homemaker I anticipated she would be upon my arrival. After that, I will hand over my lodging fee like every truthful boarder and depart! Oh, it is quite uncomplicated. Zero doubt—zero confusion—a direct path to the edge of the earth!
“And I will tread it—there is no need for you to doubt that I shall, Mrs. Carrow. Yet treading on glowing hot ploughshares would be less difficult.”

The sharpness of his tone caused Nell to recoil. Little that she might utter could properly address such circumstances. Accusations were entirely improper—counsel was uncalled for—and the man’s unmitigated anguish made any condolences seem absurd. Lost in a tangle of pity and remorse, she could merely share in his grief. How her soul grieved for Lorna! Was it not true that the unfortunate young woman had already endured plenty prior to this?

“If she were simply happy, departing and abandoning her would not be quite so difficult,” Adrian continued with intense emotion. “However, considering her living death—comprehending the exact nature of the situation to which I am abandoning her! THAT constitutes the most terrible part of everything. I would trade my own existence to bring her happiness—yet I am powerless to even assist her—powerless. She remains tied for eternity to that miserable creature—having no prospect except aging throughout a series of vacant, purposeless, infertile years. The thought of it makes me insane. Nevertheless, I have to live out my existence, never beholding her, yet perpetually aware of what she suffers. It is ghastly—ghastly!”
“It is extremely difficult,” Nell said with grief. “We—those of us who are her friends here—are all aware of how difficult it is for her.”
“And she possesses such abundant gifts for living,” Adrian stated in a tone of defiance.

“Her attractiveness represents the smallest part of her inheritance—and she is the most gorgeous female I have ever encountered. That chuckling sound she makes! I have spent the entire summer scheming to bring forth that chuckle, merely for the joy of listening to it. And her gaze—it possesses a depth and blue hue matching the gulf yonder. I have not witnessed such azure before—and gilded shades! Have you ever observed her tresses loose, Mrs. Carrow?”
“No.”

“I did—on one occasion. I had traveled down to the Point aiming to go fishing with Captain Saul, but the water was too rough for us to head out, which caused me to return. Taking advantage of an afternoon she assumed she would spend by herself, she had washed her hair and was standing outdoors on the veranda drying it in the sunlight. It cascaded clear down to her feet around her like a fountain of living gold. Spotting me, she rushed indoors, as the wind seized her hair and swept it all about her—resembling Danae in her cloud. Somehow, right at that instance, the awareness that I loved her struck me—and I understood that I had been in love with her since the very first moment I beheld her against the darkness in that radiant glow. And now she is forced to remain here—tending to and comforting Rufus, skimping and economizing simply to survive, while I pass my days in futile longing for her, prevented, by that exact circumstance, from providing her even the slight assistance a friend could offer. I paced the beach last night, nearly until daybreak, wrestling with the entire situation again and again. Even so, despite all of this, I am unable to bring myself to regret coming to Seven Gulls. To my mind, as awful as the situation stands, it would prove far worse had I never met Lorna. Loving her and parting from her causes a scorching, searing agony—yet never having loved her remains completely unimaginable. I imagine all of this strikes you as quite mad—these overwhelming feelings always appear absurd whenever we express them through our imperfect language. They were never intended to be voiced—merely experienced and borne. I ought not to have said anything—yet it has provided some relief. At the very least, it has supplied me with the fortitude to depart in a proper manner tomorrow morning, without causing a disturbance. You will send me letters occasionally, will you not, Mrs. Carrow, and share whatever updates there are concerning her?”

“Indeed,” Nell remarked. “Ah, I am deeply grieved that you are leaving—we shall miss you greatly—we have all been such good companions! Were it not because of this, you might return during future summers. Maybe, even now—eventually—once you have put it out of your mind, maybe—”
“Seven Gulls will never see me again, nor will the memory ever leave me,” Adrian stated succinctly.

Quietness and dusk descended upon the garden. Off in the distance, the ocean was beating softly and repetitively against the bar. The night breeze among the poplars made a noise similar to a melancholy, strange, ancient chant—a fragmented vision of former recollections. A slim, well-formed young aspen stood in front of them against the delicate yellow-orange, green, and fading pink of the western sky, a backdrop that revealed each leaf and twig in dark, quivering, magical beauty.
“Is that not lovely?” Adrian asked, gesturing toward it like someone who is setting a particular discussion aside.

“Because of its intense beauty, I feel a physical pain,” Nell uttered in a quiet voice. “Flawless objects such as this have constantly caused me distress—I can recall terming the sensation ‘the queer ache’ during my youth. Why does an agony of this nature appear to be inextricably linked to absolute flawlessness? Does it stem from the sorrow of absolute completion—the moment it dawns on us that any subsequent change can only be a decline?”
“It may be,” Adrian said in a dreamy voice, “that our own captive endlessness is crying out to the matching endlessness displayed by that seen flawlessness.”

“It appears you are suffering from a head cold. It would be wise to apply some tallow to your nose before sleeping,” remarked Miss Winifred, having entered via the small gate among the fir trees just as Adrian finished speaking. Although Adrian was well-liked by Miss Winifred, she made it a point of principle to penalize any grandiloquent speech coming from a gentleman with a snub nose.

Miss Winifred embodied the humor that constantly lurks behind the tragic aspects of existence. Having experienced somewhat frayed nerves, Nell chuckled uncontrollably, and Adrian offered a smile as well. Indeed, emotional intensity and romance tended to retreat into the background whenever Miss Winifred was around. Even so, the situation no longer appeared entirely as bleak, gloomy, and distressing to Nell as it had just a short time earlier. Nevertheless, rest remained completely elusive to her during those nocturnal hours.

It was the following morning when Adrian Treleaven departed Seven Gulls. Nell visited to check on Lorna that evening, yet she discovered no one there. Locked up tight, the house showed no illumination in a single window. A house stripped of its soul was what it resembled. Lorna failed to hurry over the next day—an omen Nell considered negative.

Because Hugh needed to head to the fishing cove during the evening, Nell went along in the vehicle with him as far as the Point, planning to spend some time with Captain Saul. However, the immense beacon, slicing its beams through the autumn evening's fog, was being tended by Hector Garrick, and Captain Saul was absent.
“What is your plan?” Hugh inquired. “Will you join me?”
“To the cove I do not wish to go—yet I will cross the channel alongside you, and wander upon the sandy beach until your return. Tonight, the rocky coast is excessively slick and forbidding.”

On the bar's sands by herself, Nell surrendered to the night's strange, enchanting mood. September felt unusually warm, and a dense fog had marked the late afternoon; nevertheless, the full moon partially diminished the mist, converting the gulf, the harbor, and the nearby coasts into a bizarre, whimsical, imaginary realm of faint silver haze, where all objects appeared like phantoms. Moving down the channel, Captain Josiah Crawford’s black schooner, loaded with potatoes destined for Bluenose ports, seemed to be a ghost vessel heading toward a distant, unmapped territory that continually pulled away and could never be attained. The shouts from hidden gulls above sounded like the wails of lost sailors' spirits. Small tendrils of foam blowing over the sand resembled magical creatures slipping out from underwater caverns. The large, slumping sand-dunes appeared as the resting giants from an ancient northern legend. Pale lights flickering over the harbor acted as misleading signals along a fairytale shoreline. Nell entertained herself with a century of imaginative thoughts while she roamed in the mist. Wandering by herself on this spellbound beach felt wonderful, romantic, and mysterious.
Yet was she by herself? An object emerged in the fog ahead of her—assumed a distinct shape—and unexpectedly advanced in her direction over the sands rippled by waves.
“Lorna!” Nell cried out, thoroughly astonished. “What in the world brings you—HERE—this evening?”

“If we are on the subject, what in the world are YOU doing in this place?” asked Lorna, attempting a laugh. It proved to be a failed attempt. A very pale and exhausted appearance marked her face; nevertheless, the love locks beneath her scarlet cap were forming curls around her face and eyes that resembled small, glistening gold rings.
“I am awaiting Hugh, who is currently over at the Cove. My plan had been to remain at the lighthouse, however Captain Saul is absent.”

“Well, I arrived at this place since I desired to walk—and walk—and WALK,” Lorna said with uneasiness. “I was unable to on the rocky coast—the water had risen too far and the boulders trapped me. It was necessary for me to come here—otherwise I would have lost my mind, I believe. I used Captain Saul’s flat to row across the passage. An hour has passed while I have been here. Come—come—we must walk. Remaining still is impossible for me. Oh, Nell!”
“Lorna, my darling, what is wrong?” inquired Nell, even though she was already far too aware.

“I am unable to inform you—do not request it of me. Your knowing would not bother me—it is my desire that you were aware—yet I am unable to inform you—I am unable to inform a single person. I have acted like such an idiot, Nell—and oh, being an idiot causes such extreme agony. No other thing in existence brings as much distress.”
Her laughter was bitter. Around her, Nell slid an arm.
“Lorna, have you come to feel affection for Mr. Treleaven?”
Lorna spun around in a passionate manner.
“In what way did you find out?” she exclaimed. “Nell, in what way did you find out? Oh, does my face display it for all to perceive? Is it that obvious?”
“Nay, nay. I—I am unable to explain to you the way I was aware. In some manner, it simply entered my thoughts. Lorna, do not regard me in that fashion!”
“Are you despising me?” Lorna asked, her voice quiet and intense. “Is it your belief that I am evil—not act as a woman should? Or am I merely a complete idiot in your eyes?”

“I do not consider you to be any of those things. Come on, my dear, let us simply discuss this in a sensible manner, just as we would discuss any other major life crisis. You have been dwelling on this matter and permitted yourself to fall into an unhealthy perspective regarding it. You are aware that you possess a slight inclination to react this way to anything that turns out badly, and you gave me your word that you would strive against it.”
“But—oh, it’s so—so humiliating,” Lorna whispered. “To be in love with him—without him asking—and at a time when I’m not at liberty to love anyone.”
“It contains no disgrace. However, your growing affection for Adrian causes me great regret, since, given the present circumstances, your sorrow will merely deepen.”

“I didn’t LEARN to care,” Lorna said, continuing her walk and expressing herself with great passion. “If that had been the case, I might have stopped it. Such a thought never crossed my mind until a week ago, on that day when he informed me that his book was completed and he would have to leave shortly. At that moment—then I realized it. It was as though a dreadful blow had been dealt to me. I remained silent—speech was impossible for me—yet I have no idea how my expression appeared. I am terrified that my face gave me away. Oh, dying of shame would be my fate if I believed he was aware—or even harbored a suspicion.”
Hindered by what she had deduced from her talk with Adrian, Nell remained unhappily quiet. Lorna continued to talk passionately, appearing to gain comfort from speaking.

“All through this summer, Nell, my happiness was greater than it had ever been before. My belief was that this stemmed from everything being resolved between us, and that our bond was what rendered existence so lovely and complete again. To an extent, it WAS—yet not entirely—no, far from entirely. The reason for everything feeling so changed is clear to me now. Now, however, it has completely ended—and his departure has happened. Nell, how am I to go on living? Upon returning inside the house earlier today following his departure, the loneliness hit me as if I had been struck across the face.”

“In time, it will not appear as difficult, dear,” stated Nell, who continuously experienced the suffering of her companions so deeply that uttering smooth, effortless words of solace was impossible for her. In addition, recalling how well-intentioned statements had pained her during her own grief, she felt fearful.

“Oh, it appears to me that it will become more difficult continuously,” Lorna stated in misery. “There is nothing for me to anticipate. Day after day will arrive—and his return will not happen—he is never coming back. Oh, whenever I reflect on the fact that he will never be seen by me again, it feels like my heartstrings have been seized by a large, cruel hand and are being torn out. Formerly, a long time in the past, love was dreamed of by me—and my thought was that it had to be lovely—and NOW—it resembles THIS. His departure yesterday morning was marked by such coldness and detachment. 'Good-bye, Mrs. Vane’ was uttered by him using the most frigid tone possible—as though friendship had not even existed between us—as though I possessed no meaning to him whatsoever. My knowledge is that I do not—his caring was not desired by me—nevertheless, he COULD have shown a bit more kindness.”

“Oh, I wish Hugh would come,” Nell thought. Torn between her pity for Lorna and the need to prevent any disclosure of Adrian’s secret, she understood the reason his farewell was so chilly—the reason it lacked the warmth their strong comradeship required—yet she was unable to inform Lorna.
“Nell, I couldn’t prevent it—I really couldn’t prevent it,” wretched Lorna said.
“I am aware of that.”
“Are you holding me so greatly at fault?”
“I do not hold you responsible in the least.”
“And you will not—you will not inform Hugh?”
“Lorna! Is it your belief that I would commit an act like that?”
“Well, I am uncertain—Hugh and you are such CLOSE FRIENDS. Telling him all the details seems unavoidable to me.”
“I will share every detail regarding my personal affairs—indeed I will. However, I refuse to reveal what my friends keep hidden.”

“I couldn’t let HIM be aware. Yet I’m pleased that YOU are aware. I would be filled with guilt if I kept anything from you out of shame. I trust Miss Winifred doesn’t discover it. At times I get the feeling that those dreadful, gentle brown eyes she has gaze right into my soul. Oh, I desire that this fog would refrain from ever clearing—I desire to remain within it for all time, concealed from all creation. I fail to understand how I can continue living. This summer was so packed with activity. Not for one second was I ever lonely. Prior to the arrival of Adrian, there were awful instances—after I was alongside you and Hugh—and subsequently was forced to depart from you. The pair of you would stroll off side by side and I would stroll off ALL BY MYSELF. Once Adrian arrived, he was constantly present to accompany me back home—the two of us would giggle and converse just as you and Hugh did—I experienced no further desolate, jealous instances. And AT THIS MOMENT! Oh, indeed, I’ve acted like a fool. Let us stop discussing my foolishness. I will never weary you with it any more.”

“Hugh is present, and you will return alongside us,” declared Nell, who possessed no desire to permit Lorna to roam unchaperoned across the sand-bar during a night like this and in a state like hers. “Our boat holds sufficient space for a trio, and the flat can be towed in the rear.”

“Oh, I guess I have to accept being the third wheel once more,” poor Lorna stated, giving another harsh laugh. “Pardon me, Nell—I was being awful. I should feel grateful—and I AM—for having a pair of great friends who happily include me as a third. Ignore my horrible remarks. It feels as though I am merely a single huge ache everywhere, and every single thing causes me suffering.”
“Lorna appeared extremely silent this evening, did she not?” remarked Hugh, as soon as he and Nell arrived at their house. “Whatever was she up to by herself over on the sandbar?”
“Oh, she was exhausted—and you are aware that she enjoys visiting the coast following one of Rufus’s difficult days.”
“It is such a shame she did not encounter and wed a man such as Treleaven years back,” pondered Hugh. “An ideal pair is what they would have been, wouldn't they?”

“For pity’s sake, Hugh, don’t develop into a match-maker. It’s an abominable profession for a man,” exclaimed Nell somewhat sharply, fearful that Hugh would stumble upon the truth were he to continue in that vein.
“Bless us, Nell-girl, I’m not matchmaking,” Hugh protested, taken aback somewhat by how she sounded. “I was merely reflecting on a thing that might have been.”
“Well, refrain from doing so. You are wasting your time,” remarked Nell. Following that, she abruptly stated:
“Oh, Hugh, I want all people to enjoy the same happiness that we have.”
“I’ve been looking through the death announcements,” Miss Winifred remarked, putting the Daily Enterprise aside and picking up her needlework.

Beneath a grim November sky, the harbor stretched out dark and gloomy, and dripping, lifeless leaves stuck thoroughly soaked to the window sills; nevertheless, the small house shone cheerful with the glow of a fire and seemed like springtime owing to the geraniums and ferns of Nell.
“In this place, it is perpetually summer, Nell,” Lorna had remarked on a certain day; and everyone who stayed as a guest in that home of dreams experienced the identical feeling.

“The Enterprise appears to specialize in death notices lately,” remarked Miss Winifred. “There are always two or three columns dedicated to them, and I do not miss a word. Reading them serves as a type of enjoyment for me, particularly if they include some home-made verse. I have found an exquisite example to show you:
She has departed to reside with her Creator, never again to wander. It was her custom to joyfully play and sing the hymn of Home, Sweet Home.

Who claims that our Island lacks all poetic skill! Nell, my dear, have you ever paid attention to how many wonderful individuals pass away? It is rather tragic. Within this paper are ten death notices, and each single one portrays a saint and a role model, including the men. This one covers old Peter Stimson, who has "left a large circle of friends to mourn his untimely loss." Good heavens, Nell, my dear, that individual had reached eighty, and anyone acquainted with him had been praying for his demise for the past thirty years. Go through the death notices whenever you feel down, Nell, my dear—most of all the notices for people you are familiar with. Provided you possess even the slightest sense of humor, they are bound to lift your spirits, trust ME. I only desire that I were tasked with composing the death notices for particular folks. Does not "obituary" strike you as a dreadfully hideous term? That precise Peter I was mentioning possessed a countenance that mirrored the term precisely. I could not glance at it without instantly remembering the word OBITUARY on the spot. I am aware of just one single term that is more hideous, and that term is RELICT. Good heavens, Nell, my dear, I might end up a spinster, yet it offers this reassurance—I shall never become the "relict" of any man.”

“It IS an ugly word,” Nell said with a laugh. “The cemetery in Brierley had a great number of aged gravestones that read 'sacred to the memory of So-and-So, RELICT of the late So-and-So.’ That phrase constantly brought to my mind a thing that was threadbare and damaged by moths. For what reason do a vast amount of terms associated with dying sound so unpleasant? I really desire that the habit of referring to a corpse as 'the remains’ might be done away with. A genuine shudder goes through me whenever the funeral director announces during a service, 'All who wish to see the remains please step this way.’ That statement constantly leaves me with the ghastly feeling that I am about to look upon the location of a cannibalistic banquet.”

“Indeed, my sole desire,” Miss Winifred remarked placidly, “is for no one to refer to me as 'our departed sister’ after my passing. My aversion to this constant referencing of sisters and brothers began half a decade back, during a itinerant preacher’s revival at the Glen. Right from the beginning, I had no time for the man. My gut told me he was untrustworthy. Which proved true. You see, he claimed to belong to the Presbyterian faith—though he pronounced it PresbyTARian—when he was actually a Methodist the whole time. Everyone was addressed by him as a brother or sister. That fellow possessed an extensive kin group. Squeezing my hand with great passion one evening, he begged, 'My DEAR sister Tolley, have you found Christ?’ After giving him a brief inspection, I responded coolly, 'MR. Fiske, my lone brother passed away fifteen years back, and I’ve taken on no new ones since then. Regarding my Christian faith, I trust and believe I possessed it while you were still a toddler wearing petticoats.’ That put an end to his talking, you may be sure. Understand, my sweet Nell, I do not despise every evangelist. Outstanding, sincere individuals have come here, accomplishing much good and causing ancient sinners to tremble. Yet this Fiske fellow was not among their number. One night, I enjoyed a quiet chuckle on my own. Fiske requested that every Christian rise. Rest assured, I remained seated! Such displays have never appealed to me. However, the majority stood up, after which he requested that everyone desiring to become a Christian stand. When no one moved for a bit, Fiske began singing a hymn as loudly as he could. Sitting right ahead of me in the Millison family bench was wretched little Ikey Pratt. As a ten-year-old placed child, he was pushed to absolute exhaustion by Millison. Because the miserable little boy was perpetually exhausted, he dropped off instantly whenever he attended service or found a spot to sit quietly for a short while. Throughout the revival, he had been resting, and I was glad the unfortunate child was obtaining a reprieve, you can be sure. Now, as Fiske’s singing rose toward the heavens and the congregation joined the song, unfortunate Ikey jerked awake. Imagining it was merely a typical hymn where everyone was expected to rise, he jumped to his feet with great haste, aware that Maria Millison would scold him severely for napping during the service. Catching sight of him, Fiske paused and yelled, 'A further soul brought to light! Glory Hallelujah!’ Yet there stood miserable, terrified Ikey, barely conscious and yawning, with no thought whatsoever for his soul. Unfortunate kid, he lacked the leisure to focus on anything beyond his exhausted, overburdened small frame.

“Lorna attended one evening, and the Fiske-man pursued her immediately—oh, he took a particular interest in the salvation of the attractive young women, trust me!—and he injured her feelings to the extent that she refused to return. Subsequently, he offered prayers aloud every single night, right before everyone, asking the Lord to soften her stubborn heart. At last, I approached Mr. Leavitt, who was our pastor at the time, and warned him that unless he ordered Fiske to cease, I would stand up the following evening and launch my hymn book at his head whenever he referred to that 'beautiful but unrepentant young woman.’ I certainly would have executed it, trust ME. Mr. Leavitt brought a halt to it, yet Fiske persisted with his assemblies until Charley Fairlie terminated his work in the Glen. Mrs. Charley had spent the entire winter away in California. She had suffered from severe depression during the autumn—a spiritual depression—which was a trait in her ancestry. Her father experienced such intense distress over the conviction that he was guilty of the unforgivable sin that he passed away in the asylum. Consequently, when Rose Fairlie developed those symptoms, Charley sent her away to stay with her sister located in Los Angeles. She recovered completely and returned home at the exact moment the Fiske revival reached its peak. She disembarked from the train at the Glen, looking quite cheerful and happy, and the very first sight that confronted her on the dark, gable-end of the freight shed was the query, painted in huge white characters two feet tall, 'Whither goest thou—to heaven or hell?’ That concept had originated with Fiske, who had hired Henry Rudge to execute the painting. Rose merely let out a scream and collapsed into a faint; and once she was brought back home, her condition deteriorated beyond before. Charley Fairlie approached Mr. Leavitt and stated that every member of the Fairlie family would abandon the congregation if Fiske remained any longer. Mr. Leavitt was forced to yield, since the Fairlies provided fifty percent of his stipend, so Fiske left, leaving us to rely on our Bibles again for guidance on reaching heaven. Following his departure, Mr. Leavitt discovered that the man was merely a Methodist in disguise, which made him feel quite ill, trust ME. Mr. Leavitt had his flaws in certain areas, but he remained a solid, genuine Presbyterian.”
“Incidentally, yesterday I received a letter from Mr. Treleaven,” Nell remarked. “He requested that I send you his kind regards.”
“I do not desire his tokens,” Miss Winifred stated sharply.
“For what reason?” Nell asked, thoroughly surprised. “It was my belief that he was to your liking.”

“Indeed, I did so, after a fashion. However, what he did to Lorna is something I will never pardon him for. That poor girl is grieving over him—as though she had not already suffered sufficient distress—while he is undoubtedly roaming about Toronto, having a good time just as he always does. That is precisely how a man acts.”
“Oh, Miss Winifred, in what way did you discover this?”

“Goodness, Nell, my love, don’t I possess eyes? Besides, Lorna has been known to me from the time she was an infant. Throughout this past autumn, a different sort of sorrow has been visible in her gaze, and I am certain that author fellow was somehow responsible for it. Making myself the instrument that brought him to this place is something I will always regret. However, I did not anticipate he would turn out as he did. My expectation was merely that he would resemble the previous gentlemen Lorna had taken in as boarders—arrogant young fools, the whole lot of them, for whom she had no time whatsoever. Indeed, a single one among them attempted to flirt with her on one occasion, and she gave him such a cold reception that I am confident he has failed to warm up ever since. Consequently, the idea of any peril never crossed my mind.”
“Do not allow Lorna to think that you are aware of her secret,” Nell said hastily. “It would cause her pain, I believe.”

“Have faith in me, my dear Nell. My life did not start yesterday. Oh, may every man be cursed! To start with, Lorna’s existence was destroyed by one of them, and currently a different member of that brood arrives and leaves her even more miserable. Believe me, Nell, this earth is a terrible location.”
“There is a thing on earth awry Will be explained in due course,”
recited Nell in a dreamy manner.
“Should that happen, it will occur in a realm devoid of men,” Miss Winifred remarked despondently.
Hugh came inside and inquired, “In what way have the crew misbehaved this time?”
“Trouble—trouble! What other thing have they ever accomplished?”
“Eve was the one who ate the apple, Miss Winifred.”
“A male creature was the one who lured her,” Miss Winifred shot back victoriously.

Once her initial agony had passed, Lorna discovered she could continue living despite everything, much like the majority of people, regardless of the specific nature of their suffering. She may have even taken pleasure in certain times, being part of the cheerful group within the small house of dreams. Yet, had Nell harbored any expectation that Adrian Treleaven was fading from her memory, the secret longing in Lorna’s gaze at any reference to his name would have disabused her of the idea. Moved to pity by that longing, Nell consistently managed to share fragments of information from Adrian’s correspondence with Captain Saul or Hugh while Lorna was present. The way the girl reddened and drained of color during these instances made the intensity of her feelings painfully clear. Nevertheless, she abstained from discussing him with Nell, nor did she ever refer to that evening on the sand-bar.
Her aged canine passed away on a certain day, causing her to mourn his loss deeply.

“He has been my friend for such a long time,” she said to Nell with sorrow. “You know, he was Rufus’s old dog—Rufus owned him for about a year before our marriage. He entrusted him to me upon sailing on the Four Sisters. Carlo grew very attached to me—and the affection of that dog sustained me during that initial terrible year following mother's death, when I was on my own. Hearing that Rufus was returning made me fear Carlo would no longer belong so much to me. Yet he appeared to care nothing for Rufus, despite having loved him so much previously. As if he were a stranger, he would snap and growl at him. I felt glad. Having a single creature whose love belonged entirely to me was sweet. Nell, that old dog provided me with such comfort. Because he became so weak during the fall, I feared his life would end soon—nevertheless, I harbored hopes of nursing him through the winter. This morning he appeared fairly healthy. As he lay on the rug in front of the fire, he suddenly stood up and slunk over to my side; placing his head on my lap, he bestowed one affectionate glance upon me from his large, gentle, canine eyes—and right after that, he simply trembled and passed away. I will miss him greatly.”
“Allow me to bestow upon you a different hound, Lorna,” Nell uttered. “A beautiful Lindsay setter is coming to me as a Yule gift intended for Hugh. Allow me to bestow one upon you as well.”
Lorna gave a shake of her head.

“I would rather not at this moment, I appreciate it, Nell. Taking on a new dog is not something I am up for right now. My capacity to care for a replacement feels completely exhausted. Maybe—eventually—I will accept one from you. Having a dog is actually necessary for me as a form of defense. However, Carlo possessed qualities that were nearly human—replacing him too quickly just would not be APPROPRIATE, poor faithful boy.”

Seven days prior to Christmas, Nell traveled to Brierley, remaining there past the festive season. Hugh arrived to collect her, leading to a joyful New Year's party at Grey Shutters, where Pembrokes, Carrows, and Ducketts gathered together to feast upon a meal that Mrs. Agatha and Thirza had planned and prepared with great diligence. Upon their return to Seven Gulls, the small dwelling was nearly buried by snow, as the third tempest of a season destined to be exceptionally severe had swept up the harbor, piling massive drifts against every obstacle in its path. Nevertheless, Captain Saul had cleared the pathways and doorways with his shovel, while Miss Winifred had visited to start a fire upon the hearth.

“My dear Nell, I am happy to see you return! However, have you ever beheld drifts like these? The Vane place is completely hidden from view unless one ascends to the second floor. Lorna will be thrilled at your return. She is practically interred over there. Thankfully, Rufus is able to clear the snow with a shovel and finds it very entertaining. Tabitha relayed a message asking me to inform you that she will be available tomorrow. To what destination are you headed now, Captain?”

“I think I’m going to make my way up to the Glen so I can keep old Martin Strong company for a while. His death is approaching, and he feels lonely. Since he spent his whole life working too hard to form relationships, he lacks many friends. Nevertheless, he has accumulated a great deal of wealth.”

“Well, he reasoned that as he was unable to serve both God and Mammon, sticking to Mammon was his best choice,” Miss Winifred stated sharply. “Because of that, he ought not to grumble if he currently finds Mammon’s companionship lacking.”
Captain Saul stepped outside, yet he recalled a detail in the yard and briefly returned.

“A letter reached me from Mr. Treleaven, Mistress Carrow, in which he states that the life-book has been accepted and will be printed coming autumn. Obtaining this information made me feel truly joyous. The thought that I shall finally view it in print fills my mind.”
“That person is utterly insane regarding his life-book,” Miss Winifred remarked with pity. “As for me, I believe the world already contains way too many books.”

Hugh set aside the heavy medical book he had been reading closely until the growing darkness of the March twilight forced him to stop. Resting back in his seat, he looked out the window in a thoughtful mood. Early spring had arrived, which was likely the most unpleasant season of all. The gloomy, waterlogged countryside and decaying, dark ice in the harbor that met his gaze could not be saved even by the setting sun. Except for a large black crow flying alone over a grey field, no living thing could be seen. Hugh found himself idly wondering about the bird. Was it a family-oriented crow, headed toward a dark yet attractive crow mate waiting in the forest past the Glen? Was it perhaps a sleek young male crow whose mind was set on romance? Or could it be a skeptical bachelor crow, holding the view that one travels quickest when journeying unaccompanied? Whichever it might be, the bird shortly vanished into the fitting darkness, causing Hugh to direct his attention to the more inviting scene inside.

The light from the hearth danced from place to place, shining upon the white and green jackets of Gog and Magog, upon the smooth, brown skull of the lovely setter resting on the mat, upon the frames of the pictures hanging on the walls, upon the vase packed with daffodils taken from the window garden, upon Nell herself, who was seated beside her small table, having her needlework next to her and her hands locked around her knee as she imagined images within the flames—Castles in Spain with delicate towers that broke through moonlit cloud and sunset bar—vessels journeying out of the Haven of Good Hopes directly toward Seven Gulls Harbor carrying valuable cargo. Because Nell had returned to dreaming dreams, even though a dark figure of dread accompanied her evening and morning to dim and obscure her imaginings.

Hugh routinely described himself as “an old married man.” Nevertheless, he continued to gaze at Nell with a lover's disbelieving eyes. That she truly belonged to him was something he was not yet completely able to accept. This entire experience MIGHT simply be a fantasy, inextricably linked to this enchanted house of dreams. Before her, his spirit still proceeded cautiously, afraid that the spell might break and the illusion vanish.
“Nell,” he uttered unhurriedly, “listen to me. I need to speak to you concerning a matter.”
Nell peered over toward him amidst the shadows illuminated by the fire.
“What’s the matter?” she inquired lightheartedly. “Hugh, your expression is terribly grave. I assure you I’ve been good all day. Check with Tabitha.”
“I do not wish to speak regarding you—or about ourselves,” I said. “It concerns Rufus Vane.”
“Rufus Vane?” repeated Nell, straightening herself with interest. “Why, whatever do you have to tell regarding Rufus Vane?”
“Lately, my thoughts have been occupied with him quite a bit. That time last summer when I provided treatment for the carbuncles on his neck, do you recall it?”
“Yes—yes.”

“I made use of the occasion to meticulously inspect the marks on his scalp. From a clinical perspective, Rufus has continually struck me as quite a fascinating subject. Recently, my research has focused on the background of trephining along with instances in which it was utilized. Nell, my deduction is that should Rufus Vane be brought to a reputable medical facility and undergo trephining across various areas of his head, it could revive his recollections and mental capabilities.”
“Hugh!” cried Nell, her tone rich with objection. “You cannot possibly be serious!”
“I certainly do. Furthermore, I have made up my mind that I am obligated to introduce the topic to Lorna.”

“You must NOT engage in anything of the sort, Hugh Carrow,” Nell exclaimed passionately. “Oh, Hugh, you will refrain—you will refrain. Such cruelty is beyond you. Give me your word that you will not.”
“Why, Nell-girl, I never thought you’d react in this manner. Listen to reason—”

“I will not be reasonable—I am unable to be reasonable—I AM reasonable. You are the one who is unreasonable. Hugh, have you at any point considered what Lorna would experience if Rufus Vane was returned to his proper mind? Merely halt and consider it! Currently her unhappiness is bad enough; however, existing as the nurse and caregiver for Rufus is a thousand times simpler for her than existing as the wife of Rufus. I know—I KNOW! It cannot be thought of. Do not interfere in this business. Allow what is adequate to remain as it is.”

“ Nell, I have given exhaustive thought to that side of the matter. However, it is my belief that a physician must place the holiness of a patient's mind and body higher than any other concerns, regardless of the repercussions. It is my conviction that his obligation is to strive to bring back health and sanity, provided any prospect at all remains.”

“However, Rufus does not belong to you as a patient in that regard,” Nell exclaimed, shifting her approach. “HAD Lorna questioned you about whether he could be helped, IT WOULD BE your obligation to reveal your true opinion to her. You possess no entitlement to interfere, though.”
“It doesn't seem like meddling to me. A dozen years back, Uncle Dave informed Lorna that Rufus was beyond help. Naturally, she accepts that as truth.”
“And if it wasn’t true, why did Uncle Dave tell her that?” Nell exclaimed, triumphantly. “Is his knowledge about it any less than yours?”

“I do not believe so—even if stating this might appear arrogant and self-important. Furthermore, it is just as clear to you as it is to me that he holds a certain bias against what he terms 'these new-fangled notions of cutting and carving.’ He is resistant even to performing surgery for appendicitis.”
“He is correct,” Nell cried out, altering her position entirely. “Personally, I am convinced that you contemporary physicians are far too eager to test your ideas on living people.”
“If I had hesitated to perform a particular test, Rhoda Allonby would not be among the living now,” Hugh insisted. “I accepted the danger—and rescued her.”

“I have had enough of listening to talk regarding Rhoda Allonby,” exclaimed Nell—unfairly in the extreme, because Hugh had not brought up Mrs. Allonby’s name a single time after the day he informed Nell about his triumph concerning her. Nor was he at fault when different individuals debated the matter.
Hugh was somewhat offended.

“Nell, I did not anticipate that you would view the issue in this way,” he remarked rather coldly, standing up and stepping in the direction of the office door. This represented their initial drift toward a disagreement.
However, Nell hurried behind him and pulled him back.
“Listen, Hugh, you must refrain from 'going off mad.’ Take a seat beside me so I can offer a most gorgeous apology, for my remark was completely out of line. However—oh, if you only understood—”
Nell stopped herself at the last second. She came exceedingly close to revealing the secret belonging to Lorna.
“Understood the way a female views the matter,” she finished haltingly.

“I believe I am aware.
