Having examined the situation from all perspectives, I have arrived at the inescapable conclusion that I am obligated to inform Lorna of my belief regarding the possibility of Rufus being restored to his former self; at that point, my duty ceases. The decision regarding her subsequent actions will rest entirely with her.”
“It seems to me you lack the right to place this kind of burden upon her. Her load is already heavy enough. She lacks money—in what way could she pay for an operation like that?”
“Her decision is what matters,” Hugh insisted with stubbornness.
“You state that it is your belief that Rufus is capable of being healed. However, are you CERTAIN about that?”

“By no means. No person could be certain about that. Lesions of the brain itself might have occurred, and their consequences can never be erased. However, if his memory loss and other impairments result simply from the pressure that particular depressed bone areas exert on the brain centers, as I suspect, he is capable of being healed.”

“But it is merely a potential outcome!” Nell declared. “Now, imagine you inform Lorna and she chooses to undergo the surgery. The expense will be huge. She will be forced to take out a loan, or dispose of her small holdings. And imagine the surgery fails and Rufus does not change.
“In what way can she return the funds she takes on credit, or earn a livelihood for her own sake and that huge dependent being if the property is sold?”
“Oh, I am aware—I am aware. However, informing her remains my obligation. That belief is something I cannot escape.”
“Oh, the stubbornness of the Carrows is familiar to me,” Nell groaned. “However, you should not undertake this entirely on your own authority. Seek advice from Doctor Dave.”
“I HAVE done so,” Hugh admitted with hesitation.
“And what was his reply?”

“To put it shortly—like you mentioned—do not disturb what is already fine. Besides his bias opposing modern surgical techniques, I fear he views the situation from your perspective—refrain from doing it, for the sake of Lorna.”

“There now,” Nell exclaimed victoriously. “Hugh, I truly believe you must defer to the verdict of a person almost eighty years old, one who has witnessed so much and personally rescued dozens of individuals—without question, what he thinks should carry greater weight than the thoughts of a simple boy.”
“I appreciate it.”
“Do not laugh. The situation is far too serious.”
“My point is precisely that. It IS serious. Present here is a man who constitutes an incapacitated burden. Reason and usefulness may be restored to him—”
“In the past, he proved immensely helpful,” Nell remarked with scathing sarcasm.

“A opportunity to prove himself and make amends for his previous actions might be granted to him. Knowledge of this is kept from his wife. I possess this information. Consequently, informing her about the existence of this chance is required of me. That, in essence, constitutes my choice.”
“Delay making a 'decision’ for now, Hugh. Get another opinion. See what Captain Saul thinks regarding it.”
“All right. However, Nell, I will not commit to following what he thinks.
“A person has to make this choice on their own. I could not have a clear conscience if I remained quiet about the matter.”
“Oh, your conscience!” groaned Nell. “Uncle Dave has a conscience as well, doesn’t he, I suppose?”

“Yes. However, his conscience is not mine to keep. Come, Nell, were Lorna not involved in this matter—if the situation were entirely abstract, you would be of one mind with me,—you are aware you would.”

“I would not,” pledged Nell, attempting to convince herself as well. “Oh, Hugh, you may debate throughout the entire night, yet you will not persuade me. Simply query Miss Winifred regarding her opinion on the matter.”

“When you summon Miss Winifred to reinforce your point, Nell, you have resorted to your ultimate defense. 'Just like a man,’ she will remark, while venting her intense anger. It does not matter. Miss Winifred has no business settling this matter. The decision rests solely with Lorna.”

“You are well aware of the way she is going to choose,” Nell said, nearly weeping. “She possesses standards of obligation as well. It is beyond me how you are able to assume that kind of burden yourself. I would be unable to.”
“'For following the right because it is right would be wise even if one disregards the outcome,'”
quoted Hugh.
“Oh, you consider two lines of verse to be a persuasive piece of reasoning!” Nell mocked. “Such behavior is typical of a man.”
And after that, a laugh escaped her against her own will. The sound mirrored Miss Winifred so closely.

“Well, provided you refuse to take Tennyson as a reliable source, maybe you’ll trust what is spoken by a Greater than he,” Hugh declared gravely. “'Ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free.’ That is something I believe, Nell, using every bit of my heart. In the Bible—or across all literature—no verse is greater or grander, and it is the TRUEST, assuming trueness possesses comparative degrees. Furthermore, speaking the truth, precisely as he perceives and trusts it, constitutes a man's primary obligation.”
“The truth, under these circumstances, will not liberate poor Lorna,” Nell sighed. “Her bondage will likely become even more bitter as a result. Oh, Hugh, I CAN’T believe you are correct.”

A swift wave of a severe form of flu at the Glen and down in the fishing village made Hugh so occupied over the following two weeks that he lacked the opportunity to make the promised call on Captain Saul. Nell continued to hope despite the odds that he had given up the notion concerning Rufus Vane, and, choosing not to stir up trouble, she mentioned the matter no further. Nevertheless, it remained constantly on her mind.

“I ponder whether revealing to him that Lorna harbors feelings for Adrian would be proper,” she mused. “He would refrain from ever letting her guess his knowledge, meaning her pride would remain unhurt, and it MIGHT persuade him to leave Rufus Vane in peace. Ought I to—ought I to? No, when all is said, I am unable to do so. A vow is inviolable, and I possess no right to expose Lorna’s confidence. Yet oh, no matter in my life has ever caused me as much distress as this does. It is ruining the spring—it is ruining all things.”

Hugh suddenly suggested one night that they travel down to visit Captain Saul. Nell assented with a heavy heart, and the two departed. Fourteen days of gentle sun had effected a wondrous change in the dreary countryside across which Hugh’s crow had traveled. Dry, brown, and warm, the hills and fields stood prepared to burst into bud and flower; the harbor was once more quivering with laughter; like a shining red ribbon lay the long harbor road; down upon the dunes, a group of boys who had gone out smelt fishing were setting fire to the dense, dry sandhill grass from the previous summer. Across the dunes, the flames surged rosily, casting their crimson banners against the black gulf past them, and lighting up the channel alongside the fishing village. Under different circumstances, this picturesque sight would have charmed Nell’s eyes; however, she took no pleasure in this stroll. Hugh was not enjoying it either. Their customary friendly companionship and Josephian harmony of preference and perspective were regrettably absent. Nell’s rejection of the entire undertaking manifested in the arrogant tilt of her head and the deliberate courtesy of her comments. Hugh’s lips were fixed in the full stubbornness of the Carrows, yet anxiety filled his eyes. Doing what he considered his duty was his intention; nevertheless, being at odds with Nell proved a steep cost. On the whole, arriving at the light brought relief to both of them—along with guilt for feeling that relief.

Captain Saul stowed the net he had been mending and greeted them with great joy. Nell realized he appeared older in the revealing brightness of the spring evening than he ever had before. His hair was significantly more gray, and a slight tremor affected his sturdy, aging hand. Nevertheless, his gaze remained sharp and unwavering in his blue eyes, through which his resolute spirit shone with courage and fearlessness.

As Hugh delivered his message, Captain Saul heard him out without uttering a word, completely astonished. Understanding the depth of the old man's devotion to Lorna, Nell was convinced he would take her part, even if she doubted this would alter Hugh's stance. Consequently, she was immensely taken aback when Captain Saul declared, with a deliberate and mournful yet steadfast resolve, that Lorna ought to be informed.
“Oh, Captain Saul, I believed you would not utter such words,” she cried in dismay. “It was my expectation that you wished to avoid creating additional difficulties for her.”
A shake of his head came from Captain Saul.

“Refusing isn't what I wish to do. Your perspective on this matter is clear to me, Mistress Carrow—because I share those exact sentiments. However, personal emotions cannot serve as our guide in life—indeed, relying on them would frequently result in disaster. A single dependable compass exists, and we are required to navigate according to its direction—namely, performing our duty. My view aligns with the doctor's. Should an opportunity exist for Rufus, informing Lorna is necessary. As I see it, no alternative interpretation exists.”
“Well,” said Nell, surrendering to hopelessness, “just wait for Miss Winifred to go after you pair of men.”

“Winifred will surely unleash a complete barrage on us,” Captain Saul agreed. “Although you female folk are delightful beings, Mistress Carrow, a small flaw in you all is a slight lack of logic. Despite your advanced schooling compared to Winifred's lack of it, the pair of you are completely identical in this regard. Whether that makes you any less desirable is something I doubt. It seems to me that logic is rather unfeeling and stern. So, I am going to make us some tea for us to enjoy while discussing agreeable topics, simply to soothe our thoughts a little.”

At the very least, her mind was pacified so much by Captain Saul’s conversation and tea that Nell refrained from causing Hugh the sharp suffering during the journey back that she had intentionally planned for him. The burning question was not mentioned by her whatsoever, yet she conversed pleasantly about different subjects, allowing Hugh to realize that his forgiveness was granted under protest.

“Captain Saul appears extremely weak and stooped this spring. He has been aged by the winter,” Nell remarked mournfully. “I fear he will shortly depart to search for lost Margaret. The thought of it is unbearable to me.”
“When Captain Saul 'sets out to sea,' Seven Gulls is going to be a different place,” Hugh concurred.
He walked to the residence further up the stream the next night. Until he came back, Nell roamed about in a state of gloom.
“So, what response did Lorna give?” was her demand upon his entry.
“Hardly anything. It seemed to me that she was quite stunned.”
“And will the operation be performed on her?”
“Her decision will be made very soon, after she thinks it over.”

Exhausted, Hugh dropped heavily into the armchair in front of the hearth. He had a worn appearance. Disclosing the news to Lorna had proven to be a difficult task. Furthermore, remembering the fright that flashed in her eyes as she grasped his words gave him no pleasure. At present, with the decision finalized, he found himself plagued by uncertainty regarding his own judgment.
Nell gave him a remorseful look; after that, she slid onto the rug next to him, resting her shiny red head against his arm.
“Hugh, I have been quite awful about this whole thing. I am not going to act that way again. Kindly just refer to me as red-headed and pardon my behavior.”

Through this, Hugh grasped that no "I told you so" would ever be uttered, regardless of the outcome. Yet his comfort remained incomplete. Duty expressed in theory is a single matter, whereas duty executed in reality is entirely different, particularly when the actor faces the desolate gaze of a woman.

A certain intuition prompted Nell to avoid Lorna throughout the subsequent three days. Upon the third night, Lorna walked down to the small home and informed Hugh of her decision; she intended to bring Rufus to Montreal so he could undergo the operation.

Her complexion was extremely pale, and she appeared to have enveloped herself once more in her former coat of detachment. Her eyes, however, no longer retained the expression that had troubled Hugh; instead, they were chilly and luminous, and she began talking over particulars with him in a sharp, matter-of-fact manner. Arrangements required making, and numerous matters needed consideration. As soon as Lorna obtained the facts she sought, she departed for home. Nell desired to accompany her on foot for a portion of the journey.
“It is best you do not,” Lorna replied abruptly. “The rain that fell today has soaked the earth. Good-night.”

“Is my friend gone?” Nell asked, sighing. “Should the procedure prove effective and Rufus Vane recovers his true self, Lorna is going to withdraw to a distant sanctuary within her spirit where she will remain lost to all of us forever.”
“It may be that she will abandon him,” Hugh remarked.

“Lorna could not possibly act in such a manner, Hugh. A powerful feeling of obligation guides her. She mentioned to me on one occasion that Grandmother West constantly instilled in her the principle that whenever she took on a duty, she was required to fulfill it without fail, regardless of the outcome. It stands as a chief principle of hers. It seems quite out of date, I imagine.”

“Do not feel resentment, Nell-girl. You are aware that you do not consider it outmoded—you are aware that you hold the exact same belief regarding the holiness of undertaken obligations yourself. And your view is correct. Evading obligations represents the bane of our contemporary existence—the hidden cause behind all the agitation and dissatisfaction that is boiling in the world.”
“Thus saith the preacher,” Nell mocked. Yet beneath her taunting tone she recognized the truth of his words; and her heart ached deeply for Lorna.
Seven days afterwards, Miss Winifred crashed down upon the small dwelling like a snowslide. Because Hugh was out, Nell had no choice but to endure the force of the collision by herself.
Barely taking the time to remove her hat, Miss Winifred started right away.

“Nell, are you trying to say that the rumors I’ve been hearing are factual—that Dr. Carrow informed Lorna that Rufus can be healed, and that she intends to bring him to Montreal so he can undergo surgery?”
“Yes, it is entirely factual, Miss Winifred,” Nell stated courageously.

“Well, it’s a matter of heartless savagery, that is what it amounts to,” stated Miss Winifred, who was immensely disturbed. “I truly believed Dr. Carrow to be a respectable gentleman. I never imagined he was capable of committing such a deed.”

“It was Dr. Carrow’s belief that he had a responsibility to inform Lorna that Rufus might survive,” Nell stated with vigor, “and,” she went on, her allegiance to Hugh winning out, “I am of the same mind as him.”
“Oh, no, you don’t, dearie,” remarked Miss Winifred. “Nobody possessing any bowels of compassion could.”
“Captain Saul does.”

“Do not repeat that foolish old man's words to me,” Miss Winifred exclaimed. “And regardless of who shares his opinion, it matters nothing to me. Consider—CONSIDER the consequences for that unfortunate, pursued, tormented girl.”
“It IS on our minds. However, Hugh holds the view that the well-being of a patient’s spirit and physique must be placed by a physician above every other concern.”

“That is typical of a man. Yet I anticipated a finer response from you, Nell,” remarked Miss Winifred, feeling additional grief rather than anger; after which she began to assault Nell using the exact same points that Nell had employed against Hugh; and Nell bravely shielded her spouse by utilizing the arguments he had deployed to defend himself. Extended was the battle, until Miss Winifred finally brought it to a close.
“It is a monstrous injustice,” she announced, nearly weeping. “A monstrous injustice—that is precisely what it is. My dear, unfortunate Lorna!”
“Wouldn’t it be right to give a bit of thought to Rufus as well?” begged Nell.
“Rufus! Rufus Vane! HE’S cheerful enough. Present day, he is a better behaved and more respectable part of the community than he was at any point prior.
“Indeed, he was a heavy drinker and possibly something worse. Is it your intention to free him once more so he can bellow and destroy?”
“He could change for the better,” stated wretched Nell, under attack by enemies on the outside and a betrayer on the inside.

“Reform your grandmother!” Miss Winifred retorted. “Rufus Vane received the harm that resulted in his current state during a drunken brawl. His fate is DESERVED. It was inflicted upon him as a retribution. The doctor, I don’t believe, has any right to meddle with God’s visitations.”
“It remains a mystery how Rufus suffered his injuries, Miss Winifred. A tavern fight might not be the cause. He could have been ambushed and mugged instead.”

“Swine MIGHT chirp, though their lips are ill-suited for the task,” declared Miss Winifred. “At any rate, the essence of your news indicates the matter is concluded, rendering further speech futile. Since that is the case, I will remain silent. I have no intention of ruining MY teeth by chewing on rasps. Whenever an outcome is inevitable, I yield to it. However, I prefer to be utterly certain beforehand that it truly IS unavoidable. At present, I shall apply MY efforts to soothing and supporting Lorna. Besides,” Miss Winifred continued, her mood lifting with optimism, “it is possible that Rufus is beyond help.”

Once Lorna had determined her course, she carried it out with her typical speed and determination. No matter what matters of life or death were waiting outside, cleaning the house had to be completed before anything else. With prompt aid from Miss Winifred, the gray house located up the brook was restored to immaculate cleanliness and order. Having voiced her mind to Nell, and subsequently to Hugh and Captain Saul—without holding back from either, rest assured—Miss Winifred refrained from ever discussing the issue with Lorna. Accepting the reality of Rufus’s surgery, she brought it up in a practical manner whenever required, and disregarded it otherwise. Lorna made no effort to speak about it. Throughout those lovely spring days, she remained extremely distant and silent. Her visits to Nell were infrequent, and despite her constant politeness and friendliness, that precise civility formed a frozen wall separating her from the inhabitants of the small house. The former jests, mirth, and easy familiarity over everyday matters were unable to touch her across that divide. Nell declined to take offense. She recognized that Lorna was held fast by a gruesome fear—a fear that isolated her from every small moment of joy and time of delight. Whenever a single grand emotion dominates the spirit, every other emotion is pushed to the side. At no point in her existence had Lorna Vane recoiled from what was to come with such unbearable horror. Yet, she advanced along her chosen track as steadfastly as the ancient martyrs trod their selected path, fully aware that its conclusion was the burning anguish of the stake.

Resolving the monetary issue proved less difficult than Nell had anticipated. From Captain Saul, Lorna obtained the required funds, and because she demanded it, he accepted a mortgage upon the small farm.

“With that settled, the poor girl has one less burden on her mind,” Miss Winifred remarked to Nell, “and so do I. Provided Rufus recovers sufficiently to resume working, his earnings will cover the interest payments; should he fail to do so, I am certain Captain Saul will find a way to spare Lorna from that obligation. He practically admitted it to me. 'Winifred, my years are advancing,’ he stated, 'and I lack any offspring. While Lorna would refuse a present from someone who is alive, she might accept it from someone who has passed away.’ Therefore, that particular matter will turn out fine. If only every other issue could be resolved just as smoothly. Regarding that miserable Rufus, his behavior over the past few days has been terrible. You must take my word for it, he was possessed! His antics prevented Lorna and me from accomplishing our chores. On one occasion, he ran her ducks all over the yard until the majority of them perished. Furthermore, he refused to assist us in any way. Occasionally, as you are aware, he renders himself rather useful by carrying in firewood and buckets of water. This past week, however, sending him to the well resulted in his attempting to descend inside it. At one point I pondered, 'If you were to simply plunge down there head-first, all our problems would be neatly resolved.’”
“Ah, Miss Winifred!”

“Now, you don't need to call me Miss Winifred, my dear Nell. EVERYONE would have come to the identical conclusion. Should the physicians in Montreal succeed in transforming Rufus Vane into a sensible person, they are truly remarkable.”

At the beginning of May, Lorna traveled to Montreal with Rufus. Accompanying her was Hugh, who wanted to assist her and handle her required preparations. Upon returning home, he reported that the Montreal surgeon they had seen shared his view regarding the high probability of Rufus’s recovery.
“Very comforting,” Miss Winifred remarked sarcastically.
A sigh was all that came from Nell. During their farewell, Lorna had acted extremely detached.

Yet she had given her word that she would send a letter. The missive arrived ten days following the return of Hugh. Within it, Lorna stated that the surgical procedure had been carried out with success and that Rufus was recovering well.
“What is her meaning when she uses 'successfully?’” Nell inquired. “Is she implying that the restoration of Rufus’s memory has truly occurred?”

“Unlikely—given that she omits any mention of it,” Hugh remarked. “The term 'successfully’ is employed by her through the eyes of the surgeon. Having been executed, the procedure yielded standard outcomes. Nevertheless, determining if Rufus’s senses will ultimately be brought back, completely or partially, remains premature. A sudden recovery of his memory would not be expected. Should it happen whatsoever, the progression is going to be step-by-step. Does her account end there?”

“Yes—that is her letter. Its length is very brief. Poor girl, the strain she is experiencing must be terrible. Hugh Carrow, I desire to say a great number of things to you, except that doing so would be mean.”

“Miss Winifred utters them on your behalf,” Hugh remarked, smiling ruefully. “Every time I cross her path, she gives me a dressing-down. She leaves no doubt in my mind that she considers me hardly superior to a killer, and that she deems it a terrible shame Dr. Dave permitted me to take over his practice. She went so far as to tell me that the Methodist doctor across the harbor ought to be chosen over me. In Miss Winifred's eyes, the intensity of disapproval can reach no higher peak.”

“Should Winifred Tolley fall ill, Doctor Dave and the Methodist physician are not the ones she would call upon,” Tabitha sniffed. “It is you who would be dragged from your well-deserved sleep during the night, doctor, dear, were she to suffer a fit of distress, indeed she would. Afterward, she would probably claim your charge exceeded all fairness. Yet pay her no attention, doctor, dear. Every type of person is required to form a world.”

For a period after this, not a single message arrived from Lorna. As the days of May slipped slowly past in a delightful sequence, green plants, flowers, and purple shades covered the coast of Seven Gulls Harbor. During the latter part of May, Hugh returned home on a certain day, and Tabitha was waiting to meet him in the stable yard.

“Doctor, dear, I fear that Mrs. Doctor is troubled by something,” she remarked with an air of secrecy. “A letter arrived for her this afternoon, and ever since, she has done nothing but wander about the garden while speaking to herself. Doctor, dear, you are aware that spending so much time standing is bad for her. She chose not to reveal her news to me, and doctor, dear, I am not a curious person and never have been, but she is clearly disturbed. And being disturbed is bad for her.”

Hugh made his way to the garden with a good deal of anxiety. Was something wrong at Grey Shutters? Sitting on the rustic seat near the brook, Nell did not appear distressed, however, even though she was undoubtedly very agitated. Her eyes had turned their deepest gray, and bright red patches glowed upon her cheeks.
“What has occurred, Nell?”
Nell uttered a strange, quiet chuckle.

“You will scarcely trust my words when I share this, Hugh. It still seems unbelievable to me. Just as Tabitha remarked recently, 'I feel like a fly coming to live in the sun—dazed-like.’ Everything is so beyond belief. Twenty times I have gone through the letter, yet each reading yields the same result—my eyes cannot be trusted. Oh, Hugh, you proved to be correct—entirely correct. That is obvious enough to me at present—and my self-reproach is so deep—and can you truly pardon me ever?”
“Nell, unless you become clear, I’ll shake you. You ought to make Wexcombe ashamed. WHAT is the matter?”
“It is unbelievable—it is unbelievable—”
“I shall call Uncle Dave on the telephone,” Hugh remarked, feigning a movement toward the house.

“Take a seat, Hugh. I will attempt to explain it to you. A letter has arrived, and oh, Hugh, the whole thing is so astonishing—so unbelievably astonishing—we never imagined—not a single one of us ever conceived—”

“In a situation like this, taking a seat with an resigned expression, the sole course of action, I presume,” Hugh remarked, “is to remain patient and address the issue step by step. Who sent you that letter?”
“Lorna—and, ah, Hugh—”
“Lorna! Wow! What does she have to report? What is the update regarding Rufus?”
Nell picked up the letter and offered it, displaying a calm sense of drama in an instant.

“Rufus does NOT exist! The individual whom we assumed to be Rufus Vane—and who all the people in Seven Gulls have accepted as Rufus Vane for twelve years—is actually his cousin, Laurence Vane, from Nova Scotia, a man who, as it turns out, constantly bore a remarkable resemblance to him. Rufus Vane passed away from yellow fever in Cuba thirteen years ago.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “It’s—it’s—just like a man,” Miss Winifred stammered weakly. Her hands shook as she removed her hat. Never before had Miss Winifred been so completely overwhelmed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Nell, it seems I am unable to feel it,” she remarked. “I have listened to you state it—and I trust your word—yet I am unable to grasp it. Rufus Vane has passed away—he has been deceased throughout all these years—and Lorna is no longer bound?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Yes. Freedom has come to her through the truth. That line was the most magnificent in the Bible, just as Hugh remarked.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Relate the entire story, Nell, dearie. Ever since receiving your call I’ve been completely baffled, believe ME. Winifred Tolley has never felt so kerflummuxed until now.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “There is not much to relate. Lorna wrote a brief letter. She omitted the details. Laurence Vane—this man—has regained his memory and realizes his identity. He states that Rufus contracted yellow fever in Cuba, forcing the Four Sisters to depart in his absence. Laurence remained to care for him. However, he passed away soon after.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “The reason Laurence refrained from writing to Lorna was his plan to return home immediately and speak to her in person.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “And what kept him from doing so?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “I think his mishap probably got in the way. Hugh mentions that Laurence Vane might very well have no memory of his mishap, or the events preceding it, and perhaps won't ever recall it. Its occurrence was likely shortly following the passing of Rufus. Once Lorna sends another letter, we might discover additional details.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Is it stated what her plans are? What is the date of her return home?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “She states that she intends to remain beside Laurence Vane up to the point when he is able to depart from the hospital. A letter has been sent by her to his relatives in Nova Scotia. It appears that the sole close family member Laurence has is an elder sister who is married. That sister was still alive at the time Laurence embarked aboard the Four Sisters, though naturally it is uncertain to us what might have occurred in the intervening time. Have you at any time met Laurence Vane, Miss Winifred?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “I did. Everything is returning to my mind. Eighteen years back, when he and Rufus must have been roughly seventeen, he stayed here to visit his Uncle Abner. You see, they were double cousins. Their mothers were twin sisters and their fathers were brothers, so they possessed a striking resemblance to one another. Naturally,” Miss Winifred appended with scorn, “this wasn't a case of those weird likenesses written about in stories where a pair of individuals are so identical that they can take each other's spots without their closest loved ones knowing the difference. Back then, provided you observed them side by side and close by, you could distinguish easily enough between Laurence and Rufus. When separated, or at a bit of a distance, telling them apart was harder. Those two scamps pulled many pranks on folks and considered it big entertainment. Laurence Vane stood slightly taller and considerably plumper than Rufus—even if neither could be deemed truly fat—for both belonged to the slim sort. Rufus possessed a cheek color higher than Laurence, along with hair a shade paler. Yet their facial traits were identical, and each shared that strange ocular quirk—one hazel eye and one blue. Outside of that, they didn't share many similarities. Although Laurence was a rascal for pranks, he was a genuinely pleasant guy, even if some claimed he enjoyed a drink even back then. Still, everyone preferred him over Rufus. He stayed in these parts for about a month. Lorna didn't ever see him; she was merely eight or nine at the time, and I recall now that the entire winter was spent by her across the harbor with her grandmother West. Captain Saul was absent as well—it was during that winter that he suffered a shipwreck on the Magdalens. I doubt that he or Lorna had ever been told about the cousin from Nova Scotia resembling Rufus so closely. Not a soul gave him a thought when Captain Saul escorted Rufus—I mean to say, Laurence—back home. Naturally, the rest of us believed Rufus had undergone a major transformation—he had grown so heavy and stocky. However, we attributed that to his ordeal, which was undoubtedly the cause, because, as I previously mentioned, Laurence wasn't heavy initially either. Furthermore, there existed no other clue for us to divine the truth, since the person's mind was completely vanished. I fail to see how our collective deception is at all surprising. Even so, it is a shocking realization. And Lorna gave up her finest years taking care of an individual who possessed no right to her devotion! Oh, curse the men! Whatever action they take, it turns out wrong. And regardless of their identity, they turn out to be someone they ought not to be. They truly irritate me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Hugh and Captain Saul are men, and the truth has finally been uncovered because of them,” Nell said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Well, I grant that,” Miss Winifred gave in with hesitation. “My harsh words to the doctor make me sorry now. Never before in my life have I experienced shame over something I uttered to a man. Even so, I doubt that I will admit it to him. He will simply be forced to assume it. Well, Nell, my dear, we are blessed that the Lord fails to grant every prayer we make. Continuously and fervently, I have prayed that Rufus would not be healed by the surgery. Naturally, I refrained from stating it in such direct terms. Nevertheless, that thought resided at the rear of my consciousness, and I am certain the Lord recognized it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Indeed, He has granted the essence of what you prayed for. Your genuine desire was that circumstances would not become more difficult for Lorna. I fear that within my private thoughts I had been wishing for the procedure to fail, a feeling for which I am properly disgraced.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “In what way does Lorna appear to handle it?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Her writing resembles that of someone stunned. It is my belief that she scarcely comprehends it so far, just as we do not. Her sole mention of her own person consists of the statement, 'It all seems like a strange dream to me, Nell.’”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Poor child! I imagine that once a prisoner’s chains are removed, he would feel strange and disoriented without them at first. Nell, dearie, there is an idea that keeps entering my head. What about Adrian Treleaven? Both of us are aware that Lorna cared for him. Did you ever consider that he might have cared for her?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “It—did—once,” conceded Nell, believing she could say that much.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Indeed, there was no cause for me to believe he was, yet it simply seemed to my mind that he HAD to be. Look here, Nell, dearie, God is my witness that I am no match-maker, and I hold every act of that nature in contempt. Even so, were I in your shoes and composing a letter to that Treleaven fellow, I would merely bring up, in a passing way, the recent occurrence. That is precisely how I would act.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Naturally, I am going to bring it up in my letter to him,” Nell remarked, speaking somewhat coldly. For some reason, Miss Winifred was not a person with whom she could converse about this matter. Even so, she was forced to acknowledge that this very idea had been secretly present in her own thoughts from the moment she learned Lorna was free. However, she refused to cheapen it through open conversation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Naturally, there isn't any huge hurry, dearie. However, thirteen years have passed since Rufus Vane died, and Lorna has spent a sufficient portion of her existence on him. We shall simply observe the outcome. Regarding Laurence Vane, who departed and then returned from the dead when his death and end were universally assumed, exactly as a man would do, I feel genuinely bad for him. He will appear out of place everywhere.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 32 MISS WINIFRED DISCUSSES THE AFFAIR
text: “Given that he remains young, he will have the capacity to establish his position once more, provided he achieves a full recovery, which appears probable. The situation must feel exceedingly peculiar to the unfortunate man. It seems to me that the entire duration following his mishap will be a blank to him.”

Two weeks afterward Lorna Vane returned by herself to the ancient residence where she had passed a great number of painful years. During the June dusk she crossed the fields toward Nell’s place, and materialized with the suddenness of a ghost inside the fragrant garden.

“Lorna!” Nell exclaimed, astonished. “From where did you suddenly appear? Your arrival was completely unknown to us. What kept you from writing? A meeting at the station would have been arranged for you.”
“Somehow I was unable to write, Nell. Trying to express anything using a pen and ink felt completely useless. Besides, returning silently and without attracting attention was what I desired.”

Nell wrapped her arms around Lorna and planted a kiss on her. Lorna affectionately returned the embrace. Looking washed out and exhausted, she uttered a soft sigh while sinking onto the grass next to a massive patch of daffodils, which shone amid the faint, silver-hued dusk like stars of gold.
“And did you return to your home by yourself, Lorna?”

“Yes. Laurence Vane’s sister arrived in Montreal and brought him back home with her. Poor guy, he regretted leaving me—even though he didn't know me when his memory began to return. He held onto me during those initial difficult days as he attempted to understand that Rufus’s death had not happened just yesterday, as he felt it had. The whole situation was extremely tough on him. I gave him as much assistance as I was able to. His sister's arrival made things simpler for him, since he felt like he had just seen her a short time ago. Luckily she looked much the same, which served to aid him as well.”
“It is completely peculiar and marvelous, Lorna. I believe not one of us comprehends it as yet.”

“I am unable to. Sixty minutes ago, when I stepped inside that house across the way, I had the sensation that it HAD to be a dream—that Rufus had to be present, displaying his innocent grin, just as he was for such a lengthy time. Nell, I still appear to be numb. I am neither joyful nor sorrowful—nor ANYTHING at all. My sensation is that a piece of my existence was abruptly ripped away, leaving a dreadful void. My sensation is that I cannot be myself—as though I have transformed into a different person and am unable to adapt. A terrifyingly solitary, confused, and powerless sensation comes over me. Being with you once more brings comfort—it feels like you serve as a kind of anchor holding my wandering spirit. Oh, Nell, every bit of it fills me with fear—the rumors, the surprise, and the inquiries. Considering that makes me desire that my return home had never happened. Dr. Dave waited by the station as I stepped from the locomotive—he drove me to my house. The unfortunate old fellow suffers greatly since he informed me a long time back that no remedy existed for Rufus. 'I genuinely believed that, Lorna,’ he uttered to me this very day. 'However, I ought to have advised you against relying on my judgment—I ought to have advised you to consult a expert. Had I done so, you would have been spared numerous painful years, and poor Laurence Vane numerous squandered ones. I hold myself deeply at fault, Lorna.’ I instructed him to refrain from that—he acted according to what he believed correct. He has constantly shown such goodness to me—I was unable to tolerate seeing him distress himself about the matter.”
“And Rufus—I mean Laurence? Has he completely recovered his memory?”

“For the most part. Naturally, numerous particulars still escape him—though his memory recovers further with each passing day. The night following the burial of Rufus, he stepped outside to take a stroll. Carrying Rufus’s watch and funds, he intended to return those items to me, together with the letter I wrote. He acknowledges visiting an establishment frequented by seamen—and he recalls consuming alcohol—and that is all. Nell, the instant his own identity returned to him is something I will always remember. His gaze met mine, filled with a wise yet confused look. I inquired, ‘Do you know me, Rufus?’ To which he replied, ‘I never saw you before. Who are you? And my name is not Rufus. I am Laurence Vane, and Rufus died of yellow fever yesterday! Where am I? What has happened to me?’ I—I lost consciousness, Nell. And from that point on, it has seemed to me as though I am living in a dream.”
“It will not take you long to adapt to this altered situation, Lorna. Moreover, you possess youth—a lifetime lies ahead—and numerous wonderful years remain for you.”

“Maybe I will manage to view it like that after some time, Nell. At this moment I am too exhausted and unconcerned to ponder the future. I am—I am—Nell, I am lonely. I long for Rufus. Isn’t it entirely very odd? Do you know, I was genuinely attached to poor Rufus—Laurence, I guess I ought to say—exactly as I would have been attached to an incapacitated child who relied on me for every single thing. I would not ever have confessed it—I was actually embarrassed by it—since, you see, I had abhorred and detested Rufus so intensely before he departed. When I learned that Captain Saul was transporting him back home I anticipated I would simply harbor the identical feelings toward him. But I never did—even though I kept on despising him as I recalled him previously. From the moment he arrived home I experienced merely compassion—a compassion that pained and distressed me. I assumed at that point that it was simply since his mishap had rendered him so incapacitated and altered. But currently I think it was since a truly distinct individual was present there. Carlo was aware of it, Nell—I realize now that Carlo was aware of it. I constantly considered it odd that Carlo had not recognized Rufus. Canines are typically so loyal. But HE recognized it was not his owner who had returned, even if not one of the others among us did. I had not ever observed Laurence Vane, you know. I recall at present that Rufus one time noted in passing that he possessed a cousin in Nova Scotia who resembled him as closely as a twin; but the matter had slipped from my mind, and regardless I would not ever have considered it of any significance. You see, it never crossed my mind to doubt Rufus’s identity. Every alteration in him appeared to me simply the consequence of the mishap.

“Oh, Nell, I will always remember that April evening when Hugh informed me of his belief that Rufus could be healed! It felt as though I had previously been confined inside a gruesome cage of torment, only for the entrance to be unlocked so I could emerge. Though still tethered to the cage, I was no longer trapped within. Yet during that night, a feeling came over me that a cruel force was dragging me backward into that cage—back toward an agony far more horrific than what I had previously suffered. Hugh was not at fault in my eyes. I believed his judgment was correct. Moreover, he acted with great kindness—stating that should I choose against taking the risk, given how costly and unsure the surgery was, he would hold no grudge against me whatsoever. Even so, the proper choice was clear to me—yet I lacked the courage to confront it. Throughout the entire night, I paced back and forth like a lunatic, attempting to force myself into confronting it. I was unable to, Nell—I believed it was beyond my power—and as dawn arrived, I clenched my jaw and determined that I WOULD NOT. Things would be allowed to stay precisely as they were. My actions were deeply sinful, I admit. Had I simply been forced to live with that choice, it would have served as fair retribution for such sinfulness. For the duration of the day, I stuck to my resolve. Later that afternoon, some errands required me to travel up to the Glen. Because it happened to be one of the calm, sleepy days for Rufus, I departed without leaving anyone with him. My trip lasted slightly past my expectations, causing him to notice my absence. A sense of solitude came over him. Upon my return to the house, he rushed toward me exactly as a youngster would, displaying an expression of immense delight. In that moment, Nell, I simply broke down. Enduring that look upon his pitiful, empty face proved to be beyond my strength. A feeling struck me that I was withholding from a child the opportunity to mature and evolve. Regardless of what the outcome might turn out to be, I recognized my duty to grant him his opportunity. Consequently, I walked over and informed Hugh. Oh, Nell, during those weeks prior to my departure, my behavior must have struck you as abominable. That was never my intention—yet my mind could focus on nothing other than my obligation, while all surrounding things and people seemed like mere phantoms.”
“I am aware—I comprehended, Lorna. And at present it has all finished—your fetter is snapped—no enclosure exists.”

“No cage exists,” Lorna said again distractedly, her slim, tan hands picking at the fringe of grass. “However—it feels like nothing else is there, Nell. You—you recall what I shared with you regarding my foolishness that evening on the sand-bar? It seems a person fails to recover from being foolish rapidly. At times I believe certain individuals remain fools eternally. And being a fool—in that manner—is nearly as terrible as being a—a dog attached to a chain.”

“When your fatigue and confusion pass, your perspective will change greatly,” stated Nell, who refrained from bestowing excessive pity because she was aware of a particular fact that Lorna was ignorant of.
Lorna rested her magnificent head of gold upon the knee of Nell.

“At all events, YOU are mine,” she stated. “Existential emptiness is impossible alongside a companion like that. Nell, stroke my head—in the exact manner you would for a small girl—give me some MATERNAL affection—and allow me to convey, while my obstinate tongue is momentarily freed, precisely what you and your fellowship have signified to me ever since the night of our meeting on the rocky coast.”

text: A windy, golden dawn was spreading across the gulf in waves of radiance one morning when a tired stork, traveling from the Land of Evening Stars, glided across the bar of Seven Gulls Harbor. A drowsy, starry-eyed small child was cradled beneath his wing. Exhausted, the stork gazed around himself yearningly. Although he understood his arrival point was nearby, it remained out of view. The large white light-house positioned upon the red sandstone cliff possessed positive attributes, yet a stork with a shred of sense would never deposit a fresh, velvet child in such a spot. Nestled in a blooming brook valley, an aged gray dwelling enveloped by willows appeared more suitable, though it still felt somewhat improper. Farther along, the gaudy green residence was obviously unacceptable. At that moment, the stork's spirits rose. The ideal location had met his gaze—a small white dwelling resting beside a large, rustling firwood, possessing a curl of blue smoke rising above its kitchen chimney—a dwelling that appeared perfectly designed for babies. Letting out a contented sigh, the stork gently touched down upon the ridge-pole.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 34 THE SHIP O’DREAMS COMES TO HARBOR
text: “Replacing Joy will be the function of this infant,” declared Thirza.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 34 THE SHIP O’DREAMS COMES TO HARBOR

chapter_title: CHAPTER 34 THE SHIP O’DREAMS COMES TO HARBOR
text: “Indeed, James Obed stands as a moniker that holds up durability and won't wash away,” Miss Winifred remarked. “It pleases me that you refrained from overburdening him with a lofty, imaginative title he might feel embarrassed by upon becoming a grandfather. Over at the Glen, Mrs. William Drew bestowed the name Bertie Shakespeare upon her infant. That makes quite a pairing, does it not? Furthermore, it delights me that selecting a title caused you little difficulty. Certain people experience terrible struggles. Following the arrival of the Stanley Flaggs’ initial son, competition regarding his namesake proved so intense that the unfortunate young spirit remained nameless across a two-year span. Subsequently, a brother arrived, resulting in the labels—'Big Baby’ alongside 'Little Baby.’ In the end, Big Baby became Peter while Little Baby became Isaac, honoring the pair of grandfathers, with their christenings occurring simultaneously. Thereupon, every child attempted to determine whether he could out-screech his brother. Are you familiar with the MacNabs, that Highland Scotch kin located behind the Glen? Twelve sons belong to them, with both the firstborn and the lastborn bearing the name Neil—Big Neil alongside Little Neil within one household. text: “I have read somewhere,” Nell said with a laugh, “that while a poem is what the first child is, the tenth is extremely prosy prose. That the twelfth was simply an old story told again might have been what Mrs. MacNab thought.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 34 THE SHIP O’DREAMS COMES TO HARBOR
