chapter_title: CHAPTER 34 THE SHIP O’DREAMS COMES TO HARBOR
text: “Oh, well, Nell, my dear,” Miss Winifred remarked with a wise nod, “that remains to be seen. You and I have fulfilled our duty, and now we are required to entrust whatever remains to Higher Hands.”

By the time Nell returned to the lower floor, a campaign before a general election was gripping both the Island and the whole of Canada. Being a passionate Conservative, Hugh was drawn into the commotion, as his presence was frequently requested to deliver speeches at several county rallies. Miss Winifred expressed her disapproval of his political involvement when she spoke to Nell.
“Dr. Dave was never responsible for that. Dr. Carrow will discover that he has committed an error, trust ME. No respectable person ought to become involved in politics.”
“Shall the country’s administration be abandoned entirely to scoundrels, in that case?” inquired Nell.

“Indeed—provided the scoundrels are Conservative,” stated Miss Winifred, departing with the victory. “Politicians and men in general possess the exact same faults. The only difference is that the Grits are coated far more heavily than the Conservatives—SIGNIFICANTLY more heavily. However, whether dealing with Grit or Tory, I counsel Dr. Carrow to avoid political affairs. Before anyone realizes it, he will be a candidate in a campaign himself, departing for Ottawa during six months of the year while allowing his medical work to fall into ruin.”

“Ah, well, let us not invite difficulty,” Nell remarked. “Its cost is far too steep. Rather, let us observe Little Kit. A G ought to be used to spell his name. Does he not look absolutely gorgeous? Look at the dimples in his elbows. You and I shall raise him to be a fine Conservative, Miss Winifred.”

“Raise him to become a righteous person,” Miss Winifred remarked. “Such men are rare and precious; all the same, remember, I would not wish him to end up a Grit. Regarding the vote, you and I can be grateful that we do not reside across the harbor. Over there, the atmosphere is foul currently. All the Kerrs, Crawfords, and MacAllisters have taken to the warpath, fully prepared for fight. Our side remains tranquil and quiet, given that men are so scarce here. Captain Saul belongs to the Grits, yet I believe he feels disgraced by it, since political talk never comes from him. Beyond any possible doubt, a massive majority will bring the Conservatives back into power once more.”

Miss Winifred had it wrong. Captain Saul stopped by the small home the morning following the election so he could share what had happened. Party politics contains a germ that is exceedingly poisonous, even to a quiet elderly gentleman, which caused Captain Saul’s cheeks to be red and his eyes to gleam with every bit of his former passion.
“Mistress Carrow, a landslide victory has brought the Liberals to power. Following eighteen years during which the Tories misgoverned, this oppressed nation will finally be given an opportunity.”

“Captain Saul, I have never listened to you deliver a speech of such sharp partisan hostility until now. I was unaware that you possessed that degree of political malice,” chuckled Nell, who felt very little agitation regarding the news. Small Kit had uttered “Wow-ga” earlier that day. How could principalities and powers, the ascension and collapse of dynasties, or the defeat of Grit or Tory bear any significance when measured against such a wondrous event?

“A long while has seen its accumulation,” Captain Saul remarked, displaying a deprecating smile. “Only a moderate Grit was what I believed myself to be, yet upon receiving the news of our success, the true extent of my Grittiness became clear to me.”
“It is known to you that the doctor and I belong to the Conservative party.”

“Ah, well, that is the single fault I am aware of regarding either of you, Mistress Carrow. Winifred shares those Tory views as well. On my journey from the Glen, I dropped by to inform her of the news.”
“Were you unaware that you were risking your life?”
“Indeed, yet I was unable to hold back from giving in to the urge.”
“In what manner did she react?”

“Relatively peaceful, Mistress Carrow, relatively peaceful. She remarks, says she, 'Well, Providence dispatches times of mortification to a nation, just as to persons. You Grits have suffered cold and hunger for numerous years. Hurry to get warm and satisfied, because your time in power will be short.’ 'Well, now Winifred,’ I remark, 'perhaps Providence believes Canada requires an exceptionally extended period of mortification.’ Ah, Tabitha, have YOU received the word? The Liberals are elected.”
Tabitha had only recently stepped out of the kitchen, accompanied by the smell of delicious food that appeared to constantly surround her.

“Now, are they?” she asked, displaying lovely indifference. “Well, I never could perceive that my bread rose with any less lightness when Grits held office than when they did not. And if a particular party, Mrs. Doctor, dear, can cause rain to fall before the week ends, thereby keeping our kitchen garden from being totally ruined, then that is the party for which Tabitha will cast her vote. Meanwhile, would you mind stepping outside for a moment to share your view regarding the dinner meat? I am afraid that it is extremely tough, and it seems to me that changing our butcher would be a good idea, just as changing our government would be.”

Seven days after that, when evening arrived, Nell journeyed to the Point in order to try to buy some fresh fish from Captain Saul, departing from Little Kit for her very first time. The event was a major tragedy. What if he began weeping? What if Tabitha lacked the precise knowledge of how to care for him? Tabitha remained untroubled and peaceful.
“Is it not true, Mrs. Doctor, dear, that my experience with him matches yours?”

“Indeed, with him—yet not with different infants. Why, three sets of twins were in my care when I was a youngster, Tabitha. Whenever they wept, I calmly administered peppermint or castor oil to them. Recalling the detachment with which I handled every one of those infants and their troubles seems rather strange today.”
“Oh, well, provided Little Kit weeping occurs, I shall simply place a hot water bag against his small belly,” Tabitha stated.
“It shouldn’t be excessively warm, you see,” Nell stated with concern. Oh, was making the trip truly a prudent idea?
“Do not worry, Mrs. Doctor, my dear. Tabitha will never burn a little man. Bless him, he does not think of crying at all.”

Nell eventually pulled herself free and ended up taking pleasure in her stroll to the Point, passing through the elongated shadows cast by the setting sun. Captain Saul was absent from the lighthouse living room, which was occupied instead by a different individual—a good-looking, middle-aged fellow possessing a firm, smooth-shaven chin, whom Nell did not recognize. All the same, the moment she took a seat, he started conversing with her as confidently as if he were a long-time friend. Neither his words nor his manner contained anything improper, yet Nell felt somewhat offended by such unceremonious familiarity from someone who was an utter stranger. She gave chilled responses, offering only the bare minimum that politeness demanded. Undeterred, her fellow occupant continued speaking for a number of minutes before offering an apology and departing. Nell felt positive that she caught a glint in his eye, which irked her. Who could this person be? An elusive sense of familiarity attached to him, yet she was sure he had never crossed her path before.
“Captain Saul, who was the person that just left?” she inquired, when Captain Saul entered.
“Ambrose Kerr,” the captain replied.

“Ambrose Kerr!” shouted Nell. “Oh, Captain Saul—it was not—yes, it WAS the sound of his voice—oh, Captain Saul, I failed to recognize him—and I acted very rudely toward him! WHY failed he to inform me? He had to have realized I failed to recognize him.”

“He would not utter a single remark regarding it—he would merely relish the jest. Do not be concerned about ignoring him—he will consider it amusing. Indeed, Ambrose has finally shaved away his beard and trimmed his hair. His political party has won, as you are aware. I failed to recognize him myself when I initially set eyes on him. He was present inside Carter Flagg’s store located at the Glen during the evening following election day, accompanied by a throng of people, anticipating the results. Around midnight the telephone message arrived—the Liberals had triumphed. Ambrose simply stood up and exited—he refrained from cheering or yelling—he permitted the rest to handle that, and I suppose they almost raised the roof of Carter’s store. Naturally, every Tory had gathered across in Raymond Russell’s store. There was not a great deal of cheering IN THAT PLACE. Ambrose proceeded directly along the street heading to the side entrance of Augustus Palmer’s barber shop. Augustus was resting in bed asleep, yet Ambrose pounded upon the door until he arose and came downstairs, desiring to learn the reason for all the noise.
“Step inside your shop and perform the finest work you have ever accomplished, Gus,’ Ambrose said. 'The Liberals have won, and you will be haircutting a fine Grit prior to sunrise.’
“Gus was furious—partially due to being pulled from his bed, but mostly because of his Tory beliefs. He swore that he would refuse to shave anyone past midnight.
“'Sonny, you’ll perform whatever I demand of you,’ Ambrose declared, 'or I’ll simply flip you across my lap and administer the type of thrashing your mother neglected to give you.’

“He would have carried it out, as well, and Gus was aware of it, because Ambrose possesses the strength of an ox whereas Gus is merely a dwarf of a person. Thus he surrendered, hauled Ambrose into the establishment, and set to work. 'Now,’ he states, 'I’ll give you a haircut and shave, but should you speak a single word to me regarding the Grits winning the election while I am at it, I’ll slit your throat using this razor,’ he states. You would not have imagined gentle small Gus capable of being so savage, would you? Demonstrates the effect party politics can have on a person. Ambrose remained silent, had his hair and beard trimmed, and returned home. As his elderly housekeeper caught the sound of him walking upstairs, she peered through her bedroom door to check if it was him or the farmhand. And upon spotting an unfamiliar man walking briskly down the hallway holding a candle, she shrieked hysterically and passed out completely. A doctor had to be summoned before she could be revived, and a number of days passed before she was able to gaze at Ambrose without trembling uncontrollably.”

Captain Saul had caught no fish. During that summer, his boat trips occurred rarely, and he had finished his lengthy walking journeys. A large portion of his time was passed beside his window facing the sea, gazing across the gulf, while his hand supported his rapidly blanched head. On this evening, he remained seated in that spot through numerous quiet minutes, maintaining a rendezvous with bygone days that Nell refrained from interrupting. Soon, he gestured toward the western twilight hues:

“Isn’t that lovely, Mistress Carrow? However, I would be glad if you had witnessed the sunrise earlier today. It was a marvellous sight—marvellous. Every sort of sunrise coming over that gulf has been seen by me. My travels have taken me across the entire globe, Mistress Carrow, and considering everything, a more splendid spectacle than a summer sunrise over the gulf has never been witnessed by me. A person is unable to choose their moment of death, Mistress Carrow—one simply must depart when the Great Captain issues His sailing orders. Even so, were the choice mine, my departure would happen as the morning moves across those waters. Numerous times I have observed it and considered how magnificent it would be to slip away through that immense white radiance toward whatever lay ahead on the other side, across a sea unmapped on any earthly chart. It is my belief, Mistress Carrow, that lost Margaret would be found by me over there.”

Ever since he had related the ancient tale to Nell, Captain Saul had frequently spoken to her about lost Margaret. In each inflection of his voice, his affection for her vibrated—an affection that had not once dimmed or lost its memory.

“Regardless, I trust that when my moment arrives, my departure will be swift and gentle. I do not consider myself a faint-hearted man, Mistress Carrow—on multiple occasions I have confronted a gruesome demise without flinching. Nevertheless, contemplating a drawn-out end instills in me a strange, nauseating sensation of dread.”

“Do not speak of departing from us, dear, DEAR Captain, Saul,” begged Nell, her voice thick with emotion, caressing the weathered, dark hand, which had former strength, but was currently exceedingly frail. “How could we manage in your absence?”
A lovely smile appeared on Captain Saul’s face.

“Oh, you would get along fine—fine—yet you would not completely forget the old man, Mistress Carrow—no, I do not believe you will ever entirely forget him. People of Joseph’s race constantly remember each other. However, it will be a recollection that will not cause pain—I enjoy believing that my memory will not cause pain to my friends—it will always be somewhat agreeable to them, I hope and trust. It will not be very long from now until lost Margaret calls me for the final time. I will be completely prepared to reply. I merely mentioned this since there is a small favor I desire to request of you. Here is this poor old Matey of mine”—Captain Saul extended a hand and nudged the large, warm, velvety, golden sphere on the couch. The First Mate opened himself up like a spring while making a pleasant, throaty, contented noise, partly a purr and partly a meow, extended his paws into the air, rolled over, and rolled himself back up. “HE will miss me when I set out on the V’yage. I cannot endure the thought of leaving the poor creature to starve, as he was abandoned previously. If something occurs to me, will you grant Matey a morsel and a spot, Mistress Carrow?”
“I certainly shall.”

“Well, that encompasses everything I wished to address. I have arranged for your Little Kit to receive the handful of unusual items I collected. Now, Mistress Carrow, it displeases me to witness weeping in such lovely eyes. Perhaps I will endure for a considerable duration still. Sometime during the previous winter, I overheard you reciting a poem by Tennyson. Should you be able to deliver it from memory, I would quite enjoy listening to it once more.”

While the ocean breeze drifted over them, Nell recited the lovely verses of Tennyson’s magnificent swan song—“Crossing the Bar”—in a quiet and distinct voice. With his lean, strong hand, the aged captain softly beat time.

“Yes, yes, Mistress Carrow,” he remarked, once she was done speaking, “that’s it, that’s it. You tell me he wasn’t a sailor—if he wasn’t one, I dunno how he could have expressed an old sailor’s emotions in words like that. He didn’t want any 'sadness o’ farewells’ and neither do I, Mistress Carrow—because all will be well with me and mine beyant the bar.”
“Is there any news coming from Grey Shutters, Nell?”

“Nothing very especial,” answered Nell, putting away the letter from Thirza. “Jake Trask has been at the place putting shingles on the roof. He is now a fully trained carpenter, so he appears to have achieved his desire concerning his chosen profession. You recall that his mother desired a college professor's career for him. That day she arrived at the school and scolded me because I did not address him as St. Clair will always remain in my memory.”
“Is he ever called that by anyone nowadays?”

“Clearly he has not. He appears to have moved past it entirely. His mother has even given in. My belief was always that a young man possessing Jake’s mouth and chin would ultimately prevail. Isolde informs me in a letter that a beau has been found by Lucy. Reflect upon that—a child like her!”
“Lucy’s age is seventeen,” Hugh said. “Both Wilfred Mott and I were crazy for you when your age was seventeen, Nell.”

“In truth, Hugh, we are certainly aging,” remarked Nell, displaying a somewhat mournful grin, “if kids who were merely six years old back when we considered ourselves adults have reached an age to attract suitors. Lucy’s companion is Ralph Pullen—the brother of Odette. My memory of him is as a small, plump, heavy-set, fair-haired boy who consistently stayed at the bottom of his grade. However, I hear that he has grown into a rather handsome youth today.”

“It is likely that Lucy is going to wed at an early age. Her nature resembles that of Belinda the Fourth—she will certainly seize her initial opportunity out of dread that a second one may not arrive.”
“Well; if Ralph becomes her husband, my wish is that he shows a bit more ambition than Barney, his brother,” reflected Nell.

“As an example,” Hugh said with a laugh, “we can pray that he manages to make a proposal for himself. Nell, if Barney had popped the question directly, rather than having Odette act as his messenger, would you have accepted him?”

“I could have.” Nell burst into a shrill laugh as she remembered her initial proposal. “Being so shocked by everything could have mesmerized me into doing something so reckless and silly. We should be grateful that he used a surrogate.”
“Yesterday, a letter arrived for me from Laurence Vane,” Lorna mentioned out of the corner where she sat reading.
“Oh, how is he?” Nell inquired with interest, though she felt strangely as if the person she was asking about was a stranger to her.

“He is fine, though adjusting to every change regarding his former home and companions proves extremely difficult for him. Once spring arrives, he will return to the sea. He claims it is in his blood, and he yearns to be back on it. However, he shared a piece of news that brought me happiness on his behalf, poor man. Prior to departing on the Four Sisters, he had been betrothed to a local girl. He refrained from mentioning her to me in Montreal, explaining that he assumed she would have put him out of her mind and wed another man years ago, whereas for him, the betrothal and affection remained entirely current. Though this was quite painful for him, his return home revealed that she had remained unmarried and still held affection for him. Their wedding is planned for this autumn. I intend to invite him to bring her here for a brief visit; he mentions a desire to come observe the location where he resided for so many years unaware.”

“What a sweet little love story,” remarked Nell, who possessed an undying fondness for romance. “And to consider,” she continued while sighing remorsefully, “that Laurence Vane would have remained in the grave where his true self was entombed had I gotten what I wanted. I battled so fiercely against the idea Hugh had! Well, my retribution has arrived: never again will I be permitted to disagree with Hugh! Should I attempt to, he will crush me by bringing up Laurence Vane’s situation!”

“Even that wouldn't hush a woman!” Hugh scoffed. “At any rate, Nell, stop echoing me. Life is made more interesting with a bit of disagreement. My desire is not for a spouse resembling John MacAllister’s across the harbor. Whatever statement he makes, she immediately observes in her dull, spiritless small voice, 'That is very true, John, dear me!’”
Nell and Lorna giggled. A musical perfection like a flawless chord was created by blending Nell’s silvery laugh with the golden tone of Lorna’s.
Tabitha, entering right after the laughter occurred, mirrored it by letting out a deep sigh.
“Why, Tabitha, what is wrong?” Hugh inquired.
“Little Kit isn’t unwell, is he, Tabitha?” Nell shouted, leaping up in fright.

“No, no, settle down, Mrs. Doctor, dear. A thing has occurred, however. Dear me, all things have gone completely wrong for me during this week. I ruined the bread, as you are only too aware—and I burned the doctor’s finest shirt bosom—and I shattered your large platter. And now, to cap it all off, news arrives that my sister Matilda has fractured her leg and desires that I travel to remain with her for a time.”
“Oh, I am deeply sorry—that is to say, sorry that your sister suffered such a mishap,” cried Nell.

“Ah, well, human beings were created to grieve, Mrs. Doctor, dear. It seems like something that should belong in the Bible, yet I am informed that an individual called Burns composed it. Furthermore, it is certainly true that we are destined for sorrow just as sparks ascend. Regarding Matilda, I am at a loss as to what I should believe about her. Never before has any member of our family fractured a leg. Nevertheless, regardless of her actions, she remains my sister, and I believe it is my obligation to travel there and attend to her, provided you are able to manage without me for a couple of weeks, Mrs. Doctor, dear.”
“Naturally, Tabitha, naturally. Someone else can be found to assist me during your absence.”

“Should you be unable to, I shall refrain from attending, Mrs. Doctor, dear, despite Matilda’s leg. I refuse to cause you anxiety, and to have that sweet child disturbed as a result, for all the legs in existence.”
“Oh, Tabitha, you ought to travel to your sister immediately. I am able to obtain a girl from the cove, who will manage for now.”

“Nell, will you allow me to come and live with you during Tabitha’s absence?” Lorna cried out. “Please do! I’d delight in it—and you would be performing a charitable deed. I am so terribly isolated over there inside that large barn-like home. I have so few tasks to occupy me—and during the night I am more than just isolated—I am scared and edgy even with the doors secured. A tramp was lurking about two days back.”
Nell delightfully accepted, and on the following day, Lorna took up residence in the modest house of dreams. Miss Winifred enthusiastically favored the plan.

“It appears to be Providential,” she privately remarked to Nell. “I feel regret for Matilda Clow, yet given that breaking her leg was unavoidable, the timing could not have been superior. Lorna is going to reside here during the period that Adrian Treleaven remains in Seven Gulls, preventing those old cats up at the Glen from having an opportunity to meow, which they certainly would if she were residing over there by herself while Adrian visited her. They are already engaging in enough gossip because of her refusal to wear mourning clothes. I observed to one among them, 'If you imply that she ought to wear mourning clothes for Laurence Vane, it strikes me as resembling his resurrection far more than his funeral; whereas if you are referring to Rufus, I admit I fail to perceive the appropriateness of wearing weeds for an individual who passed away thirteen years back, whose departure was a good riddance at the time!’ Furthermore, when old Louisa Baldwin commented to me that she considered it extremely odd for Lorna to have never harbored a suspicion that he was not her actual husband, I replied, 'YOU failed to ever suspect he was not Rufus Vane, despite being his next-door neighbor throughout his entire existence, and by temperament you possess ten times more suspicion than Lorna.’ Nevertheless, one is unable to silence certain individuals' tongues, Nell, dearie, and I feel truly grateful that Lorna will reside beneath your roof throughout the time Adrian is courting her.”

On an August evening, Adrian Treleaven arrived at the small home while Lorna and Nell were fully occupied with doting on the infant. Unobserved by the pair inside, he stopped at the open doorway of the living room, taking in the lovely scene with hungry eyes. Lorna was seated on the carpet holding the baby on her lap, delightedly touching his chubby little hands as he waved them about in the air.
“Oh, you dear, beautiful, beloved baby,” she murmured, grabbing a tiny hand and pressing kisses all over it.

“Is he not the most darling little thing,” Nell murmured, leaning over her chair's arm in adoration. “Those little tiny pads are the sweetest hands in the entire wide world, are they not, you darling little man.”

Nell, during the months preceding the arrival of Little Kit, had studied several erudite books with great diligence, and she placed her trust particularly in one, “Sir Oracle on the Care and Training of Children.” Parents were implored by Sir Oracle, by everything they deemed sacred, never to speak “baby talk” to their offspring. From the very moment they are born, infants must always be spoken to in classical language. Thus would they acquire the ability to utter pure English from their very first words. “How,” Sir Oracle inquired, “can a mother reasonably expect her child to learn correct speech, when she continually accustoms its impressionable gray matter to such absurd expressions and distortions of our noble tongue as thoughtless mothers inflict every day on the helpless creatures committed to their care? Can a child who is constantly called 'tweet itty wee singie’ ever attain to any proper conception of his own being and possibilities and destiny?”

This left a deep impression on Nell, who told Hugh that she intended to establish a strict rule to never, no matter what, use “baby talk” with her offspring. Hugh concurred with her, leading them to form a serious pact regarding the matter—a agreement that Nell flagrantly broke as soon as Little Kit was placed in her embrace. “Oh, the darling itty wee sing!” she had cried out. Furthermore, she had persisted in breaking it from that time onward. Whenever Hugh mocked her, she treated Sir Oracle with complete contempt.

“Hugh, he was without any offspring himself—I am certain he lacked them, otherwise he could not have penned such nonsense. Speaking baby talk to an infant is simply unavoidable. It happens instinctively—and it is PROPER. Addressing those small, gentle, downy little beings the way we address large boys and girls would be heartless. Infants require affection, embraces, and every bit of sweet baby talk available to them, and Little Kit will receive it, bless his sweet itty heartums.”

“However, you are the most terrible I ever listened to, Nell,” objected Hugh, who, since he was merely a father rather than a mother, had not been completely persuaded yet that Sir Oracle was mistaken. “The manner in which you speak to that child is unlike anything I ever listened to.”

“It is highly probable that you never did. Leave—leave. Before reaching eleven years of age, did I not raise three sets of Rudge twins? Sir Oracle and you are merely dispassionate theorists. Hugh, ONLY take a glance at him! He is grinning in my direction—he understands what is being discussed by us. And oo dest agwees wif evy word muzzer says, don’t oo, angel-lover?”
Hugh wrapped an arm around the pair. “Ah, all of you mothers!” he remarked. “You mothers! When God created you, He certainly knew what He was doing.”

Thus Little Kit received speeches, affection, and hugs; and he grew well as was fitting for a infant from the home of dreams. Lorna displayed just as much folly regarding him as Nell did. Once their chores were finished and Hugh had departed, they surrendered to unabashed sprees of affection and fits of worship, like the one where Adrian Treleaven had caught them unawares.
Lorna noticed him before anyone else did. Even as the light faded, Nell was able to observe the abrupt paleness that spread across her lovely face, erasing the red color from her lips and cheeks.
Adrian stepped toward us, full of eagerness, briefly taking no notice of Nell.

“Lorna!” he uttered, extending his hand. Never before had he addressed her by her first name; yet the hand Lorna proffered him felt cold; and throughout the entire evening she remained extremely quiet, whereas Nell and Hugh and Adrian shared laughter and conversation. She made her excuses and ascended the stairs prior to the conclusion of his visit. The cheerful mood Adrian possessed waned, and he departed shortly thereafter looking disheartened.
Hugh's eyes turned toward Nell.

“Nell, what are you doing? There is something happening that escapes my understanding. Tonight, the entire atmosphere in this place has been filled with tension. Lorna is seated resembling the muse of tragedy; Adrian Treleaven makes jokes and laughs outwardly, while observing Lorna with his soul's eyes. You appear constantly on the verge of exploding with a hidden excitement. Confess. What secret have you been hiding from your misled husband?”
“Do not be silly, Hugh,” Nell answered her husband. “Regarding Lorna, she is ridiculous, and I am heading upstairs to inform her of that.”

Nell discovered Lorna located at the dormer window belonging to her room. The rhythmic thunder of the ocean filled the small space. Lorna was sitting with clasped hands in the misty moonlight—a lovely, accusing presence.
“Nell,” she uttered quietly and critically, “were you aware that Adrian Treleaven was traveling to Seven Gulls?”
“I did,” Nell stated without shame.

“Oh, Nell, you ought to have informed me,” Lorna exclaimed with intensity. “Had I been aware, I’d have left—I’d not have remained in this place to encounter him. You ought to have informed me. You weren’t being fair, Nell—oh, you weren’t being fair!”
Lorna’s entire body was stiffened by feeling, and her lips shuddered. Nell, however, uttered a cruel laugh. She leaned down to place a kiss upon Lorna’s turned-up, accusatory face.

“Lorna, you are an adorable goose. Adrian Treleaven didn’t hurry from the Pacific to the Atlantic out of a desperate craving to see ME. I also do not think that he was motivated by any fierce and frantic devotion to Miss Winifred. Shed your tragic demeanour, my dear friend, and fold it up and store it away in lavender. You will not require it ever again. There are certain individuals who are capable of seeing through a grindstone when a hole exists in it, even though you are unable to. I do not claim to be a prophetess, yet I will risk making a forecast. Life’s bitterness has come to an end for you. From now on you will experience the delights and expectations—and I imagine the griefs, as well—of a contented woman. The omen of the shadow of Venus really did come to pass for you, Lorna. The year when you witnessed it delivered your life’s finest present to you—your love for Adrian Treleaven. Now, retire straight to bed and get a restful sleep.”

Lorna conformed to instructions to the extent that she retired to bed, though it is doubtful whether she enjoyed much sleep. I doubt she permitted herself to indulge in daydreams; existence had proven so difficult for this unfortunate Lorna, and the route she was forced to tread had been so narrow, that she was unable to murmur to her inner self the expectations that the times ahead might hold. Nevertheless, she observed the immense rotating beacon ornamenting the brief hours of the summer darkness with star-like brightness, and a youthful, soft, and luminous quality returned to her eyes. Furthermore, she did not refuse Adrian Treleaven when he arrived the following day to request her company for a visit to the beach.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: Miss Winifred made her way down to the small dwelling on a sluggish afternoon, at a time when the gulf displayed the pale, faded blue characteristic of August waters, and the orange lilies standing by the gate of Nell’s garden raised their majestic blossoms to catch the liquefied gold of August sunlight. It was not that Miss Winifred paid any mind to colorful seas or thirsty lilies. She was seated in her preferred rocking chair in an uncharacteristic state of rest. She was neither sewing nor spinning. Neither did she utter a solitary disparaging remark regarding any part of humanity. To be brief, Miss Winifred’s talk lacked its customary bite on that particular day, and Hugh, who had remained at home so he could hear her talk, rather than venturing out to fish as he had planned, considered himself wronged. What had occurred to alter Miss Winifred? She failed to appear depressed or anxious. Rather, an undeniable mood of restless triumph hung about her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Lorna, where is she?” was her question—spoken without much genuine concern, either.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “In the woods behind her farm, she and Adrian were picking raspberries,” Nell replied. “Before supper—if even by that time—they will not return.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “It appears they lack all awareness of the existence of clocks,” Hugh remarked. “That business remains a complete mystery to me. My conviction is that you women manipulated matters behind the scenes. Yet Nell, disobedient spouse that she is, refuses to enlighten me. Are you willing to, Miss Winifred?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “No, I will not. However,” stated Miss Winifred, assuming the manner of a person resolved to leap in and finish it, “I am going to share a different matter with you. My reason for coming today was specifically to convey it. I shall be getting married.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: Nell and Hugh kept quiet. Had Miss Winifred declared that she intended to go out to the channel and drown herself, the statement could have been believed. This, however, was unbelievable. Consequently, they waited. Naturally, Miss Winifred had committed an error.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Well, the pair of you appear somewhat kerflummexed,” Miss Winifred said, her eyes twinkling. With the uncomfortable instant of disclosure behind her, Miss Winifred had regained her self-possession. “Is it your belief that I lack the age and experience required for marriage?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “You know—it IS quite shocking,” Hugh said, attempting to collect his thoughts. “I’ve listened to you state twenty times that you wouldn’t wed the finest man on earth.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “I will not be marrying the world’s finest man,” Miss Winifred countered. “Ambrose Kerr falls far short of being the best.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Will you be marrying Ambrose Kerr?” Nell cried out, regaining her ability to talk beneath this second jolt.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Indeed. I was able to secure him at any moment throughout the past twenty years had I raised a finger. However, do you imagine I intended to stroll into a house of worship alongside a moving haystack such as he?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “I am sure we are very glad—and we wish you all possible happiness,” said Nell, expressing herself, in her own opinion, quite dully and insufficiently. For such an event, she lacked preparation. Never had she pictured herself extending engagement congratulations to Miss Winifred.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “I knew you would, thanks,” Miss Winifred said. “My friends do not know it yet, except for you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Although, dear Miss Winifred, we shall be so sorry to lose you,” said Nell, starting to become slightly sentimental and sad.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Oh, I am not going to be lost to you,” Miss Winifred remarked without sentiment. “Do you truly imagine I could reside across the harbor alongside every one of those Crawfords, Kerrs, and MacAllisters? ‘Good Lord, save us from the pride of the MacAllisters, the conceit of the Kerrs, and the vain-glory of the Crawfords.’ Ambrose will move into my house. Hired men have completely exhausted my patience. The one I have hired for this summer, Saul Hastings, is without question the most awful of his kind. Anyone would be driven to matrimony by him. Can you imagine? Yesterday, he knocked the churn over, covering the yard in a large batch of spilled cream. Yet he felt not the slightest bit of remorse! He merely chuckled foolishly, declaring that the soil benefited from cream. Is that not typical male behavior? I informed him that using cream as fertilizer for my back yard was not my custom.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Well, I wish you every kind of joy as well, Miss Winifred,” Hugh said, gravely; “however,” he continued, failing to withstand the urge to poke fun at Miss Winifred, even though Nell looked at him beseechingly, “I am afraid your period of freedom has come to an end. As you are aware, Ambrose Kerr is an exceedingly resolute person.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “A person who is capable of adhering to a course of action appeals to me,” replied Miss Winifred. “That was not the case with Amos Hollis, a former suitor of mine from years back. A more fickle individual you have never observed. On one occasion, he leapt into the body of water to end his life, yet he altered his intention subsequently and paddled back to shore. Was that not typical masculine behavior? Ambrose would have persevered in the act and perished.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “They also inform me that his temper is somewhat quick,” Hugh pressed on.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “He would fail to be a Kerr if he had done otherwise. That he did makes me grateful. Stirring his anger will be genuine entertainment. Furthermore, one is usually able to accomplish something with an ill-tempered man once the moment for remorse arrives. Conversely, a man who merely remains calm and exasperating offers no leverage at all.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Miss Winifred, you are aware that he is a Grit.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Yes, he IS,” Miss Winifred conceded quite mournfully. “And naturally he cannot possibly be turned into a Conservative. Yet he is a Presbyterian, at any rate. Therefore I must assume that will have to content me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “If he happened to be a Methodist, Miss Winifred, would you take him as your husband?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “No, I wouldn’t. While politics belongs strictly to this world, religion pertains to both.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “And you could end up a ‘relict’ in the end, Miss Winifred.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “I will not. Ambrose is going to outlive me. Longevity is a trait of the Kerrs, whereas it is absent in the Bryants.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “When is your wedding to take place?” Nell inquired.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “In roughly four weeks. The gown for my wedding will be made of navy blue silk. Furthermore, Nell, my dear, I would like your opinion on whether wearing a veil alongside a navy blue gown is appropriate. My desire has always been to wear a veil should I ever wed. According to Ambrose, I should wear one if it pleases me. Is that not typical of a man?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “If you wish to wear it, why ought you not to?” Nell asked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Well, a person prefers not to stand out from everybody else,” stated Miss Winifred, who did not bear a striking resemblance to any other human being in the world. “Like I mentioned, I really would like a veil. Still, perhaps a person ought not to wear it unless the dress is white. Nell, my dear, kindly share your true opinion with me. I will follow whatever you advise.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Except with white dresses, veils are not typically worn,” Nell acknowledged, “yet that is just a custom; and like Mr. Kerr, I feel the same, Miss Winifred. If you desire a veil, I see no valid cause why you should be without one.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: Yet Miss Winifred, who conducted her visits wearing calico wrappers, shook her head.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Should it not be the correct item, I shall refrain from wearing it,” she uttered, sighing mournfully over a vanished fantasy.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Because you have made up your mind to get married, Miss Winifred,” Hugh stated gravely, “I will bestow upon you the superb guidelines for controlling a husband that were handed down by my grandmother to my mother upon her marriage to my father.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Indeed, I suppose Ambrose Kerr is within my control,” Miss Winifred stated calmly. “However, allow us to listen to your regulations.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Capturing him is the initial step.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “He is trapped. Continue.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Give him plenty to eat is the second rule.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Given a sufficient amount of pie. What comes after?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “Pay attention to him—those are the third and fourth.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 37 MISS WINIFRED MAKES A STARTLING ANNOUNCEMENT
text: “I take you at your word,” Miss Winifred declared with force.

That August, bees frequented the garden of the small dwelling, which was made red by late-blooming roses. Its inhabitants spent a great deal of time there, often eating picnic suppers in the lawn-covered space past the stream and lounging in it during the dusk hours as large night moths glided across the soft darkness. Adrian Treleaven discovered Lorna by herself in it one night. Nell and Hugh had gone out, while Tabitha, whose return was anticipated that evening, was still absent.

Above the fir summits, the northern sky displayed tones of amber and light green. August was drawing close to September, making the air chilly, so Lorna had draped a crimson scarf above her white dress. Side by side, without speaking, they walked along the small, welcoming paths packed with flowers. Adrian was obliged to depart before long. His time off had almost come to an end. Lorna sensed her heart pounding furiously. She was aware that this cherished garden would serve as the setting for the binding spoken vows that had to finalize their currently unspoken agreement.

“On certain nights an odd smell drifts along the breeze in this garden, resembling a ghostlike scent,” remarked Adrian. “From which exact flower it originates, I have never managed to find out. It is evasive, lingering, and remarkably sweet. I enjoy imagining that it is the spirit of Grandmother Tremayne dropping by for a brief call to the ancient place she adored so much. Plenty of welcoming phantoms ought to linger around this small aged dwelling.”
“Though I have resided beneath its roof for merely a month,” Lorna said, “my affection for it surpasses any love I felt for the house across the way, where my entire life was spent.”

“Love was the foundation upon which this home was constructed and blessed,” Adrian remarked. “Dwellings like this are BOUND to affect their inhabitants. Consider this garden, too—it has existed for more than six decades, with its flowers recording a thousand moments of anticipation and delight. Certain blossoms were in fact planted by the bride of the schoolmaster, who passed away three decades ago. Even so, their blooms return each summer. Observe those red roses, Lorna—they reign supreme over all the rest!”

“I adore the red roses,” Lorna stated. “Nell prefers the pink ones, whereas Hugh favors the white. However, I desire the crimson ones. No other flower fulfills a particular longing within me the way they do.”

“These roses arrive so late—their blossoms appear when every other flower has faded—and they preserve the entire heat and essence of the summer at its peak,” Adrian remarked, picking several of the vibrant, opening buds.

“For ages, humanity has recognized the rose as the emblem of affection. While love that is full of hope and anticipation is embodied by pink roses, and love that has been abandoned or perished is signified by white roses, the red ones—tell me, Lorna, what do red roses represent?”
“Love triumphant,” Lorna said softly.

“Indeed—affection victorious and faultless. Lorna, you are aware—you comprehend. I have adored you since the beginning. And I KNOW you adore me—I have no necessity to inquire of you. Yet I desire to listen to you state it—my precious—my precious!”

Lorna uttered words with an extremely quiet and shaking tone. Touch united their lips and hands; this represented the ultimate instance of their lives, and while they remained in that ancient garden, which possessed a long history of affection, joy, grief, and splendor, her glowing hair was adorned by him using the intensely red rose of victorious affection.

Shortly thereafter, Nell and Hugh came back, with Captain Saul alongside them. Because she loved the pixy flames, Nell set fire to a couple of driftwood sticks in the hearth, and they gathered about it to enjoy an hour of friendly company.
“Viewing a fire made of driftwood makes it simple for me to feel like I am youthful once more,” Captain Saul remarked.
“Are you able to foresee what lies ahead within the flames, Captain Saul?” Adrian inquired.
Captain Saul gazed with affection at everyone present, after which his eyes returned to Lorna's expressive features and shining eyes.

“To read your futures, I don’t need the fire,” he said. “For every one of you, I see happiness—for all of you—for Lorna and Mr. Treleaven—and the doctor here and Mistress Carrow—and Little Kit—and children who are not yet born but will be. Happiness for all of you—though, remember, I expect you will also have your troubles and worries and sorrows. They are sure to arrive—and no house, whether a palace or a little house of dreams, is able to bar ’em out. However, provided you face ’em TOGETHER with love and trust, they won’t get the better of you. With those two for compass and pilot, you can weather any storm.”
The aged man abruptly stood up, resting a hand upon the head of Lorna and another upon that of Nell.

“A pair of good, sweet women,” he remarked. “Loyal and devoted and worthy of trust. On account of you, your husbands will receive honor in the gates—in the time ahead, your children will stand up and proclaim you blessed.”

A peculiar gravity hung over the small gathering. Receiving a blessing, Nell and Lorna inclined their heads. Hugh abruptly wiped his eyes with his hand; Adrian Treleaven was absorbed like a person beholding visions. A period of silence fell upon everyone. To its repository of recollections, the small dwelling of visions attached yet another deeply moving and indelible instance.
“Now I need to depart,” Captain Saul finally uttered in a deliberate manner. Picking up his hat, he cast a long, reluctant gaze around the chamber.
“Good night, every one of you,” he remarked while leaving.
Nell was struck by the exceptional melancholy in his goodbye, prompting her to hurry to the doorway in his wake.
“Return shortly, Captain Saul,” she shouted, while he went past the small gate suspended in the middle of the fir trees.
“Ay, ay,” he answered her in a cheerful voice. Captain Saul, however, had occupied his place beside the familiar hearth in the house of dreams for the final time.
Nell returned to the rest of the group with deliberate steps.
“To imagine him traveling entirely by himself to that solitary Point is just so—so tragic,” she remarked. “Plus, nobody is present to greet him upon his arrival.”

“Captain Saul provides such pleasant fellowship to everyone else that his own presence must surely be agreeable to him,” Adrian remarked. “He has to experience solitude frequently, however. This evening, he resembled a prophet somewhat—his words sounded like those of a person granted a special message. In any case, I need to depart now as well.”
Nell and Hugh quietly slipped out of sight; nevertheless, after Adrian’s departure, Nell came back and discovered Lorna beside the fireplace.
“Oh, Lorna—I am aware—and it brings me such happiness, darling,” she stated, encircling her in a hug.

“My joy terrifies me, Nell,” Lorna murmured softly. “Its magnitude feels impossible—I fear giving it voice—or dwelling on it. I feel as though this is merely one more illusion born of this dwelling of phantoms, bound to disappear the moment I depart.”

“Indeed, you shall not depart from this spot—before Adrian comes to fetch you. Up to the arrival of that moment, you will remain in my company. Is it your belief that I would allow you to return to that desolate, gloomy location?”

“I am grateful to you, my dear. My intention was to inquire whether I could remain in your home. Returning to that place was something I wished to avoid, as it would feel as though I were stepping once more into the coldness and gloom of my former existence. Oh, Nell, Nell, you have proved to be such an incredible friend—'a good, sweet woman—true and faithful and to be depended on’—as Captain Saul described you.”

“He uttered ‘women,’ rather than ‘woman,’” Nell smiled. “It may be that Captain Saul views the two of us via the rose-colored glasses of his affection for us. Nevertheless, we are able to endeavor to fulfill his faith in us, anyway.”

“Do you recall, Nell,” Lorna murmured deliberately, “how I mentioned—the evening our paths crossed on the beach—that my attractive appearance was something I despised? At that time, I truly did. I was convinced that had I been plain, Rufus wouldn't have given me a second thought. My allure was repulsive to me since it drew him in, yet at present—oh, my looks bring me joy. They represent the sole gift I can present to Adrian,—and his artistic nature revels in them. It makes me sense that I am not arriving before him completely without a offering.”

“Adrian is in love with your beauty, Lorna, as anyone would be. However, you are being silly to state or believe that your beauty is the sole thing you offer him. HE is going to inform you of that, so there is no need for me to do so. I have to lock up at this point. Tabitha was expected to return this evening by me, yet she is absent.”
“Oh, yes, here I am, Mrs. Doctor, dear,” stated Tabitha, coming in without warning from the kitchen, “and blowing like a hen pulling rails at that! Coming down here from the Glen is quite a walk.”
“It pleases me that you have returned, Tabitha. What is the state of your sister’s health?”

“Though she can sit up, walking is still out of the question for her, naturally. Even so, she can manage quite fine without my help at present, since her vacationing daughter has returned home. Mrs. Doctor, dear, I am truly grateful to return. There was certainly no doubt about Matilda’s leg being broken, yet her tongue remained completely fine. Mrs. Doctor, dear, even if I am saddened to speak this way about my sister, she would talk endlessly without stopping. Her chatter was always constant, nevertheless she married before any of us in our family. Her feelings about marrying James Clow were actually quite indifferent, but she simply lacked the heart to refuse him. I am not saying James is not a decent man—my sole grievance regarding him, Mrs. Doctor, dear, is the eerie groan he invariably utters when beginning to offer thanks before meals. My appetite is invariably scared right off by it. And on the subject of weddings, Mrs. Doctor, dear, does truth lie in the rumor that Winifred Tolley will marry Ambrose Kerr?”
“Indeed, that is correct, Tabitha.”

“Indeed, Mrs. Doctor, dear, it DOES NOT appear just to me. Here I am, having never uttered a single word opposing men, yet I am completely unable to marry. On the other hand, Winifred Tolley constantly criticizes them, yet she only needs to extend her hand to take one, so to speak. Mrs. Doctor, dear, the world is remarkably peculiar.”
“Tabitha, you know there is another world.”
“Indeed,” Tabitha uttered while sighing deeply, “and yet, Mrs. Doctor, my dear, no one is married or given in marriage in that place.”

text: Hugh departed, and Nell stowed Little Kit’s short dresses with shaking hands. Sewing any more that day was impossible for her. Its grounds were lovely, and the dwelling was sufficiently old to possess dignity, repose, and traditions, yet modern enough to remain cozy and up-to-date. She loved EVERYTHING regarding it—the garden she had cared for, which a great number of women had cared for prior to her—the shimmer and glisten of the small brook sliding so playfully through the corner—the gate set among the creaking fir trees—the aged red sandstone step—the majestic Lombardies—the pair of small, unusual glass cupboards above the hearth in the living-room—the lopsided pantry door inside the kitchen—the pair of amusing dormer windows on the upper floor—the small turn in the stairs—indeed, such details formed a portion of her being! How was she to abandon them?

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: And in what manner this small home, hallowed in the past through affection and delight, had been hallowed anew for her via her gladness and grief! Within these walls she had passed her honeymoon; within these walls tiny Joyce had existed for her single fleeting day; within these walls the tenderness of maternity had returned alongside Little Kit; within these walls she had listened to the wonderful melody of her infant’s bubbling chuckles; within these walls cherished companions had lingered beside her hearth. Happiness and sorrow, nativity and mortality, had rendered holy for all time this small home of visions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: And now it was time for her to depart from it. Even as she had argued against the notion to Hugh, she was aware of that truth. Their small home had become too small for them. Nell understood that the conclusion of their time in this beloved home was approaching, and she had to meet the reality with courage. Yet her heart suffered so greatly!

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Tearing a piece out of my life is what it will be like,” she wept. “And oh, if I might only pray that lovely people would settle here after us—or that nobody at all would live here. Even that would surpass being swamped by a crowd that possesses no understanding of the geography of dreamland, nor any knowledge of the history that has endowed this dwelling with its soul and identity. Furthermore, should that kind of clan move in, this spot will fall apart extremely fast—a historic dwelling deteriorates rapidly when it lacks diligent care. They are going to uproot my garden—and allow the Lombardies to grow untidy—and the fence will start resembling a mouth that lost half its teeth—and leaks will develop in the roof—and plaster will drop—and broken window panes will be stuffed with rags and pillows—and every single thing will grow shabby.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: Nell’s mind envisioned the future ruin of her beloved small home so intensely that it caused her as much pain as though it were already a completed reality. Dropping onto the steps, she wept lengthily and bitterly. Tabitha discovered her in that spot and asked with great anxiety what was wrong.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Have you fallen out with the doctor, then, Mrs. Doctor, dear? Even if you have, do not be anxious. I am told that such an occurrence is very probable for wedded partners, even though I possess no personal experience of that nature. He will feel regret, and the two of you can quickly reconcile.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “No, no, Tabitha, a quarrel hasn’t occurred. It is just that—Hugh intends to purchase the Varley property, which forces us to move to the Glen. And my heart will be broken by it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: Nell’s emotions were not shared by Tabitha in the slightest. On the contrary, the likelihood of residing at the Glen delighted her immensely. The solitary situation of her dwelling was her single complaint regarding her life in the small cottage.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Oh, Mrs. Doctor, darling, that will be magnificent. Such a grand, spacious place is the Varley house.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “I despise large dwellings,” Nell wept.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Ah, well, once you possess six offspring, your hatred for them will cease,” Tabitha observed in a tranquil manner. “Furthermore, our present dwelling has already become insufficient in size for our needs. With Mrs. Vane staying with us, we lack a guest chamber, and no workspace has ever brought me as much annoyance as that pantry. Whichever direction one pivots, a corner is encountered. In addition, this location is completely isolated from society. Nothing whatsoever exists here aside from the landscape.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “It may be out of your world, Tabitha, though it is not out of mine,” Nell said, smiling faintly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “I cannot entirely follow your meaning, Mrs. Doctor, dear, though naturally my education is lacking. However, should Dr. Carrow purchase the Varley property, it will certainly be a sound decision, you can rely on that. Running water is installed there, the pantries and closets are delightful, and I have heard that no other cellar on St. Brendan’s Island compares to it. Indeed, the cellar in this house, Mrs. Doctor, dear, has caused me great sorrow, as you are well aware.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Oh, go away, Tabitha, go away,” Nell said forlornly. “A HOME isn’t made by cellars and pantries and closets. Why don’t you weep with those who weep?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Well, weeping was never something I was skilled at, Mrs. Doctor, dear. Rather than weep alongside folk, I prefer to get to work and brighten their spirits. Now, avoid crying and ruining those pretty eyes of yours. Having served your purpose, this house is fine enough, yet you are long overdue for a superior one.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: It appeared that Tabitha held the same perspective as the majority of folk. Only Lorna offered Nell a sympathetic understanding. Upon learning what had happened, Lorna also wept copiously. After that, having wiped away their tears, the pair set to work preparing for the move.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Because we have to leave, let’s leave as quickly as possible and get it done,” expressed miserable Nell with resentful acceptance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “You are aware that the beautiful old home at the Glen will become dear to you once you have resided there for a sufficient time to form precious memories around it,” Lorna remarked. “Companions will visit you there, just as they have visited here—joy will bestow splendour upon it on your behalf. At present, you view it merely as a house—however, time will transform it into a home.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: The following week, Nell and Lorna wept once more as they put Little Kit into shorter clothes. The tragic feeling stayed with Nell until nightfall, when his long nightgown restored her precious child to her once more.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “However, rompers will follow—and after that, trousers—and before long, he will be an adult,” she uttered with a sigh.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Well, you would not desire him to remain an infant forever, Mrs. Doctor, dear, would you?” Tabitha remarked. “Bless his innocent heart, he appears far too sweet for anything in his little short dresses, with his dear feet protruding. And consider the reduction in the ironing, Mrs. Doctor, dear.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Nell, I have just received a missive from Adrian,” Lorna declared, coming in with a glowing countenance. “And, oh! Such wonderful tidings I have. He informs me in his letter that he intends to purchase this property from the church trustees so we can retain it for our summer holidays. Nell, does this not make you happy?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Oh, Lorna, saying I am 'glad' does not even begin to describe it! It appears nearly too wonderful to be real. My distress will be far less now that I am aware this cherished place is not going to be profaned by a horde of vandals, nor abandoned to collapse into ruins. Indeed, it is wonderful! It is wonderful!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: When Nell awoke on an October morning, she realized she had spent her final night beneath her small house's roof. Regret could not be indulged on so busy a day, and the house stood stripped and bare by the time evening arrived. To bid it goodbye, Nell and Hugh were by themselves inside. Along with the final load of furniture, Lorna, Tabitha, and Little Kit had departed for the Glen. Through the windows, which lacked curtains, the light of the sunset poured in.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Does not every bit of it appear so full of grief and rebuke?” inquired Nell. “Oh, my longing for home will be so great at the Glen this evening!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Nell-girl, we’ve been extremely happy in this place, haven’t we?” asked Hugh, speaking with deep emotion.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: Nell gasped, incapable of responding. Hugh stood waiting for her by the gate of fir trees, during the time she walked through the residence and bade goodbye to each room. She was departing; yet the aged house would remain in that place, gazing out to sea via its unusual windows. The winds of autumn would circle it dolefully, and the gray rain would strike it and the white mists would arrive from the ocean to envelop it; and the light of the moon would descend upon it and illuminate the aged tracks where the schoolmaster and his bride had strolled. Upon that aged harbor coast the magic of tale would remain; the wind would continue to blow invitingly across the silver sand-dunes; the waves would continue to summon from the red rock-coves.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Yet we shall be no longer here,” Nell remarked while weeping.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: Upon stepping outside, she shut and locked the door in her wake. Awaiting her with a smile was Hugh. Toward the north, the light from the lighthouse shone brightly. Shadows were already wrapping themselves around the small garden, in which marigolds were the sole remaining blossoms.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: Nell dropped to her knees and pressed her lips to the threadbare old step that she had walked over when she was a bride.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 40 FAREWELL TO THE HOUSE OF DREAMS
text: “Farewell, sweet tiny home of visions,” she uttered.
